92d3b671a5d41a16: PETALING JAYA, Oct 18 — Of the soup-filled dumplings to come out of Shanghai, shengjian bao has enjoyed far less love than its sibling, the xiaolong bao, famous the world over.
Maybe it just isn’t dainty enough.

After all, the thin, delicate skin of the xiaolong bao is a big part of its appeal: successfully wrangling one with our chopsticks and slurping the soup in a genteel manner feels like the work of an erudite epicure, especially when a friend reaches for a straw and still spills soup all over themselves.
The ensuing feeling is a momentary but powerful hit of that sweet, sweet dopamine.
Straws are for suckers, we say, more smug than any dumpling has a right to make us.
But all of this is likely just fantasy.
Realistically, the global popularity of the xiaolong bao came about almost entirely from the success of a single company: Din Tai Fung.
Without that kind of corporate backing, shengjian bao has had to rely on the disparate, grassroots efforts of countless street vendors and mom-and-pop shops.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
The huge sign with calligraphy on it is quite hard to miss. — Picture by Ethan Lau
Fitting, as it has always been the more rustic of the two — in every way.

Closer to a bun than a dumpling, shengjian bao is made with semi-leavened dough — it rises more than a flatbread, but not like a puffy bun — and envelops the same pork and gelatin mixture that turns into soup after cooking. Instead of being gently steamed in a bamboo basket, it is traditionally fried in an oiled pan, with water sprinkled or sprayed over the top during cooking.
The moisture steams the inside through while the bottom of the bun crisps up on the pan, like wo tip (potstickers) or gyoza.

More substantial and durable than xiaolong bao, shengjian bao has been a popular breakfast and street food in Shanghai since the 1920s, its crunchy bottom and thicker dough making it considerably more portable.
But it hasn’t quite broken through in Malaysia, so your best bet for shengjian bao is places like Jia Yu Fang.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
The interior of the excellent ‘shengjian bao.’ — Picture by Ethan Lau
Located in Damansara Utama, the restaurant is barely a month old and has done little to update the decor left by the previous tenant.
Instead, all the attention seems to have gone into the shengjian bao (RM3 per piece).
For what looks like a quick, simple snack, they take a while to arrive — on my third and most recent visit, I learned that each bao is cooked to order.

A fresh batch is made every day, but steaming and frying them takes close to 10 minutes, which feels like an age thanks to the restaurant’s insistence on playing an endless loop of smooth jazz à la Kenny G.
When they do arrive, however, they are more than worth the wait — even the additional one or two minutes you’ll need to avoid burning the roof of your mouth.
The inside was scalding hot, but when it had cooled enough to eat, the soup was sweet, very sweet, but resulting in a clean, refreshing sensation rather than a cloying one.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Shanghainese red-braised pork is much sweeter and stickier than the Hunan variant, and this version stays true to that. — Picture by Ethan Lau
The pork and soup had a fresh, pure depth of flavour that’s often called xian tian (鲜甜) in Chinese, while the bottom of the bun was crunchy and caramelised too.
Whether you’re eating it on its own or dipping it in some vinegar, these shengjian bao are some of the best you’ll find in the Klang Valley.
Much of the rest of the menu was deserving of praise, but the red braised pork (RM46) in particular stood out.
Shanghai-style red braised pork is well known for being much sweeter and richer than the classic Hunan variation, and this was no different.
Where the sweetness described earlier carried a refreshing, crisp undertone, this was on the other end of the spectrum: rich, sticky and clinging to the lips long after the last bite of pork.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
It looks incredibly simple, but the chilli green egg is one of the most satisfying dishes on the entire menu. — Picture by Ethan Lau
All that soft, fatty cloyingness calls for something tangy, sharp and crunchy to balance it out, which the restaurant provides… in the form of a housemade kimchi that’s well impressive.

But the biggest surprise on the menu has to be the chilli green egg (RM18). It’s an exceedingly simple dish of eggs stir-fried with green peppers and onions, yet there is something unbelievably addictive about it.
The eggs are formed into thin, fluffy strips, similar in shape and length to the slivers of pepper, which boast a wonderfully smoky and savoury flavour. A bowl of rice and this? My happy place.
Will shengjian bao ever get its own Din Tai Fung to carry it into malls around the world?
It seems unlikely.
For now, the case in Malaysia is being made one bun at a time by Jia Yu Fang, barely a month old and making a very fine argument on the dumpling’s behalf.
Yes, you’ll wait, and yes, there will probably be smooth jazz. But come and order it anyway.
Jia Yu Fang Restaurant
72G, Jalan SS21/62,
Damansara Utama, Petaling Jaya.
Open Tuesday to Sunday, 10.30am—10pm
Facebook: Jia Yu Fang Restaurant

b36e1edce1969b43: KUALA LUMPUR: A young boy has won hearts online after he was seen guiding a blind elderly man at Maluri LRT station, helping him navigate the station safely.
Threads user @syifanadine92 shared the moment, praising the boy's kindness.
"May all the goodness you give find its way back to you, kind soul," the user wrote.
The post drew warm responses from other users, many of whom shared similar experiences of helping visually impaired people in public.
One user, @careyryan_, recounted helping a blind man exit an MRT station despite being late for a train.
"Although I was late for my train, I helped the man exit the station.
"As I went down the escalator, another man, whom I believe was a doctor, chased after me, tapped me on the shoulder and thanked me for helping before running back upstairs.
"It really made my day," the user wrote.
Another user, @ieya.az, praised the gesture, writing: "Such a beautiful soul. May he always be blessed!"

Meanwhile, @hi_mayahhhhh said they had witnessed a similar scene at Pasar Seni LRT station, where a young man helped a blind elderly man by asking him to place his hand on his shoulder as they chatted.
"May the goodness in your heart lead you to beautiful things," the user wrote.
Another user, @panadol_cat_, said people in their neighbourhood often helped blind residents cross roads, including those who walked about 20 minutes to reach the MRT station.
c5563cc5c489774d: KUALA LUMPUR: Pasir Gudang in Johor recorded the highest Air Pollutant Index (API) reading in the country at 190, as 25 areas nationwide registered unhealthy air quality as of 8am today.
Johor was the worst-hit state, with eight of its monitoring stations in the unhealthy category.

According to the Department of Environment's Air Pollutant Index Management System portal, the other affected areas in Johor were Larkin (181), Kota Tinggi (181), Pengerang (178), Batu Pahat (169), Kluang (163), Tangkak (160), and Segamat (157).

In the Klang Valley, Johan Setia recorded 163, followed by Shah Alam (161), Klang (159), Petaling Jaya (157), and Banting (156). In Kuala Lumpur, Cheras recorded 156, and Batu Muda registered 155, while Putrajaya logged 159.
The readings came despite heavy rain in the Klang Valley over the past few days.
In Negri Sembilan, Nilai recorded 172, followed by Seremban (169) and Port Dickson (152). Melaka's Bukit Rambai, Alor Gajah, and Bandaraya Melaka recorded 164, 161, and 155, respectively.
In East Malaysia, Sandakan and Serian each recorded 153, while Tawau registered 103.
Only Limbang in Sarawak (45) and Balik Pulau in Penang (42) recorded good air quality.
Yesterday, Pasir Gudang recorded a very unhealthy reading of 203, with Johor remaining the state hardest hit by the haze.
Readings between 0 and 50 are categorised as good, 51 to 100 as moderate, 101 to 200 as unhealthy, 201 to 300 as very unhealthy, and 300 and above as hazardous.
7d5d2e48875b54cc: KYIV, Oct 18 — Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky said yesterday that he feared the United States would lift more sanctions on Russia and that President Donald Trump’s action only “rewards” Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin.
Trump heightened a battle with Zelensky on Friday when he signed an executive order that waived sweeping US sanctions targeting Russia’s energy revenues.
The decision came despite Russia increasing strikes on Ukraine in the fifth year of its war, which has killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions.
Trump had already announced that he has agreed a deal with Putin to allow exports of Russian diesel in exchange for the easing of sanctions, and Zelensky said he feared more concessions.
“Unfortunately, the lifting of sanctions will continue. I believe the ‘diesel deal’ is just the first step,” Zelensky told reporters.

He said he still “personally” hoped that Trump will do “everything in his power” to make Putin end the war but added: “You cannot achieve this by limiting Ukraine’s responses to Russia for killing our people. And certainly not by lifting sanctions.”
Ukraine said at least two people were killed in Russian air strikes on Saturday.
Pressure needed
Zelensky said the US decision on Friday came the same day as Russia attacked 15 critical power generation facilities across Ukraine in “one of the largest” attacks on Ukraine’s energy grid.
Officials said one person was killed in the southern city of Kherson in an attack that also wounded 22 people, including two children, and that another was killed in the northeastern city of Sumy.
Zelensky said the US decision on Friday came the same day as Russia attacked 15 critical power generation facilities across Ukraine in “one of the largest” attacks on Ukraine’s energy grid.

The Lindsey Graham Act—named after the late US senator who sponsored the bill—targeted Russia’s energy and defence sectors, as well as Putin and the so-called “shadow fleet” of tankers used by Moscow to circumvent Western sanctions.
“It is important that everyone in America also sees what is really happening,” Zelensky said on social media.
The Lindsey Graham Act, he said, was “supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end” adding that the act “could have helped enormously—and still can!”.
“A U.S. sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, financial rewards for Putin—all of this only encourages him to keep attacking,” he warned.

The Ukrainian leader said Russia wanted to cause a “blackout” in Ukraine ahead of winter: “Russia is trying to leave millions of our people without electricity and heating.” He called on allies to pressure Moscow to “stop this.”
Last winter saw hundreds of thousands in Ukraine consistently without heat and electricity in freezing temperatures.
Russia hails Trump move as ‘historic’
The Kremlin and Putin have not yet reacted to Trump, but several Russian officials celebrated the move as a win.
“The Trump administration’s suspension of the Graham Act is an important and truly historic moment,” Kirill Dmitriev, a Putin envoy, said on social media.
Dmitriev said the act would have caused “serious damage first and foremost to the US economy and global markets”.
Trump announced the sanctions waiver in an executive order Friday, shortly after Putin appeared in military uniform and said Moscow aims to capture the rest of east Ukraine.
US-led talks to end the war have failed to bring a breakthrough. Putin and Zelensky have frustrated Trump in the past.

Zelensky rallied his allies Friday on a visit to Brussels for a European Union summit, urging them to keep financing Ukraine’s fight and insisting he was standing up for his country amid the row with Trump.
Putin vows more
Ukraine has been struggling to shoot down Russian missiles and has been left scrambling to boost defences ahead of winter.
Russia controls large swathes of eastern and southern Ukraine and Putin has repeatedly said Moscow intends to seize the rest of east Ukraine by force.
“On the whole I see a positive trend in the operations of the troop groupings,” Putin told army leaders Friday, dressed in military attire.
“Undoubtedly, one of the main objectives remains the liberation of the Donetsk People’s Republic,” he added, using the Kremlin’s name for the eastern Donetsk region. — AFP
ef466b7d1bba2f47: KOLKATA, Oct 18 — At least 19 people were killed and two dozen more injured yesterday in eastern India after a stampede that occurred during sudden rainfall at a Hindu religious gathering, officials and Indian media said.

West Bengal’s Chief Minister Suvendhu Adhikari told reporters the fatalities included a seven-year-old girl, adding that 25 other people were injured outside a pavilion “in a stampede” at the Hindu festival of Durga Puja in the city of Kolkata.
“Six bodies have so far been identified,” Adhikari said.

A senior police official at the scene told AFP an announcement caused “commotion” after it started raining at night and the “crowd waiting outside the pandal (pavilion) was pushing, pulling and rushing forward and fell on the ground, leading to the stampede.”

Afterwards medics were seen moving injured people on stretchers, including a police officer, into a local hospital. Several relatives of victims cried and held one another as they mourned the loss of loved ones.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi addressed the tragedy in a short statement on Facebook.
“The stampede in Kolkata is saddening. Condolences to the bereaved families. Wishing the injured a speedy recovery,” he wrote.
“The West Bengal Government is providing all possible help to the affected families.”
Adhikari originally announced 17 fatalities. The Press Trust of India (PTI) reported the death toll rose by two to 19, quoting Adhikari in a later statement.
Nine dead bodies have been released to their families, the PTI reported.

It also said police have taken the closed circuit footage of the festival and authorities would initiate action against those seen on CCTV who appeared to fail in their responsibility for crowd control.

Videos shot before the stampede appeared to show large crowds of people waiting to enter the pavilion, in an area with narrow lanes that allow only a few people to walk in at a time, according to Indian Express.
Deadly crowd incidents are a frequent occurrence at Indian mass events, such as religious festivals, due to poor management and safety lapses.

Last year, a stampede at India’s Kumbh Mela religious fair killed 30 people and injured several others, and 11 fans were crushed to death in Bengaluru during celebrations for the local cricket team’s first Indian Premier League title.
The same year, 36 people were killed after a stampede broke out at a campaign rally of a popular actor-turned-politician in southern Tamil Nadu state.
In 2024, 121 people were killed in northern Uttar Pradesh state during a Hindu religious gathering. — AFP
498dc005dfc5f011: BEND, Oct 18 — Liz’s seven-year-old-nephew hasn’t been able to sleep since a teenage shooter opened fire at his Oregon elementary school, killing three children and a teacher.
“He kept hearing the sound of gunshots” ringing through his head, even as his parents spent all of Thursday night comforting the Silver Rail Elementary pupil, she told AFP.
Parents and caregivers in this city, known for its mountain skyline and outdoor activities, are reeling from the tragedy and searching for ways to discuss what happened with their children.

Sixteen-year-old Griffin John II killed three children and a teacher in the same special needs class he previously attended, before a father who happened to be passing the school grabbed his own gun and killed the attacker, authorities said.
Another student, a seven-year-old girl, and another teacher were wounded, but are in stable condition.
Vigil
Communication is crucial after such an event, local pediatrician Logan Clausen told CNN.
“Talk to them about what they know, talk to them about what they’re feeling. You can gently correct inaccurate facts,” the doctor said.
Dozens of people gathered on a street in Bend, many accompanied by children of various ages, to hold a vigil late on Friday.
Jeff Michaels, a father of three, told AFP that he and his wife have let their children know it is OK to talk about what happened and ask questions.
“We want to know how they feel, and they do ask questions,” he said, hugging one of his daughters. “They want to know why this happened, why people are sad.”
Special needs
The challenge of helping little ones process the trauma is acute for caregivers of children with special needs.
Since the Thursday rampage, Sherry Lauer, 56, has been watching her five-year-old granddaughter for signs of how she is processing the tragedy.
“She’s nonverbal, so we’re not sure how much she is comprehending about what is going on at the moment,” Lauer told AFP.
While the little girl is not a student at Silver Rail, she “stopped what she was doing and paid attention” to a news conference about the school shooting.
So far, the girl has not shown any negative reactions, her grandmother added.

Art centers, restaurants and parks in Bend, a city of around 100,000 people in central Oregon through which the Deschutes River winds, opened their doors and organized special activities for children over the weekend.
She missed me
“My mom’s been crying a lot, and I’m sad too,” an eight-year-old girl who attended the Friday vigil with her aunt told AFP.
The girl attends another school, but when news alerts about the shooting began circulating, her mother picked her up and took her home, where she explained what had happened.
The aunt, who asked not to be identified, said her sister has been encouraging the girl “to just ask questions and just answering them as they come up.”
“She kept saying she missed me so much after it happened,” the child said. — AFP
b778850f337a42bf: PARIS, Oct 18 — Clashes between police and protesters, massive looting and multiple blazes gripped France yesterday, as nationwide marches against soaring inflation degenerated into street violence of “extreme intensity”.
The widespread unrest follows weeks of student protests and deepens political uncertainty as the country readies for elections in six months’ time to replace President Emmanuel Macron.
Whole streets in Paris “have been devastated”, the city’s mayor, Emmanuel Gregoire, said as groups of masked young men torched parked cars and ransacked many shops.
French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu, who earlier slammed the “violence of extreme intensity”, said late Saturday that 1,200 people had been arrested and 150 police officers hurt.

The violence began on the sidelines of marches in the capital and other cities over the cost of living that the interior ministry said were attended by 550,000 people. The CGT union, which took part, said 800,000 people participated.

Police used tear gas and water cannon against protesters who threw projectiles and aimed fireworks. A 17-year-old boy had his right hand blown off by a crowd-control grenade in the southern city of Saint-Etienne.
Looting in many cities
During and after those demonstrations, gangs of youths roamed city streets, sporadically confronting police, while setting fires and attacking shuttered stores to break in and empty their shelves.

Scores of shops—supermarkets, pharmacies, luxury boutiques, clothing retailers, opticians, cosmetic vendors and consumer electronics stores—were looted in Paris, Marseille, Nice, Nantes, Bordeaux, Limoges, Lille, Toulouse and Strasbourg.

AFP reporters in Paris saw groups of half a dozen young men often attacking the shops in an organised way: wearing masks and gloves, they first disconnected security cameras before smashing windows to get in.
The looting added to a day of destruction and vandalism, with town halls in several cities targeted.

The one in the city of Limoges—more than 140 years old—was largely destroyed by a blaze set by masked protesters who broke in, according to the region’s top official. Two others were broken into and vandalised in Marseille and Lille.
A police compound in Bordeaux was also vandalised, while in Lyon protesters set ablaze a tourist office.
Macron vowed on X that “those who carried out vandalism, attacked administrative offices or businesses, or carried out looting—even in our town halls, will be prosecuted and punished”.
Opposition politicians vying to replace Macron in presidential elections in April and May seized on the chaos.
Far-right candidate Marine Le Pen condemned “the rioters” and claimed that the party of her far-left rival for the presidency, Jean-Luc Melenchon, had “legitimised the violence”.
She said on X that, if she came to power, she would protect the French “from the violence of the extreme left”.
Melenchon, who had prominently supported the demonstrations and the student protests preceding them, urged demonstrators to stay away from any looting, describing it as “contrary to our methods”.
A ‘revolution’
France’s Yellow Vest movement, which eight years ago staged street protests against Macron’s government over planned fuel tax hikes, had called for Saturday’s “yellow and youth” demonstrations.
The principal grievance was the cost of living, pushed up in part by the war in the Middle East that has helped send inflation soaring in Europe as elsewhere.
But there were other issues too.
In Paris, tens of thousands marched across the east and north of the city in one major march, some shouting “Everyone hates the police” and “Macron, resign”.

High school student Kamil Alahyan, 18, said he was protesting “for so many reasons—the elections coming up in 2027, politicians who lie, the ultra-rich who’ve been taking more and more wealth over the past 10 years”.
Several protesters sought to draw parallels with the French Revolution of 1789.
“It’s the Revolution—we’re taking the Bastille!” some shouted in Marseille during the forced entry of the mayor’s offices.
In the western city of La Rochelle, marchers streamed behind a placard reading: “Revolution or death.”
And in the southern city of Montpellier, a giant blue sign reading “The people will win” was unfurled above a central square.

“The government is trembling and it’s right to tremble because when the French people are angry, they never let up,” Ryad Rani, the head of the LSU high school student representative body, told journalists in Paris. — AFP
432dac4c7cd18dbd: Paris, France, Oct 17, 2026 (AFP) -

Lions put up a gritty fight on an emotional Champions Cup debut on Saturday but came up short 31-14 at La Rochelle as both sides paid tribute to South African lock Hyron Andrews, who died suddenly at the team's hotel in western France.
The whole stadium observed a minute's silence while Andrews's No.5 shirt was laid on the pitch before kick-off.
La Rochelle's three South African players presented a jersey to their visitors in memory of the player, who died on Friday at Lions' hotel on the nearby Ile de Re.
A source close to the investigation said that Andrews, who was 31, was found in cardiac arrest in a shower cubicle that was locked from the inside.
Andrews's death came exactly 10 years after Munster coach Anthony Foley died in his hotel room ahead of their match at Racing 92.
Those two teams paid tribute to both Foley and Andrews ahead of their match in Cork on Saturday night.
"Yesterday was very, very tragic. And our sincere condolences go out to Hyron's family, his wife and his two boys," said La Rochelle's South African lock Salmaan Moerat.

"We cannot begin to imagine just how difficult it must be for them," added Moerat, who alongside compatriots Dillyn Leyds and David Kriel, and head coach Ronan O'Gara had visited the Lions team at their hotel on Friday.
"It was a very difficult occasion and I can only imagine how difficult it must have been for the Lions, and they showed so much courage to come out and play."
O'Gara, who was a coach at Racing when Foley died, said he had "never imagined we would play a match after yesterday's news."
"There are more important things than rugby," he added. "Our thoughts should be about Hyron's family and it's another example of the fragility of life."
Wingers Tevita Ofa and Davit Niniashvili were on the scoresheet in the first half for hosts La Rochelle, who led 19-14 as Lions replied through Henco van Wyk and Morne Brandon.
Second-half scores from Australia hooker Silatolu Latu and Fijian winger Avakuki Niusalelekitoga earned La Rochelle a bonus point.
- 'Thick and fast' -
In Cork, Munster and Racing both laid No.8 jerseys on the pitch in memory of Foley and held a moment of silence for Andrews.
They put on a show to befit the occasion, with the hosts edging an absorbing contest 33-25.
Scrum-half Craig Casey sealed the victory with a late try and flashed eight fingers to the cameras in celebration.
Ireland fly-half Sam Prendergast starred as four-time winners Leinster opened their Champions Cup account with a bonus-point 48-23 win at Clermont.
Prendergast scored one of the Irish province's seven tries, adding four conversions and a penalty for a personal haul of 16 points, while captain Dan Sheehan scored twice.
"Lots of really good stuff in the game," Leinster head coach Leo Cullen said.
"Games come thick and fast so we've got to move on."
Prendergast's brother Cian scored two tries as Connacht stunned Saracens 45-36 in a 13-try thriller.
Ciaran Frawley also scored a brace for Connacht, while Tongan Sione Va'enuku did so for Sarries, whose back five were all on the scoresheet.

Stade Francais, who have not won away in the competition since 2015, succumbed to the heat, the altitude and a string of defensive errors in South Africa as they crumbled 56-20 against the Bulls, who outscored their visitors by eight tries to two to earn a bonus point.
Stormers made light of hooker JJ Kotze's first half red card to thrash an under-strength Bristol 49-12.
Bath fell to a surprise 32-14 defeat at home to Montpellier as French winger Donovan Taofifenua scored a brace for the visitors.
Glasgow fought back from an early deficit to beat Andrews's former club Sale 47-27.

04ce75a3ba4f3bf3: TUMPAT: "Although there were slight wounds on the side of her face, she looked peaceful," said the brother of Norhazwani Ibrahim, who was believed to have been killed by her husband in Nilai, Negri Sembilan, last Thursday.
Mohd Hazwan Ibrahim, 38, said he was overcome with emotion when he saw his sister's face for the final time after her shroud was opened.
"Her face looked calm. I am relieved that everything has been settled," he said when met after the burial at the Tanjung Muslim Cemetery here at 1.50am today.
"After two days, Wani's remains have finally been safely laid to rest."
Norhazwani, a Customs officer who had transferred to the Malaysia Border Control and Protection Agency (MCBA) scheme, was stationed at Kuala Lumpur International Airport (KLIA).
It was previously reported that she was allegedly stabbed by her husband at their home in the KLIA quarters in Nilai on Thursday.
She suffered two stab wounds to the left abdomen and one to the right cheek.
The suspect surrendered to police shortly after the incident and was remanded for seven days from yesterday to assist investigations under Section 302 of the Penal Code for murder.
A post-mortem found that Norhazwani died from pressure applied to her neck.
Negri Sembilan police chief Datuk Alzafny Ahmad said the cause of death was determined following a five-hour post-mortem at the Forensic Medicine Department of Hospital Tuanku Ja'afar yesterday.
He said physical examinations also found three stab wounds caused by a sharp weapon — two to the abdomen and one to the right cheek.
About 200 people, comprising family members, MCBA personnel, Customs Department personnel, police officers and local villagers, attended the funeral.
Also present were MCBA deputy director-general (Operations) Datuk Mohd Nasaruddin M. Nasir and Tumpat police chief Assistant Commissioner Mohd Khairi Shafie.
Hazwan said he and his family were focusing on settling the remaining matters, including the tahlil prayers, for now.
He said they had yet to decide on long-term plans for Norhazwani's two daughters, aged five and six.
"They were already under the care of my elder sister here previously. So, we intend to keep them with us," he said.

e99052c068d9ef03: JOHOR BAHRU, Oct 18 — The Johor government has extended the closure of schools and educational institutions across the state for another five days from tomorrow (October 19) due to the haze.
State Education and Information Committee chairman Dr Muhammad Naqib Md Ghazali said the decision was made following a meeting of the Johor Haze Management Coordination Committee at noon yesterday.
He said the extension would remain subject to developments in air quality, weather forecasts and ongoing health assessments.
“Monitoring reports indicate that Air Pollutant Index (API) readings remain at concerning levels, with no significant improvement.

“The decision also takes into account wind movement towards the north and weather forecasts for the next three to four days, which will be considered before determining when schools can reopen,” he said in a statement.
Muhammad Naqib said the measure was in line with the directive of the Regent of Johor, Tunku Mahkota Ismail, who consistently prioritised the safety, health and well-being of the people.
He said the decision also reflected the state government’s commitment to placing public health and safety at the forefront.
Meanwhile, he said Teaching and Learning at Home (PdPR) would continue throughout the closure in accordance with the Ministry of Education’s (MOE) PdPR Manual Version 2.0.
However, the needs of students sitting for examinations and assessments would be taken into account, with limited exceptions possible.

“These exceptions are subject to coordination by the Johor Education Department (JPNJ) and strict compliance with health standard operating procedures (SOPs), with no additional activities permitted,” he said.

Muhammad Naqib said JPNJ would review the implementation SOPs daily in line with MOE directives and obtain the latest updates from the Examination Board to coordinate examination and assessment schedules for MOE schools and Johor religious schools.
He stressed that face masks must be worn and all established health guidelines followed.
Regarding private educational institutions (IPS) and childcare centres, Muhammad Naqib said the decision on whether to continue operating or close rested with the respective institutions.
“However, this is subject to compliance with the established guidelines, including conducting activities in enclosed spaces and ensuring that face masks are worn,” he said.

Meanwhile, he said health authorities had raised concerns over the public health risks of prolonged exposure to air pollution and recommended more comprehensive preventive measures, particularly for children and vulnerable groups.
“Throughout October, 30,648 cases of asthma and upper respiratory tract infections (URTI) were recorded in the state, representing a weekly increase of 20.7 per cent,” he said.

The state government had earlier announced the closure of all schools for two days from October 8, before extending the closure to cover educational institutions for another five days from October 12. — Bernama
5d072d9fe53bdff6: JOINT BASE ANDREWS: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Saturday that President Donald Trump's waiver of sweeping sanctions and tariffs on Russia would be a 60-day pause to "analyse" their impact on the global economy.

"The president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyse what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the US economy," Rubio said, noting that the economic restrictions involved a number of countries, not just Russia.
He said various conflicts were impacting global energy prices, including the US war on Iran and attacks on Saudi Arabia by Yemen's Houthis.
"These conflicts around the world are starting to crash into each other, and they're having an impact not just on global oil and diesel prices" but on economies as well, he said.

US lawmakers on both sides of the political aisle have sharply criticised Trump after he signed an executive order Friday that waived sweeping sanctions and tariffs targeting Russia – measures adopted by Congress last month.

The law passed in September, and signed by Trump, included sanctions targeting Russian officials, oligarchs and financial institutions, and provided Trump with the authority to impose sanctions on major buyers of Russian oil and gas.
The idea was to cut off sources of funding to supporters of Russian President Vladimir Putin, as well as his war on Ukraine.
But late Friday, two days before the law was due to take effect, Trump exempted Russia from those economic restrictions.
"Beyond irresponsible," Republican Senator Thom Tillis, a frequent Trump critic who will leave office in January, said in a post on X.
"If the President wants to actually bring down energy prices, he can do it by solving the Iran problem, not by doing a solid for Vladimir Putin."
Ted Cruz, a senior Republican senator from Texas, called the move "a mistake" in comments aired on Fox News.
Trump's executive order came after he struck a deal with Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin to allow exports of Russian diesel in exchange for the easing of sanctions.

The impact of steep diesel price hikes due to the Iran war are beginning to filter into the US economy, and cost of living worries are top of mind for voters ahead of key midterm elections next month.
Polls show Trump's Republicans are likely to receive a drubbing at the polls.

"The diesel that Putin was going to sell, they were (going to) make it available to the global market one way or the other. The only difference is how much of it the United States was going to get," Rubio said, underscoring the importance of the vital fuel powering US road hauling, agriculture and construction.
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he feared the United States would lift more sanctions on Russia and that Trump's action "rewards" Putin.--AFP
2cb763dd2fbe6582: KYIV: Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Saturday that he feared the United States would lift more sanctions on Russia and that President Donald Trump's action only "rewards" Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin.
Trump heightened a battle with Zelenskyy on Friday when he signed an executive order that waived sweeping US sanctions targeting Russia's energy revenues.
The decision came despite Russia increasing strikes on Ukraine in the fifth year of its war, which has killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions.
Trump had already announced that he has agreed a deal with Putin to allow exports of Russian diesel in exchange for the easing of sanctions, and Zelenskyy said he feared more concessions.
"Unfortunately, the lifting of sanctions will continue. I believe the 'diesel deal' is just the first step," Zelenskyy told reporters.

He said he still "personally" hoped that Trump will do "everything in his power" to make Putin end the war but added: "You cannot achieve this by limiting Ukraine's responses to Russia for killing our people. And certainly not by lifting sanctions."
Ukraine said at least two people were killed in Russian air strikes on Saturday.
- 'Pressure' needed -
Zelenskyy said the US decision on Friday came the same day as Russia attacked 15 critical power generation facilities across Ukraine in "one of the largest" attacks on Ukraine's energy grid.
Officials said one person was killed in the southern city of Kherson in an attack that also wounded 22 people, including two children, and that another was killed in the northeastern city of Sumy.
Zelenskyy said the US decision on Friday came the same day as Russia attacked 15 critical power generation facilities across Ukraine in "one of the largest" attacks on Ukraine's energy grid.

The Lindsey Graham Act – named after the late US senator who sponsored the bill – targeted Russia's energy and defence sectors, as well as Putin and the so-called "shadow fleet" of tankers used by Moscow to circumvent Western sanctions.
"It is important that everyone in America also sees what is really happening," Zelenskyy said on social media.
The Lindsey Graham Act, he said, was "supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end" adding that the act "could have helped enormously – and still can!".
"A U.S. sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, financial rewards for Putin – all of this only encourages him to keep attacking," he warned.

The Ukrainian leader said Russia wanted to cause a "blackout" in Ukraine ahead of winter: "Russia is trying to leave millions of our people without electricity and heating." He called on allies to pressure Moscow to "stop this."
Last winter saw hundreds of thousands in Ukraine consistently without heat and electricity in freezing temperatures.
- RUSSIA HAILS TRUMP MOVE AS 'HISTORIC' -
The Kremlin and Putin have not yet reacted to Trump, but several Russian officials celebrated the move as a win.
"The Trump administration's suspension of the Graham Act is an important and truly historic moment," Kirill Dmitriev, a Putin envoy, said on social media.
Dmitriev said the act would have caused "serious damage first and foremost to the US economy and global markets."
Trump announced the sanctions waiver in an executive order Friday, shortly after Putin appeared in military uniform and said Moscow aims to capture the rest of east Ukraine.
US-led talks to end the war have failed to bring a breakthrough. Putin and Zelenskyy have frustrated Trump in the past.

Zelenskyy rallied his allies Friday on a visit to Brussels for a European Union summit, urging them to keep financing Ukraine's fight and insisting he was standing up for his country amid the row with Trump.
- PUTIN VOWS MORE -
Ukraine has been struggling to shoot down Russian missiles and has been left scrambling to boost defences ahead of winter.
Russia controls large swathes of eastern and southern Ukraine and Putin has repeatedly said Moscow intends to seize the rest of east Ukraine by force.
"On the whole I see a positive trend in the operations of the troop groupings," Putin told army leaders Friday, dressed in military attire.
"Undoubtedly, one of the main objectives remains the liberation of the Donetsk People's Republic," he added, using the Kremlin's name for the eastern Donetsk region. --AFP

38a9d17ed366bf07: BENGALURU, (India) :India and West Indies were forced to settle for a 2-2 stalemate in their five-match Twenty20 International series after Saturday's deciding match lasted just 48 minutes before it met a watery end.

10407dd0660efd00: PETALING JAYA: With less than two weeks to go before nomination day for the Melaka state election, Umno’s silence over a possible pact with PAS may signal a desire to test the party’s electoral strength by going solo, according to an analyst.

Mazlan Ali of Universiti Teknologi Malaysia said Umno’s performance in the Melaka polls would likely shape its decision on whether to forge a nationwide electoral pact ahead of the 16th general election (GE16).
“If it can win on its own, it will be in a better position to decide how much it needs PAS for GE16,” he told FMT.

Mazlan also said Umno was hesitant about forming an alliance with PAS for the Nov 14 polls because it was confident of retaining the 21 seats it won in the 2021 state election and saw little need to compromise.

Barisan Nasional chairman Ahmad Zahid Hamidi previously said that while Umno intends to defend its 21 seats, it was open to negotiating with potential partners over the remaining seven constituencies.
Zahid, who is also the Umno president, said the party was also open to potential seat swaps.
Mazlan said the main concern was whether these swaps would involve PAS strongholds, and questioned how many seats the Islamic party would be willing to hand over to BN.

Hisommudin Bakar, who heads the think tank Ilham Centre, attributed Umno’s silence to concerns over whether cooperation would benefit BN or strengthen PAS, which competes for the same pool of Malay voters.
“Umno needs to assess whether cooperation would help revive the party or give PAS a boost,” he said.
Hisommudin said BN’s recent victories in the Johor and Negeri Sembilan state polls were partly due to PAS supporters who wanted to vote out Pakatan Harapan.
In Johor, BN won 48 of the 56 seats it contested, while in Negeri Sembilan, it secured 18 of the 25 seats contested.

“The question is whether BN can retain its seats without the support of PAS voters,” he said, adding that, by going solo, BN risked facing three-cornered contests that cost it seats in the 2018 and 2022 general elections.
Still, Hisommudin said, Umno’s silence allows it to keep its options open while weighing the pros and cons of an alliance with any party and negotiating seat allocations.

Jayum Jawan of the Academy of Sciences Malaysia said Umno had little reason to seek an alliance following BN’s successes in Johor and Negeri Sembilan, adding that the party appeared to be “on the rebound”.
He said an alliance with PAS could slow Umno’s revival by forcing it to give up seats it could win on its own.
Jayum also dismissed suggestions that Umno feared PAS as a national rival, although he acknowledged that the Islamic party had enough influence to demand concessions in future negotiations.
“Surely no political party would want to give up seats to a new partner, especially when it believes it can win those seats on its own merit,” he said.
57cda0c91fea0493: PETALING JAYA: Langkah Umno mendiamkan diri mengenai kemungkinan pakatan dengan PAS berbaki kurang dua minggu sebelum penamaan calon PRN Melaka dilihat mahu menguji kekuatan pilihan rayanya secara solo, kata penganalisis.

Mazlan Ali daripada Universiti Teknologi Malaysia berkata, prestasi Umno pada PRN Melaka berkemungkinan membentuk keputusannya sama ada mahu menubuhkan pakatan pilihan raya di peringkat kebangsaan, menjelang PRU16.
"Sekiranya Umno boleh menang sendiri, mereka akan berada pada kedudukan lebih baik menentukan sejauh mana parti itu memerlukan PAS pada PRU16," katanya kepada FMT.

Mazlan turut berkata, Umno teragak-agak membentuk pakatan dengan PAS pada PRN Melaka 14 Nov ini kerana yakin dapat mengekalkan 21 kerusi dimenanginya dalam PRN 2021, selain melihat tidak banyak keperluan berkompromi.

Mazlan berkata, kebimbangan utama adalah sama ada pertukaran kerusi ini akan melibatkan kawasan kubu kuat PAS, serta mempersoalkan berapa banyak kerusi yang sanggup diserahkan PAS kepada BN.

Hisommudin Bakar yang mengetuai badan pemikir Ilham Centre, mengaitkan sikap berdiam diri Umno dengan kebimbangan sama ada kerjasama akan menguntungkan BN atau memperkasakan PAS, yang berebut kumpulan pengundi Melayu sama.
"Umno perlu menilai sama ada kerjasama akan membantu membangkitkan semula parti itu atau memberi dorongan kepada PAS."
Hisommudin berkata, kemenangan BN baru-baru ini pada PRN Johor dan Negeri Sembilan sebahagiannya berpunca daripada penyokong PAS yang menolak Pakatan Harapan (PH).

"Persoalannya ialah sama ada BN boleh mengekalkan kerusinya tanpa sokongan pengundi PAS," katanya, sambil menambah dengan bergerak solo, BN berdepan risiko persaingan tiga penjuru yang menyumbang parti itu hilang kerusi pada PRU 2018 dan 2022.

Namun, Hisommudin berkata, sikap berdiam diri Umno membolehkan parti berkenaan kekal mempunyai pilihan terbuka, sambil menimbang kebaikan dan keburukan pakatan dengan mana-mana parti serta perundingan pembahagian kerusi.

Jayum Jawan daripada Akademi Sains Malaysia berkata, Umno tidak mempunyai banyak sebab untuk mencari pakatan susulan kejayaan BN di Johor dan Negeri Sembilan, sambil menambah parti itu nampaknya 'kembali bangkit'.
Beliau berkata, pakatan bersama PAS mampu merencatkan kebangkitan semula Umno apabila memaksa parti itu menyerahkan kerusi berpotensi dimenanginya.
Jayum turut menolak tanggapan Umno takut kepada PAS sebagai pesaing nasional, walaupun beliau mengakui PAS mempunyai pengaruh menuntut konsesi dalam perundingan akan datang.
"Sudah tentu tiada parti politik yang mahu menyerahkan kerusi kepada rakan kongsi baharu, terutamanya apabila ia percaya mampu memenangi kerusi atas kekuatan sendiri."
302ca2bfc8c0c9b8: KUALA LUMPUR: Muhammad Syahir Azali still remembers the fear of watching his nine-year-old daughter struggle to breathe.
Puteri Hannah Amelia had started with a cough and inflamed throat, but within days her condition worsened into chest pain and breathing difficulties.
Syahir rushed her to hospital, where she remained for five days after being diagnosed with a mycoplasma infection and bronchitis that doctors linked to haze exposure.
“At first, she had been coughing for two days, so I took her to a nearby clinic to consult a doctor and get some medication,” the 35-year-old said.
“However, her condition did not improve. By the third day, it had worsened, and she began experiencing breathing difficulties and chest pain.”

The episode was the first time Hannah had been hospitalised because of a haze-related illness. She missed school during her recovery, and doctors advised the family to make sure she wore a face mask even indoors.

For Syahir, the experience stripped the haze of its familiar, almost seasonal quality. What can look like little more than a grey sky or distant smell of smoke can become something far more serious when a child is already vulnerable.
When exercise becomes exposure
Healthy adults can be affected, too, particularly when exercising outdoors.

Running enthusiast Syahirah Atikah, 36, recently took part in a city marathon after checking that the Air Pollutant Index (API) reading remained below 100. She felt confident enough to continue, but the haze thickened as the morning went on.
“After completing my run, I experienced chest tightness and difficulty breathing,” she said. The following day, she took sick leave after developing a headache and severe cold.

Paediatric respiratory physician Dr Noor Zehan Abdul Rahim said prolonged or repeated exposure to haze can inflame the respiratory tract because fine particles such as PM2.5 penetrate deep into the lungs.
Children are particularly vulnerable because their lungs are still developing, while older adults may have less capacity to clear inhaled particles.

Symptoms can include persistent coughing, wheezing, mucus production, chest tightness and breathlessness. For children with existing respiratory conditions such as asthma, repeated exposure can also trigger flare-ups and worsen symptoms.
Exercise brings another problem: the harder people work, the more deeply they breathe.

Tolullah Oni, chair of Global Public Health and Sustainable Urban Development at the University of Cambridge, said runners may inhale greater quantities of polluted air simply because their breathing becomes faster and deeper during exercise.

The route matters, too: running beside busy roads can increase exposure to vehicle pollution, while even small changes in distance from traffic can reduce the amount inhaled. Transboundary haze is harder to escape, however, because it can cover a much wider area.
“Under severe haze conditions, exposure would undoubtedly be worse. It is not something I would recommend for outdoor running,” Oni said.
Knowing when to stay indoors

The health ministry has already reported increases in some haze-related illnesses, including upper respiratory tract infections and conjunctivitis. But for individuals and families, the more immediate question is often how to judge when an ordinary day outside is no longer worth the risk.

Respiratory physician Dr Syed Ajmal Syed Ali advises limiting outdoor exposure when air quality deteriorates, avoiding strenuous exercise, staying hydrated and continuing prescribed medication for existing respiratory conditions.
Anyone who experiences worsening breathlessness, wheezing or chest tightness should seek medical attention rather than wait for the haze to clear.

Weather can bring temporary relief, with rainfall helping reduce pollutants in the atmosphere. But changing winds can also carry smoke from forest and land fires in neighbouring countries back across Malaysia, meaning conditions can shift quickly.

For families like Syahir’s, that uncertainty makes the haze more than an inconvenience. Once you have watched a child fight for breath, checking the air outside becomes less about whether the sky looks hazy - and more about whether it is safe to step out at all.
01a626d46fe01e8b: PETALING JAYA: The air quality was unhealthy in 25 areas this morning as haze continued to envelop parts of the country.
Johor continued to be the worst-hit state as of 8am, with six locations occupying the top 10 places in the air pollutant index (API) readings.
Schools in Johor will remain closed for five more days from Monday because of the unhealthy air quality, executive councillor Naqib Ghazali said yesterday.

Pasir Gudang recorded the highest reading of 189, followed by Larkin (181), Kota Tinggi (180), Pengerang (178), Batu Pahat (169) and Kluang (163). Elsewhere, Tangkak had an API reading of 160, and Segamat 158.
API readings of between zero and 50 are categorised as good, 51 to 100 as moderate, 101 to 200 as unhealthy, 201 to 300 as very unhealthy, and 301 and above as hazardous.
In Negeri Sembilan, Nilai had an API reading of 173, Seremban (170) and Port Dickson (153).
Bukit Rambai in Melaka recorded an API reading of 164, Alor Gajah (161) and Bandaraya Melaka (155).

The areas with unhealthy air quality in Selangor included Johan Setia (163), Shah Alam (162), Klang (160), Petaling Jaya (158) and Banting (157). Putrajaya recorded an API reading of 159, and Cheras, Kuala Lumpur, 157.
Forty-one areas nationwide had moderate air quality, and two - Limbang, Sarawak, and Balik Pulau, Penang - enjoyed good air quality.
b84507bf381c5ed1: KOLKATA: At least 19 people were killed and two dozen more injured Saturday in eastern India after a stampede that occurred during sudden rainfall at a Hindu religious gathering, officials and Indian media said.

West Bengal's Chief Minister Suvendhu Adhikari told reporters the fatalities included a seven-year-old girl, adding that 25 other people were injured outside a pavilion "in a stampede" at the Hindu festival of Durga Puja in the city of Kolkata.
"Six bodies have so far been identified," Adhikari said.

A senior police official at the scene told AFP an announcement caused "commotion" after it started raining at night and the "crowd waiting outside the pandal (pavilion) was pushing, pulling and rushing forward and fell on the ground, leading to the stampede."

Afterwards medics were seen moving injured people on stretchers, including a police officer, into a local hospital. Several relatives of victims cried and held one another as they mourned the loss of loved ones.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi addressed the tragedy in a short statement on Facebook.
"The stampede in Kolkata is saddening. Condolences to the bereaved families. Wishing the injured a speedy recovery," he wrote.
"The West Bengal Government is providing all possible help to the affected families."
Adhikari originally announced 17 fatalities. The Press Trust of India (PTI) reported the death toll rose by two to 19, quoting Adhikari in a later statement.
Nine dead bodies have been released to their families, the PTI reported.

It also said police have taken the closed circuit footage of the festival and authorities would initiate action against those seen on CCTV who appeared to fail in their responsibility for crowd control.

Videos shot before the stampede appeared to show large crowds of people waiting to enter the pavilion, in an area with narrow lanes that allow only a few people to walk in at a time, according to Indian Express.
Deadly crowd incidents are a frequent occurrence at Indian mass events, such as religious festivals, due to poor management and safety lapses.

Last year, a stampede at India's Kumbh Mela religious fair killed 30 people and injured several others, and 11 fans were crushed to death in Bengaluru during celebrations for the local cricket team's first Indian Premier League title.
The same year, 36 people were killed after a stampede broke out at a campaign rally of a popular actor-turned-politician in southern Tamil Nadu state.
In 2024, 121 people were killed in northern Uttar Pradesh state during a Hindu religious gathering.--AFP
373fefe13adf0b47: SAN SALVADOR: El Salvador's President Nayib Bukele has clarified that possible early releases for people detained in his anti-gang crackdown would only cover about 10,000 suspects who allegedly helped the criminal groups on occasion, not actual members.
Bukele on Tuesday unveiled a plan for early releases that he said "that would benefit more or less 50% of prisoners in El Salvador who collaborated with gangs."
More than 90,000 suspected gang members have been arrested in the Central American country since Bukele declared a state of emergency in 2022.

But in response to an AFP request for clarification, Bukele said Friday the early release plan would cover roughly 10,000 people identified as occasional gang associates, but who did not formally belong to gangs.

"We are going to review the cases of those 10,000 or so people, and based on a preliminary review, we believe about 50 percent could enter the 'Zero Idleness' program so they can get out sooner," he said.
"No gang member is going to be freed. Ever," Bukele said at a press conference alongside Costa Rican President Laura Fernandez, who was visiting El Salvador.
"No one in the history of humanity, in any country, has achieved what we have achieved," said Bukele, an ally of US President Donald Trump.
Bukele first revealed his plan Tuesday when asked about statements by his brother, Ibrajim Bukele, who said a "commission" was reviewing the cases of people detained in the crackdown.
The state of emergency established by Bukele has slashed crime rates to record lows, but rights groups have denounced abuses including arbitrary detentions, torture and deaths in custody.
According to an Amnesty International tally, hundreds of people have died in custody.
1a4e33bac488c7e6: CYBERJAYA: The misuse of artificial intelligence (AI) to create sexually explicit images, particularly of children, is on the rise, prompting calls for stronger safeguards and closer parental supervision.

Multimedia Content Forum of Malaysia (CMCF) chief executive officer Mediha Mahmood said AI tools could be used to turn images of people into sexually explicit materials or deepfake videos in inappropriate situations.
"It is not an authentic image. It is a manipulated image or deepfake video altered by AI to depict the victim in a sexual or inappropriate manner," she said recently.
Mediha said the growing use of AI tools by children is another concern, as unrestricted applications and websites may make it easier to create illicit content.
"The most glaring issue is the proliferation of unrestricted apps, websites and open-source tools that can be repurposed for these malicious purposes.
"There are so many of them," she said.
She said easy accessibility of these applications has made it difficult to monitor or control the use of AI platforms.

"These AI-generation platforms cannot always be fully monitored or controlled. Most concerningly, they are accessible to anyone with a connected device, without verifying whether the user is an adult or a child.
"Access remains largely unrestricted for minors and other vulnerable groups," she said.
Mediha said distributing sexually explicit material involving children is an offence under the Sexual Offences Against Children Act 2017, even if the person circulating it is a minor.
"This is a critical point that must be impressed upon parents, guardians, teachers and anyone who interacts regularly with children."
She said Malaysians have embraced AI for creativity and efficiency, but malicious users have taken advantage of the technology.
"Like any other service or application, bad actors will exploit and manipulate it.
"We see amazing uses of AI for creativity and efficiency. But because it is available to everyone, we also see bad actors using it for nefarious purposes," she said.
Mediha said existing laws, including the Penal Code, the Communications and Multimedia Act 1998 and the Online Safety Act 2026, may be used to address AI misuse.
However, gathering digital evidence is a challenge for enforcement agencies.
She called on those who have fallen victim to AI manipulation or those aware of such incidents to lodge reports with the police and relevant agencies.
She said even after the online content has been taken down or deleted, this does not mean that the evidence can no longer be recovered.
"People often assume that once a link is deleted, nothing more can be done.

"But in discussions with enforcement agencies, such as the police and the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission (MCMC), there are technical avenues to recover links and trace digital forensic evidence.
"People should not assume an incident cannot be reported. Reports can and should be filed, and action will be taken," she said.
Mediha said digital platforms should adopt the "Safety by Design" and "Safety by Default" principles.
They include restricting certain image-manipulation features for minors and requiring verifiable consent before images can be altered.
While social media platforms have been working with MCMC to comply with regulatory frameworks and licensing requirements, she said collaboration with generative AI providers remains limited.
"From CMCF's perspective, there has not yet been meaningful collaboration, largely because engaging these independent AI developers and providers is quite difficult."
Mediha said the problem is not a lack of legislation.
"Rather, it is a lack of awareness among parents who do not fully grasp the potential harm their children face.
"It is fundamentally an advocacy and digital literacy issue," she said.
She cited MCMC's Internet Selamat (Safe Internet) campaign as an initiative to educate parents about online risks, platform safety features and how to configure them.
"Parents need to understand the threats, learn about the safety features offered by platforms and know how to configure them," she said.
Mediha wants parents to supervise their children's use of AI applications, particularly when providing them with Internet-connected devices or devices with recording capabilities.
"Whether they like it or not, if parents provide Internet-connected devices or devices with recording capabilities to their children, they must ensure the usage is supervised," she said.
She added that the government's stand of not allowing children under 16 to open social media accounts should serve as a benchmark for other online services.
Mediha said preventing AI misuse requires shared responsibility among regulators, enforcement agencies, digital platforms, parents and the wider community.
"We also need everyone to help these children understand the grave dangers of using AI to generate inappropriate imagery of themselves or their peers and sharing it."

af22c58b6ff5ca29: WHEN Muhammad Usamah Zaid Yasin talks about the making of Ejen Ali, the Malaysian animated spy series about a schoolboy recruited into a secret intelligence agency, he doesn't begin with a stroke of genius. He begins with a burger stall.
In the early days of WAU Animation, the studio he co-founded in 2013, Usamah and his partners were brainstorming ideas for their first original series.
Over lunch one afternoon, a colleague suggested imagining a burger-stall operator as a spy, passing customers something secret when they placed a special order.
Elements of that casual exchange eventually found their way into the show. Agent Bakar, a supporting character, came before the protagonist Ali.
The lead character, his gadgets and the people around him took shape through many discussions, sketches and revisions.
"It's not really something that sparked and we felt like this is it.
"It was more like we decided on this and then... okay, let's run with it," begins Usamah, who's clad all in black, with a cap perched jauntily on this head.
For someone behind one of the country's best-known animated properties, creativity is less about the lone genius than the collective effort required to make an idea work.

Over two decades in animation, Usamah has gone from working at Les' Copaque Production, the Malaysian studio behind the hugely popular Upin & Ipin, to building WAU Animation and creating Ejen Ali, which has expanded from a television series into feature films and a wider commercial brand.
The journey, however, has been anything but straightforward.
WORLD OF HIS OWN
Growing up in Kuala Lumpur, Usamah gravitated towards comics, cartoons, video games and drawing.
He also sketched stories in exercise books, though he never seriously imagined these interests could become a profession.
The possibility emerged almost by accident while he was choosing a university.
A brochure for Multimedia University's Faculty of Creative Multimedia caught his eye because its imagery reminded him of Final Fantasy VII, the video game he was playing at the time.
He thought he might learn to create games like it.
His father had hoped he would pursue architecture or engineering, but Usamah went with the opportunity to study creative multimedia.

At university, he began to understand the design principles behind the visual worlds he'd always loved, from composition and positive and negative space, to the deliberate choices that make an audience feel something.
Animation didn't come easily at first, but he persevered and eventually became one of the stronger students in his class.
"My dream was to land in an international studio... Pixar," he recalls.
Disney and DreamWorks were also part of that ambition. But an opportunity soon after graduation brought him into Malaysia's animation industry instead.
His early career included work at Les' Copaque Production and on Geng: The Adventure Begins, a Malaysian animated feature.
The experience gave him a grounding in production and the possibilities of creating animation for local audiences.

In 2013, he and his partners established WAU Animation, hoping to develop original intellectual property — stories and characters they could own and grow, rather than simply provide creative services for others.

The beginnings were modest. The team worked out of Usamah's apartment before moving into an incubator and eventually a more permanent workspace. They pitched ideas and tried to separate genuine interest from polite encouragement.
A 2½ minute proof-of-concept animation eventually helped attract attention, but getting a foot in the door was only the start.
The young studio had underestimated the demands of production and had to build its capabilities along the way.
A ransomware attack cost the team about a month's work, while production gaps and financial pressures added to the strain.
Although Usamah managed to steer WAU through the Covid-19 pandemic without laying off staff or cutting salaries, the gap between projects left the studio struggling to recover.
At one point, the team was "barely making ends meet". Eventually, financial pressures forced a painful decision to downsize.
For Usamah, the experience was a reminder that building a creative studio demands more than imagination.
The business of keeping it alive — managing people, financing projects and navigating the gaps between productions — is inseparable from the work of making animation.
STORY TO BUSINESS

Usamah understood that a successful animated property could eventually generate opportunities through merchandise, licensing and other commercial ventures. But none of that would matter without a compelling story and characters audiences wanted to spend time with.
The making of Ejen Ali was an iterative process. The team worked through more than 25 ideas before narrowing its choices to a Malaysian spy story.
Ali emerged after a discussion about making the lead character a child, allowing young viewers to identify with him.
His personality and gadgets took further experimentation. Initially conceived as clumsy and less academically gifted, Ali was at one stage meant to wield an elastic weapon.
The yo-yo came later, after Usamah saw a child playing with one and recognised how its unpredictable movement suited the character.
Alicia, Ali's disciplined classmate and fellow young agent, provided a foil to his more impulsive nature, adding another dynamic to the cast.

Usamah credits the people around him for helping ideas evolve. Creators can become too close to their work to see its weaknesses, he shares, which is why he encourages younger artists to seek honest feedback rather than work in isolation.

A successful creation, however, brings complications of its own. After Ejen Ali: The Movie 2 was released last year, unauthorised recordings circulated online, including on messaging platforms and social media.
Merchandise featuring the characters also appeared without the studio's permission.
Usamah understands the affection behind fan-made creations, but draws a distinction between fans expressing their enthusiasm and sellers reproducing official artwork for commercial gain.
In a labour-intensive industry, piracy does more than undermine a business; it deprives the people who create the work of income that could sustain their craft and fund future projects.
For Usamah, protecting intellectual property is ultimately about protecting the livelihoods of the artists behind it.
COST OF CONVENIENCE
That same concern shapes Usamah's view of generative artificial intelligence (AI), which can produce images, text and other material in response to prompts.
While he accepts that AI tools may have a place in the creative process, he draws the line at systems that displace artists or use their work without consent or compensation.
He likens it to ordering food from a microwave and claiming to have cooked it.
For Usamah, creativity isn't simply about the finished product, but the decisions, compromises and discoveries that shape it along the way.
Animation, he explains, is an exercise in problem-solving, with storyboard artists, concept artists and other collaborators bringing different perspectives to the table.
Through experimentation and exchange, an idea evolves into something no one person might have arrived at alone.
Even when a project succeeds, the creative work is far from over.
After the first season of Ejen Ali was well received, the team had to figure out how to build on that success.
A feature film, meanwhile, brought an entirely different set of challenges from a television series.
Explains Usamah: "You don't always stop once you've found what you're happy with.
"Most of the times we stop the creation process because we're out of time, and we have to live with what we've created."
His concern isn't simply about the technology itself, but the future it could leave for those entering the profession.
What happens to young graduates trained in animation if the work they aspire to do is taken away?
And what of the 8-year-old drawing pictures today, dreaming of becoming an artist, if there's no viable path to making a living from that passion?
"I'm actually very... hopeful," says the father-of-two, pushing back against the notion that his stance is rooted in fear.
"I'm certain there are enough hope in humanity that at the end of the day, the true creators will prevail."

For Usamah, the stakes extend beyond WAU. Malaysia has begun building successful animated properties, but sustaining that momentum means nurturing new generations of artists and giving them the opportunity to develop their skills and earn a living from their work.

The bigger question, then, isn't just how technology can make animation faster or cheaper, but what kind of industry Malaysia wants to build — and whether there'll still be room for the people whose imagination brings its stories to life.
WHAT MATTERS
For all his conviction, Usamah is candid about the compromises that come with building a studio.
He and his partners had set out to create something of their own, but had not fully anticipated the demands of financing, production schedules, commercial partnerships and carrying a brand.
As the studio grew, there was less time for the creative freedom that had brought them together.
"I miss the days when all of us were not as busy as we're now. Like, the five of us, the core, right? Get to spend more time sitting and creating," he muses reflectively.

9fd1af01b713f727: From Moaz Nair

In the noble effort to elevate Bahasa Melayu as the core of national identity, a topic frequently discussed among language enthusiasts is the level of mastery and fluency of the national language among multi-ethnic communities.
Most narratives typically focus on daily communication, the corporate sector, or administrative affairs.

However, from a sociolinguistic perspective, there is a dimension that is rarely explored deeply but carries significant influence over language assimilation: the use of the national language within the religious and cultural expressions of non-Muslim communities.
On one hand, there are high expectations for all citizens to anchor their lives around Bahasa Melayu. On the other, when touching upon the spiritual realm, a more complex dynamic emerges.

Understanding these contrasting approaches is not meant to assign blame, but rather to examine how language can function more inclusively as a bridge for unity without disrupting established socio-religious sensitivities.
Historical framework and the unique situation in the peninsula

The difficulty of expanding the use of Bahasa Melayu in non-Muslim religious affairs in Peninsular Malaysia is rooted in a combination of legal history, demographics, and the evolution of the language's corpus itself.

Under Article 160 of the Federal Constitution, Malay identity is clearly defined by three main elements: professing the religion of Islam, habitually speaking the Malay language, and conforming to Malay custom. This close alignment has caused Bahasa Melayu to evolve with a heavy Islamic imprint over hundreds of years through the absorption of Arabic theological terms into everyday vocabulary.

To preserve harmony and prevent theological confusion, most states in the peninsula enforce the Enactment on the Control and Restriction of the Propagation of Non-Islamic Religions, guided by the principles of Article 11(4) of the Federal Constitution. These laws restrict the use of certain religious terms to ensure the doctrinal integrity of the majority community remains protected.
Aware of these legal and social sensitivities, non-Muslim communities in the Peninsula—comprising largely Chinese and Indian ethnic groups—opt for a cautious approach.

To maintain racial harmony and safeguard their respective theological purity, they feel more comfortable retaining their mother tongues (such as Mandarin or Tamil) or English in their religious affairs. This situation inadvertently creates a linguistic divide in spiritual matters, even though they are fluent in Bahasa Melayu in other daily affairs.
Diverse models in East Malaysia and Indonesia

The reality in the peninsula presents a stark contrast when looking at the socio-political models in Sabah, Sarawak, and Indonesia. In East Malaysia, a unique demographic structure has long positioned Bahasa Melayu as the primary unifying vessel.

For hundreds of indigenous sub-ethnicities such as the Iban, Kadazandusun and Bidayuh, Bahasa Melayu has served as the daily lingua franca, including in church services and their Alkitab (Bible) texts.

The general practice and sharing of religious terms rooted in the same language are accepted with high tolerance as a historical norm, in line with the socio-political guarantees under the Malaysia Agreement 1963 (MA63).

Looking at our neighbour, Indonesia underwent a comprehensive language assimilation process because Bahasa Indonesia was established as a neutral and inclusive national asset. There, all recognised religions fully utilise Bahasa Indonesia in rituals and scripture translations.
Major Islamic figures and organisations like Nahdlatul Ulama (NU) and Muhammadiyah play a mature role in guiding society.
They have successfully educated the public by decoupling the language’s function as a national communication tool from the essence of an individual's personal faith.
This approach allows for the harmonious sharing of certain religious vocabularies, anchored by the concept of inter-citizen brotherhood or “ukhuwah wathaniyah”.
Building harmony through mutual understanding
These differing linguistic approaches have a tangible impact on daily social relations. In the peninsula, the separation of language in religious affairs shapes a model of "cautious coexistence".

Multi-ethnic communities deeply respect each other’s boundaries, yet opportunities for deeper cross-cultural dialogue can sometimes be limited by fears of stepping on legal sensitivities. Social interactions remain largely concentrated in secular spaces like economics, education and sports.

Conversely, the dynamics in Sabah, Sarawak and Indonesia demonstrate that when a national language is shared in the most deeply personal aspect of life—spirituality—it can erode suspicion and strengthen a sense of togetherness. The national language is no longer seen as the exclusive property of one group, but as a grand canopy sheltering all citizens.
Conclusion
The desire to see Bahasa Melayu fully embraced by all Malaysians is a noble dream that deserves support. However, discourses on elevating the language must look beyond casual conversation.

We must acknowledge the sociolinguistic challenge that arises when the national language is restricted in non-Muslim spiritual realms to safeguard faith, while simultaneously expecting these communities to assimilate the language into every facet of their lives.

To move forward, the best path is to construct a harmonious, localised understanding. Drawing from the spirit of tolerance in East Malaysia, we can begin to view Bahasa Melayu not as a tool of division, but as a bridge that unites.

Without compromising the legal protections that safeguard the faith of Muslims in the peninsula, the cultivation of the national language in cultural and literary spaces across all communities must continue to be nurtured maturely—for the future of a truly integrated Bangsa Malaysia.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
b8494dd74ddf100a: KUALA LUMPUR: Twenty-five Malaysians from government, business and civil society have been selected for the inaugural ilmu Fellowship, a leadership programme aimed at nurturing a new generation of leaders committed to nation building.

The 25 fellows were chosen from more than 800 applicants, with 54 reaching the final stage. The selection process involved 25 panelists from various sectors, who assessed candidates on their leadership qualities, contributions to their organisations and communities, and willingness to learn from different perspectives.

Developed in partnership with the University of Oxford's Blavatnik School of Government, Acumen Academy, Pemandu Associates and leadership coach Alvin Ung, the programme is designed to accommodate participants' existing professional commitments.

It combines immersive retreats, workshops, coaching, peer learning and practical leadership initiatives, culminating in a four-day residential programme at the University of Oxford. There, fellows will explore leadership, public policy, systems change and cross-sector collaboration, gaining insights they can apply to challenges back home.
Leon Jala, vice-chairman and group CEO of Pemandu Associates, said the diversity of the inaugural cohort was one of the programme's strengths.

"The ilmu Fellowship creates an environment for individuals with different experiences and perspectives to learn from one another, challenge their assumptions and develop a broader understanding of leadership," he said.
He added that exposure to different sectors would help participants navigate complex challenges and contribute beyond their own organisations.

YTL Foundation programme director Kathleen Chew said the fellowship would provide participants with the space and support to grow as leaders while building relationships that could lead to meaningful collaboration.

"We are excited to bring them together across sectors, where they can learn from one another, challenge their perspectives and build the relationships needed to work towards a shared purpose," she said.
Among the inaugural fellows is former world squash champion Nicol David, who now leads the Nicol David Organisation, which empowers communities through sport, education and wellbeing.
David said her transition from professional athlete to community advocate had introduced her to new challenges and opportunities for growth.
"My journey in squash has taught me the value of discipline, perseverance and a willingness to keep learning," she said.
"I see the ilmu Fellowship as an opportunity to learn from people with different experiences, challenge my own perspectives and grow in how I serve our communities."
Beyond the programme itself, YTL Foundation hopes to build a lasting network of leaders who can continue working together on issues affecting Malaysia.
With 25 fellows selected annually, the foundation aims to develop at least 250 values-driven leaders over the next decade, fostering greater integrity, trust and collaboration across sectors.
The initiative reflects YTL Foundation's wider commitment to education and leadership development, rooted in the belief that investing in people is essential to Malaysia's long-term progress.
