8b4307aa50ece14e: Dalam usaha murni memartabatkan bahasa Melayu sebagai citra identiti negara, satu topik yang sering dibincangkan oleh para pencinta bahasa ialah tahap penguasaan dan kefasihan bahasa kebangsaan dalam kalangan masyarakat pelbagai kaum. Kebanyakan naratif yang diutarakan lazimnya tertumpu kepada ruang komunikasi seharian, sektor korporat, atau urusan pentadbiran. Namun, dari perspektif sosiolinguistik, terdapat satu dimensi yang jarang diterokai secara mendalam tetapi mempunyai pengaruh besar terhadap asimilasi bahasa, iaitu penggunaan bahasa kebangsaan dalam ruang ekspresi keagamaan dan kebudayaan komuniti bukan Islam.

Di satu sudut, terdapat harapan tinggi agar seluruh warganegara meletakkan bahasa Melayu sebagai pasak utama dalam kehidupan. Namun di satu sudut yang lain, apabila menyentuh ranah spiritual, wujud dinamik yang lebih kompleks. Memahami perbezaan pendekatan ini bukan bertujuan mencari kesalahan, sebaliknya untuk meneliti bagaimana bahasa boleh berfungsi dengan lebih inklusif sebagai jambatan perpaduan tanpa mengusik sensitiviti socioreligious yang sedia termaktub.
Kerangka sejarah dan keunikan di Semenanjung

Kesukaran memperluas penggunaan bahasa Melayu dalam hal ehwal agama bukan Islam di Semenanjung berakar umbi daripada gabungan sejarah perundangan, demografi, dan evolusi korpus bahasa itu sendiri. Berdasarkan Perkara 160 Perlembagaan Persekutuan, identiti Melayu ditakrifkan secara jelas melalui tiga elemen utama: menganut agama Islam, bertutur dalam bahasa Melayu, dan mengamalkan adat istiadat Melayu. Hubungan yang erat ini menyebabkan bahasa Melayu berkembang dengan acuan Islam yang sangat tebal selama beratus-ratus tahun, menerusi penyerapan istilah teologi Arab ke dalam kosa kata harian.

Atas dasar memelihara keharmonian dan mengelakkan kekeliruan konsep ketuhanan, kebanyakan negeri di Semenanjung menguatkuasakan Enakmen Kawalan dan Sekatan Pengembangan Agama Bukan Islam berpandukan prinsip Perkara 11(4) Perlembagaan Persekutuan. Undang-undang ini mengehadkan penggunaan istilah-istilah keagamaan tertentu bagi memastikan keaslian akidah masyarakat majoriti sentiasa terpelihara.

Sedar akan sensitiviti perundangan dan sosial ini, komuniti bukan Islam di Semenanjung -- yang sebahagian besarnya terdiri daripada kaum Cina dan India -- memilih pendekatan berhati-hati. Demi menjaga keharmonian kaum serta memelihara ketulenan teologi masing-masing, mereka lebih selesa mengekalkan penggunaan bahasa ibunda (seperti Mandarin atau Tamil) mahupun bahasa Inggeris dalam urusan keagamaan. Keadaan ini secara tidak langsung mewujudkan garis pemisah linguistik dalam aspek kerohanian, walaupun mereka fasih berbahasa Melayu dalam urusan harian yang lain.
Kepelbagaian acuan di Malaysia Timur dan Indonesia

Realiti di Semenanjung ini memberikan gambaran yang berbeza apabila kita melihat acuan sosiopolitik di Sabah, Sarawak, dan Indonesia. Di Malaysia Timur, struktur demografi yang unik meletakkan bahasa Melayu sebagai wadah penyatu utama sejak sekian lama. Bagi ratusan sub-etnik bumiputera di sana seperti Iban, Kadazandusun, dan Bidayuh, bahasa Melayu menjadi lingua franca harian, termasuk dalam urusan gereja dan teks Alkitab mereka. Amalan am dan penggunaan kalimah keagamaan yang berkongsi akar bahasa ini diterima dengan penuh toleransi sebagai sebahagian daripada kelaziman sejarah, sejajar dengan jaminan sosiopolitik di bawah Perjanjian Malaysia 1963 (MA63).

Melihat pula kepada negara jiran, Indonesia melalui proses asimilasi bahasa yang menyeluruh kerana bahasa Indonesia diletakkan sebagai hak milik nasional yang neutral dan inklusif. Di sana, semua agama yang diiktiraf menggunakan bahasa Indonesia sepenuhnya dalam ritual dan terjemahan kitab suci.

Tokoh-tokoh dan organisasi Islam terbesar seperti Nahdlatul Ulama (NU) dan Muhammadiyah memainkan peranan matang dalam membimbing masyarakat. Mereka berjaya mendidik umat dengan memisahkan fungsi bahasa sebagai alat komunikasi kebangsaan daripada intipati akidah individu. Pendekatan ini membolehkan perkongsian beberapa kosa kata agama berlaku secara harmoni berteraskan konsep persaudaraan sesama warganegara (Ukhuwah Wathaniyah).

Perbezaan pendekatan linguistik ini memberikan impak yang ketara kepada hubungan sosial dalam kehidupan seharian. Di Semenanjung, pengasingan bahasa dalam hal ehwal agama membentuk model hubungan yang berhati-hati (cautious coexistence). Masyarakat pelbagai kaum sangat menghormati sempadan satu sama lain, namun ruang untuk dialog silang budaya yang lebih mendalam kadangkala menjadi terhad kerana bimbang menyentuh sensitiviti undang-undang. Interaksi sosial lebih banyak bertumpu kepada ruang sekular seperti ekonomi, pendidikan, dan sukan.

Sebaliknya, apa yang berlaku di Sabah, Sarawak, dan Indonesia menunjukkan bahawa apabila bahasa kebangsaan dikongsi bersama dalam aspek yang paling peribadi (kerohanian), ia berupaya mengikis rasa curiga dan memperkukuh rasa kebersamaan. Bahasa kebangsaan tidak lagi dilihat sebagai milik eksklusif satu kelompok, tetapi sebagai bumbung besar yang menaungi seluruh warga.

Hasrat untuk melihat bahasa Melayu dihayati sepenuhnya oleh seluruh rakyat merupakan satu impian murni yang harus disokong. Bagaimanapun, wacana pemartabatan bahasa ini perlu melihat melampaui sekadar perbualan harian. Kita perlu mengakui wujudnya cabaran sosiolinguistik apabila penggunaan bahasa kebangsaan disekat dalam ranah spiritual bukan Islam atas faktor penjagaan akidah, sementara pada masa yang sama, komuniti tersebut dituntut untuk mengasimilasikan bahasa Melayu ke dalam segenap aspek kehidupan.

Untuk bergerak ke hadapan, jalan terbaik adalah dengan membina kefahaman dan formula tempatan yang harmoni. Mengambil semangat toleransi dari Malaysia Timur, kita boleh mula melihat bahasa Melayu bukan sebagai alat pemisah, tetapi sebagai jambatan yang menyatukan. Tanpa perlu mengorbankan perlindungan undang-undang yang melindungi akidah umat Islam di Semenanjung, ruang pembudayaan bahasa kebangsaan dalam aspek kebudayaan dan sastera merentas komuniti harus terus disuburkan secara matang demi masa depan sebuah bangsa Malaysia yang benar-benar bersepadu.

2ea2863ac3805dd9: LONDON: Daniel Dubois scored a crushing second-round knockout victory over fellow Briton Fabio Wardley to retain his World Boxing Organisation heavyweight crown on Saturday.
In a much-anticipated rematch of their bruising 11-round classic earlier this year, Dubois dominated Wardley from the opening bell to batter his rival into submission in the second round.
Dubois dropped Wardley after 17 seconds of the contest at the O2 Arena in London, catching the challenger flush on the chin with a huge overhand right.
The 29-year-old Dubois continued to land punches at will throughout the first round, which finished with Wardley clinging on desperately under a barrage a punches on the ropes.
The second round started as the first had ended, with the 6ft 5in Dubois uncorking an array of punches that left Wardley in desperate trouble.
With Dubois unloading on a defenceless Wardley, the towel came in after two minutes and 21 seconds of the round.
The fight's explosive opening was a role reversal from the two fighters' first meeting in May, when Wardley floored Dubois after just 16 seconds.
Dubois said afterwards he had been determined to set the tone in Saturday's rematch.
"I had bad intentions from the beginning," Dubois said in his post-fight television interview in the ring.

"Our back was against the wall the first time; this time we just had to go out there and show that we mean business and that's what we did tonight," added Dubois, who improved to 24-3-0 (23 knockouts) with the win.
Dubois is now eyeing a series of potential unification fights in a heavyweight division that has been splintered since Ukraine's Oleksandr Usyk vacated his WBC, WBA and IBF belts in June.
"I'm the champion now and I want to get some big fights in," Dubois said. "This stage of my career, big money, big fights."
Wardley, who fell to 20-2-1, meanwhile had no complaints about his loss.
"It's never fun to lose but it is what it is," said Wardley, who took up professional boxing relatively late after starting fighting in white-collar bouts.
"The game is the game. I've always thrown myself in with the best competitors out there, the best in the business, the toughest, the biggest, hardest, meanest guys around.

"There's no shame in a loss when you're putting yourself in and testing yourself against the best ... Boxing is a game of fine margins – it can be done and over in a round or two, or it can be a big old war like it was last time.
"I didn't execute the game plan properly tonight. That was all. I hold my hands up to that." --AFP

47935c4e33f64e43: ANYTHING, it seems, can go between two buns.

That's what I'm beginning to think as I study the colourful printed posters fluttering around the menu board of a burger stall in Puchong. There's a matcha burger, a mac and cheese burger, a cili padi burger and a crispy chicken burger, including combinations I'd never have thought to try.

The stall sits beneath a leafy tree on the pavement, with shoplots, warehouses and busy roads all around. It's easy for passing motorists to spot and pull over. For now, a tarp covers it, while the smell of food wafts from a restaurant across the road.
I check the address Waze has brought me to. Burger Ji Legend, Puchong Headquarters, it says.
A WhatsApp message pings. "You see the stall?" Ganesh Moorthy writes.
I tell him I do. It's the only stall here, an inviting patch of shade amid the bustle. After all, a humble burger is just the thing for a quick, satisfying meal.
Except Ganesh's burgers are not so humble. Judging by the posters, he has thought of everything. Or so I think, until we meet and I suspect there's always another idea waiting to be tried.

Wearing a baseball cap turned backwards, the earnest 34-year-old shares that the stall will open at 5pm. He introduces his wife, Anneseletta Peter, who's a year younger, before we settle at the mamak restaurant across the road.

In 2019, Ganesh made headlines, including in the New Straits Times, as a delivery rider whose politeness, honesty and work ethic touched Malaysians' hearts. I remember reading about him then. Seven years later, I want to know what happened after the headlines faded, and how he found his way into burgers.
INSPIRATION AND IDEAS
"I want to be different," he declares, eyes sparkling. He reels off his creations, including a pappadom burger, featuring the thin, crisp Indian wafer usually served with rice and curry.
Then he mentions a pickle burger.
"Pickle?" I repeat.
He grins. "You know… oorukka… the Indian pickles."

He means the punchy, spicy preserves made from fruits or vegetables, such as mango or lime. Before I can imagine that flavour between two buns, he moves to another creation. "I did the daun pisang burger," he says, referring to his banana leaf burger.
"That time daun pisang burger kaw kaw viral (went hugely viral). Then we came up with the ice-cream burger."

He experiments in his kitchen at home, with his wife as his first taste-tester. His regular customers then help him decide which ideas are worth pursuing. "We try it with our regular customers and they give us feedback," he shares, smiling.

He glances at his watch and pats his phone. Soon, his workers will arrive to prepare for the evening. Even as we chat, he seems conscious of every passing minute. I begin to wonder where that urgency comes from.
HUMBLE BEGINNINGS
As our conversation turns to his early years, Ganesh grows quieter. The Puchong native who was so eager to describe his burgers now seems less certain where to begin.
"When I was 6 months old, my mother passed away," he confides.

After his taxi driver father remarried, his grandparents took care of him. Eventually, an uncle took over. He shrugs as he recounts these changes, although he was only a child, dependent on others for a home and a place to belong.
Money was scarce. Even milk was something he grew up going without. "I lived on coffee and tea," he says matter-of-factly.
That simple statement stays with me. While other children might have taken a glass of milk for granted, Ganesh learnt early to make do.
"I also didn't really study," he readily admits. He left school before reaching Form Two and picked up whatever work he could find.
"I would follow the lorry drivers and help them, angkat barang (carry goods)… mostly carry canned drinks to fast food restaurants," he recalls.
At an age when his days should have revolved around lessons and homework, he was hauling cartons of drinks. Other jobs followed, from working as a security guard to selling shoes as a sales promoter.
At 17, he found work at a fast-food restaurant, where his lack of qualifications left him with some of the hardest, least-paid tasks.

"It was hard," he confesses, adding: "I didn't have any certificates, so I worked menial jobs there, from wiping tables to cleaning the toilets. I mean, it was around RM2.80 an hour, but still it was honest work."
Alongside the work, he remembers the tears, shed in the very place he was tasked with cleaning.
"I remember crying in the toilet on more than one occasion," he reveals quietly.
Still, he stayed for many years, learning the job from the ground up until he was managing the outlet. The teenager who'd cried in the toilets was now trusted to run the place.
"I didn't know how to speak Malay. I didn't speak proper English. The restaurant taught me everything," he says.
With those skills came the confidence to consider what else he might try.
STEPPING OUT
After years of struggling, a steady salary meant a great deal. But Ganesh wanted to build a better life beyond the outlet. Leaving was difficult, and his family couldn't understand it.
"They were upset because I was giving up a steady income for a pipe dream of doing something else. They got angry and threw me out of the house," he shares.
Even so, he understands their worries.
Says Ganesh: "I think I can understand their frustration. My regular income helped support the household. Now they didn't know whether I would be able to keep contributing."
He began making deliveries for shopping platforms and tried multi-level marketing, but that venture failed. It became one of the lowest periods of his life.
"I just wanted to do more. Try other things," he says simply.
Wanting to go further had left him starting over, without his family's support. Yet he continued looking for work.
"I needed to prove that I could make it. My family is poor. Most of them are rubber tappers earning a meagre income. I wanted to be the first to break that cycle," he confides.
FINDING FAMILY
His efforts caught businessman Aiman Manan's attention during a delivery pick-up.

In reports at the time, Aiman recalled being impressed by his courtesy, punctuality and initiative. Ganesh had started GRS Delivery Service to supplement his income and asked Aiman to try it. He did, and his customers were soon praising Ganesh too.

Aiman shared their encounter on Facebook to promote the business. Thousands of Malaysians liked, shared and commented, recognising something to be proud of in this young man working hard to get ahead.
"That story which went viral completely changed my life," Ganesh exclaims, a smile softening his serious face.

As he talks about Aiman, it's clear that their friendship means far more than the attention Ganesh received. What began with a few deliveries grew into a lasting bond, and Ganesh eventually joined Aiman's healthcare and supplements company, Natura, where he managed inventory and orders while continuing his delivery work. Their partnership grew further when they established Goosy Delivery, a business they continue to run together to this day.
Among those who came across his story was Anneseletta, neither knowing it would be the beginning of their own.
"I kept seeing the post about Ganesh on my social media," she recalls, adding: "Eventually, I wanted to engage him to deliver the products I was selling."
Their friendship deepened into love, and they made plans to marry in 2020.

Then, a month before their wedding, Ganesh lost both motorcycles he used to earn a living in a fire at the Gombak Setia People's Housing Project. He was suddenly without the means to carry out his deliveries.

Once again, Aiman stepped in, rallying his customers, most of them Malay, to pool money for a replacement motorcycle. They continued giving Ganesh delivery jobs, helping him earn again as his wedding approached.
The young Indian rider had earned their trust. When he needed help, they came together to give him a chance to recover.
"Aiman expected nothing in return," he says, voice full of emotion. "All he advised me to do was to help others the same way when I get the chance."
Benny James, the boss of one of Aiman's friends, also gave Ganesh a car to help him get further in life and build his delivery business.

There's something wonderfully Malaysian about this coming together, the spirit of muhibbah expressed through practical kindness. People who'd met Ganesh through deliveries helped him rebuild his livelihood and look forward to his wedding.
For someone once asked to leave his family home, that sense of belonging meant a great deal.
"My customers are my family. Aiman is my family," declares Ganesh.
BIGGER DREAMS

Ganesh had tried the burger business before, setting up a stall with a friend. His long hours on deliveries left his partner struggling to manage alone, and they closed. There was another setback when someone they rented the stall to disappeared with it.
After getting married, he wanted to give the idea another chance. This time, Anneseletta was beside him. "It wasn't easy," he recalls.
A canopy was beyond their means. On wet evenings, they ran for shelter and waited for the rain to stop before returning to the stall. Their plans depended as much on the skies as on customers.
Ganesh recalls using a rechargeable lamp that cast a bluish glow over the stall. They laugh together at the memory, although those early days gave them plenty to worry about.

He continued deliveries while they got the business going. Then, after their daughter was born, he was involved in a bad accident. The risks of spending so many hours on the road became harder to put aside, and he decided to focus more on burgers.
That renewed effort became Burger Ji. Fellow delivery riders called him "Ji", a name he carried into his new working life.

Today, the couple manages seven outlets in the Klang Valley and two in Johor — and Ganesh is considering expanding to Singapore. The ambition that once worried his family has given him a business to build with his wife.
fc9376d971a1a760: PORT KLANG: Beneath Malaysia's vast maritime waters lies a dramatic landscape of underwater mountains, ridges, valleys and canyons, much of which remains unmapped to modern hydrographic standards.
National Hydrographic Centre (NHC) director-general Rear Admiral Dr Najhan Md Said said understanding this hidden terrain was vital to safe navigation, maritime security and sovereignty.
"If you drain the water from the South China Sea, you will see a terrain just as breathtaking as anything on land.
"There are underwater mountains, massive ridges, steep trenches and ancient riverbeds that once ran above water thousands of years ago," he told the New Sunday Times.

Najhan also serves as the vice-chair of the International Hydrographic Organisation — Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission General Bathymetric Chart of the Oceans Sub-Committee on Undersea Feature Names, comprising 12 international experts.

The sub-committee is responsible for establishing internationally consistent nomenclature and naming guidelines for undersea features, ensuring uniformity across nautical charts, bathymetric maps and scientific publications worldwide.
He said high-resolution bathymetric surveys had mapped extreme depths across Malaysia's maritime domain.
Seabed mapping, he added, shared some principles with astronomy, but also carried a strong connection to national identity and heritage.

"When astronomers discover a new star, individual scientists are often allowed to put their names on it. But under international maritime rules, individuals cannot name undersea features. That privilege belongs strictly to sovereign nations.
"To date, Malaysia has secured official recognition for 17 undersea feature names, most of them in the bathymetrically rich waters off Sabah and Sarawak," he said.
The New Sunday Times was provided with advanced 3D acoustic renderings from the NHC, showing the varied topography of some seabeds in Sabah and Sarawak.
Among them are the Santubong Seamount, a jagged, volcanic-like spire; Kenyalang Hill, with its sharp, conical summit; and the Rafflesia Hill, a massive dome-shaped mound.
Measured against the Kuala Lumpur skyline, the seabed's peaks hold their own.
Santubong Seamount rises about 1,400m from the ocean floor, roughly twice the height of Merdeka 118, the country's tallest building. Yet its summit lies about 500m below the surface.
Rafflesia Hill, at about 450m, matches the Petronas Twin Towers, while Kenyalang Hill, at about 320m, is 100m shorter than KL Tower (421m).
Rungus, Kadazandusun and Bidayuh Hills each rise about 900m, a third taller than Merdeka 118.
Submerged mountain chains include Iban Ridge, Bajau Ridge and Kimaragang Ridge, which stretch across the ocean floor.
The seabed also features deep chasms and valleys, including the steep-walled Meranti, Chengal and Anggerik canyons, and the broad, flat-bottomed Mawar Valley.

Najhan said naming undersea features has helped preserve Malaysia's cultural identity, with internationally recognised names documenting the country's heritage on global maps and in scientific records.

"Through ongoing high-resolution bathymetric surveys, the NHC has identified and prepared another 45 undersea features for formal registration and submission to the sub-committee on undersea feature names.
"Imagine looking at an international ocean gazetteer or a global map and seeing an underwater mountain in your home waters named in a foreign tongue.
"It feels like a personal sting to national pride," said Najhan.
He added that hydrographers had a duty to not only map the seabed, but also ensure its features bore the names reflecting Malaysia's history, culture and identity.

2b1348b46a5d6af5: TIRANA: Albania's capital saw violent clashes for a fifth straight day on Saturday as police fired rubber bullets on protesters demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama and setting buildings ablaze.
Violent demonstrations have rocked Tirana since Tuesday, with thousands of protesters calling for Rama to step down as they rally against university conditions and high tuition fees.
Protesters on Saturday threw rocks, Molotov cocktails, metal objects and pyrotechnic devices at police, and torched cars and litter bins, using them as blazing barricades to stop police advancing.
In a sign of the escalating violence, police fired rubber bullets on the demonstrators for the first time since the protests began, AFP journalists on the ground saw.
The protests continued into the night, with buildings -- including a court, banks and post office -- set on fire or severely damaged.
Ambulances were seen rushing to pick up injured people as the protest entered its tenth hour.
The health ministry told AFP that 35 people were wounded on Saturday, of which 18 were police and 17 were protesters.
Officers also used water cannon, pepper spray and tear gas against the crowd, leaving the streets of Tirana shrouded in thick smoke.

Paula, who together with other young people set up a provisional first-aid station in a lawyer's office, told AFP three people had been treated for head, eye and leg injuries allegedly from rubber bullets.
Albanian law allows the police to use rubber bullets during protests only in extreme cases.
Sport student Redi Taku told AFP the move was indeed extreme "considering that there are minors aged 16 to 17 among the protesters".
Director of the state police, Skender Hita, told a press conference that "rubber bullets were used in a limited manner".
"All the means used have been used in a limited manner and only certified equipment is used, which is allowed for such cases in European Union countries," he said.
During the week's protests 167 people were arrested while criminal proceedings were initiated against 388, he said.
Seven police officers were suspended and are under disciplinary investigation for overstepping their authority.

He added that over the five days of protests 132 officers primarily in Tirana have sustained injuries, and called "those committing these acts of violence to cease their illegal activities immediately".
Protesters managed to set on fire the Supreme Court building and the entrance of the Bank of Albania, as firefighters rushed to extinguish the blaze.
Minister of justice Toni Gogu said that this was "not strike at the government" but at "two independent institutions" that "serve the country and its citizens".
Suitcase protest
At the beginning of the protest demonstrators set a suitcase on fire and threw it in the education ministry courtyard -– symbolically showing they do not want to leave Albania.
Journalism student Sinan Billa said the protest was "a reaction to express discontent at the silence of our government."
"Young people have awoken for our parents, too," Billa told AFP.
"We are not asking for privileges. We are demanding our rights, our future and a better country," he said.
While visiting local businesses damaged in the demonstrations, Rama said he respected the students and added that "their right to protest must and will be protected".
"Their voices, the voices of young people and of every citizen who has taken part in protests today, must and will be heard with respect," Rama said.
However, he added that he "will not allow anyone to jeopardise the future of this country".
Local media reported further protests in the coastal town of Durres, where demonstrators smashed the windows of the post office and blocked roads with burning barricades.
This week's unrest comes after months of anti-government protests in the Balkan nation, initially sparked by a controversial resort development linked to US President Donald Trump's family.
cf603bf7bd0b9b90: SOME of the most revealing stories aren't necessarily the ones that announce themselves. They may lie in a family silence passed from one generation to the next, a familiar neighbourhood whose history has been forgotten, or a seemingly convincing account that begins to unravel when examined more closely.
In an age of artificial intelligence (AI), online scams and competing versions of the truth, learning to look beyond appearances has taken on an urgency that extends well beyond the pages of a book.

It's this territory that the Singapore Writers Festival (SWF) explores when it returns from Nov 13 to 22, bringing together more than 300 writers, speakers and moderators across over 200 programmes under the theme "Hidden in Plain Sight".

Now in its 29th edition, the festival spans fiction, memoir, literary translation, crime writing, journalism and documentary film, bringing Singaporean, regional and international voices into conversation. Its central invitation, however, is deceptively simple: to look again at the stories we think we know, and consider what might have escaped our attention.
For festival director Yong Shu Hoong, himself a writer, literature offers precisely this opportunity.

"As a writer myself, I know how the power of literature lies in its ability to open our eyes to what's beyond the façade, to find hidden meanings in stories and poetry that beckon us to understand the world with deeper perspectives," he says.
The theme also reflects the challenges of navigating contemporary life, he adds.

"Aside from the literary context, it also reflects the current times of AI and scams, where it gets harder to distinguish between what might be obvious but untrue, and the concealed reality requiring additional effort to decipher. I hope festivalgoers will engage with this year's topical and thought-provoking conversations with an open mind."
The 2026 edition will be Yong's final one at the helm, bringing his tenure to a close with a programme that draws together literary traditions, voices and perspectives from Singapore and beyond.
LOOK CLOSER

One of this year's major additions, the "Crime and Mystery Spotlight", takes the festival's theme into a genre built on the art of looking closer. In "Old Crimes, Fresh Takes", Silvia Moreno-Garcia joins Singapore writers Jean Tay and Ovidia Yu to explore how histories and archival material can be transformed into crime fiction.

British writer Robin Stevens and Irish writer Louise Hegarty consider the enduring appeal of Agatha Christie, while China's Shuang Xuetao and Singapore's Jeremy Tiang examine how crime and thriller conventions can illuminate questions of memory, precarity and contemporary life.

But the things left unsaid aren't just confined to mysteries and investigations. Families, too, carry stories that may take generations to surface. In "What the Family Doesn't Say", Amitav Ghosh, Jemimah Wei and Balli Kaur Jaswal consider the sacrifices and histories that shape families, including those that remain unspoken.
In "Off the Record", Malaysian writers Janet Tay and Tan Twan Eng, longtime friends and former lawyers, offer candid reflections on writing and the realities of life beyond the public eye.

Elsewhere, the festival turns to the larger forces shaping our collective future. Ghosh examines the stories societies tell about the planet's future; Stephen Witt explores Nvidia's rise as an AI powerhouse; and Ruha Benjamin considers the hidden biases embedded in technology and society.
Together, these conversations invite audiences to look beyond technological spectacle and examine the assumptions, histories and human consequences beneath it.

The region receives a similarly searching treatment through SEA xChange, a programme bringing Southeast Asia into focus through literature, architecture, folklore, migration and everyday life. Among its offerings are explorations of regional beliefs and superstitions, Southeast Asian architecture, journalism in the Malay world and the different ways migrant and local writers experience the city.

There's also a concerted effort to bring Singapore's multilingual literary landscape into sharper view. Chinese, Malay and Tamil programming, shaped by guest curators Chan Cheow Thia, Muhammad Ilyia Kamsani and Neelakandan Sivanantham, connects local writers with voices from the wider language communities of the region.

In "Writing Fiction to Remember and Heal", Singapore's Teoh Hee La joins Wang Zhanhei from China and Hon Lai Chu from Hong Kong to consider how fiction can preserve memory and offer comfort in times of change.

"Royal Syair and Journalism in the Malay World" examines the relationship between classical Malay poetic traditions and contemporary reportage, while Tamil-language writers Uma Kathir and Krishnasamy Subramaniam revisit the histories and communities of Little India. Indian poet Yuvan Chandrasekar, meanwhile, explores poetry's capacity to resonate across time, nation and language.
SOMETHING FOR EVERYONE

At the heart of this multilingual focus is SWF Homage, which examines how Singapore literature has travelled across languages and borders, from the 18th and early 19th centuries to the present. Alongside translation-focused programmes, an interactive microsite and a public installation travelling to libraries and community spaces will explore how local writing reaches readers beyond its original language.

The festival also brings literature to families and young readers. Children can create illustrated stories at "Bring Your 'Chou Chou' Day!" with Singaporean author-illustrator Quek Hong Shin, while families can join "Treasure Hunting in Dunhuang", co-presented with the Asian Civilisations Museum. SWF Playground features Robin Stevens and Jessica Townsend discussing rebellious heroines in "Girls Who Don't Follow the Rules".

Youth Fringe equips participants aged 13 to 25 with curation, moderation and marketing skills. Its "Storytelling Shiok!: The Value of Humour", developed by youth curator Lim Yuxuan and led by writer Suffian Hakim, explores Singaporean wit in storytelling. SWF Classroom, meanwhile, challenges students aged 10 to 18 to devise their own endings to a mystery.

Elsewhere, architectural historian Yeo Kang Shua leads a tour of the restored Tan Yeok Nee mansion, revealing the stories behind its history. Audiences can experiment with writing prompts at "Poetry Game Night with Ella Frears" or explore the female writers who have shaped Pooja Nansi at The Salon, hosted at COMO Cuisine.

Ahead of the festival, book clubs, Book Doctor sessions and pop-up activities bring literature into the community. "Reading by the River" invites visitors to browse and read by the Singapore River, while SWF Digital extends the festival's conversations to global audiences through recordings, podcasts and online programmes.
ENDURING PROMISE

Organised by Arts House Group and commissioned by Singapore's National Arts Council, SWF also takes literature into everyday spaces. A new collaboration with CapitaLand Investment will bring arts initiatives to retail and workspace properties, including Undercurrents at the Funan Underground Pedestrian Link, featuring Malaysian illustrator Tang Yau Hoong and Singaporean illustrator Quek Hong Shin on how people process thoughts and navigate everyday challenges.
For Arts House Group executive director Sharon Tan, the festival is about more than presenting writers.

"Our efforts extend beyond presenting outstanding writers, with a greater focus on creating encounters that encourage audiences to read more widely, question more deeply and discover stories beyond those they already know," she concludes.

4dc0be6df918002f: PETALING JAYA: A pact between the Selangor government and Bersatu could allow the Pakatan Harapan-led administration to serve out its full term and hold the next state election after the 16th general election (GE16), according to an analyst.

With ties between PH and Barisan Nasional increasingly strained, Universiti Malaya’s Awang Azman Pawi said a confidence and supply agreement (CSA) with Bersatu would allow the Selangor administration to remain in office even after Parliament is dissolved.

“National issues could dominate the considerations of voters,” he said. “On the other hand, holding the state polls concurrently with GE16 would allow for election machinery to be consolidated.”
Nonetheless, he said the bigger question was whether PH could retain voters’ confidence in its ability to govern, particularly on bread-and-butter issues such as the cost of living.

“Holding the state polls concurrently with GE16 would also demonstrate confidence on PH’s part, something that is especially important as the coalition continues to face challenges in Peninsular Malaysia’s Malay belt,” said Fauzi.
Last week, menteri besar Amirudin Shari said Bersatu’s assemblymen were close to inking a pact with the Selangor government ahead of the state budget’s tabling.
The proposed deal comes amid growing tensions between PH and BN in Selangor, as well as strains within Perikatan Nasional, where PAS has emerged as the dominant partner.
The 56-member Selangor assembly comprises 32 PH assemblymen, followed by Bersatu (11), PAS (10), BN (two) and one independent.

7af1c50a402457e6: PETALING JAYA: Rising sharply from the landscape like giant stone walls, Malaysia’s limestone hills are easy to admire from a distance. What is less obvious is how much they hold inside - caves, fossils, unusual wildlife, and traces of human history stretching back thousands of years.

A new exhibition at Muzium Negara is shining a light on that hidden world. "Pameran Khazanah Kars Malaysia", which runs until Dec 31, brings together 87 collections, including mammal, bird, amphibian and reptile specimens, rocks and fossils, archaeological finds, snail specimens and herbarium material.

Karst is a type of landscape that forms when water gradually dissolves soluble rock, especially limestone. Over immense periods of time, that process can create caves, sinkholes, underground drainage systems, cliffs and the steep-sided limestone formations familiar in many parts of Malaysia.

The exhibition is divided into three main segments covering the formation of karst landscapes; fossil and archaeological discoveries; the plants and animals associated with these environments; and efforts to conserve and manage them.
The exhibition is designed to help visitors understand not only cave ecosystems and biodiversity, but also the links between karst landscapes, archaeology, history and local culture.
A natural archive beneath our feet

Part of the appeal of Malaysia’s limestone landscapes is that they can act like natural archives. Layers of rock and cave deposits may contain clues to ancient environments, extinct or long-vanished animals, and the people who once lived in or used these spaces.

At the same time, modern karst environments remain very much alive. Their caves provide roosting sites for bats and shelter for specialised invertebrates, while plants growing on isolated limestone outcrops can sometimes be found nowhere else.

This combination of geology and life is one reason karst areas can be particularly vulnerable. Damage to a small limestone hill or cave system may affect species with nowhere else to go, while quarrying, development and careless tourism can permanently alter geological features that took millions of years to form.
Conservation, therefore, forms part of the exhibition, including examples of work by government agencies, private organisations and non-governmental groups to protect and manage karst areas.

For visitors, the exhibition offers a chance to look at Malaysia’s limestone scenery as more than a backdrop for caves, temples or weekend trips. The rocks themselves help tell a story about how the landscape formed, while the fossils, archaeological finds and animal specimens reveal what those environments have supported over time.

It also makes for an accessible introduction to a subject that can otherwise sound highly technical. You do not need to know your geomorphology from your palaeontology to appreciate the idea that a limestone cave can preserve both geological history and evidence of human life.
Where: Central Hall @ Muzium Negara, Kuala Lumpur
When: 9am-5pm daily, with last admission at 4.30pm

02da00e99273c2bb: PORT KLANG: Malaysia needs a dedicated national hydrography act to give its hydrographic authority statutory backing and replace a 54-year-old administrative memorandum that can be amended or rescinded by the cabinet.

National Hydrographic Centre (NHC) director-general Rear Admiral Dr Najhan Md Said said despite operating for more than half a century and representing Malaysia in the International Hydrographic Organisation (IHO) since 1975, the centre is still relying on a cabinet memorandum produced in 1972.
He said an act of Parliament was needed to establish the NHC as the sole national authority responsible for official nautical charting, bathymetric data governance and maritime safety declarations.
"Without a statutory foundation, the NHC faces administrative hurdles that hamper its agility, as even routine operational and inter-agency approvals require lengthy administrative processes.
"Enacting the National Hydrography Act will give the NHC institutional permanence, streamline decision making and provide long-term funding stability," he told the New Sunday Times.

Najhan said the proposed law would give the national hydrographic authority formal legal recognition and strengthen its ability to maintain continuous maritime domain awareness, safeguard navigation and protect Malaysia's maritime interests.

"For more than 50 years, the NHC has operated under a 1972 cabinet memorandum rather than a formal Act of Parliament. Administrative memorandums remain legally fragile because any sitting cabinet can amend or rescind them."

He said national reviews, including the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Batu Puteh, had recommended a national hydrography act to replace the existing administrative framework and give the NHC explicit statutory authority to fulfil its national responsibilities.

"Under the proposed legislation which has received support from the Defence Ministry and its policy division, the NHC is envisioned as a standalone department directly under the ministry, similar to the Veterans Affairs Department and the Science and Technology Research Institute for Defence.
"It would report directly to the defence minister, while operational personnel would continue to be drawn from the Royal Malaysian Navy."
c3466f03cdc0f290: FOR months, Negri Sembilan had been embroiled in an extraordinary constitutional and adat crisis, pitting the palace, state government and customary chiefs against one another over questions of authority.
The dispute also cast a spotlight on a centuries-old system of customary rule unique to the state.

At its heart is Adat Perpatih, the matrilineal system of customary law and social organisation practised in Negri Sembilan, where descent is traced through the mother's line and ancestral property is traditionally passed down through women.
The crisis has introduced Malaysians to many unfamiliar words, such as Undang, Lembaga, Buapak, waris and luak. Yet, one title has received far less attention: Ibu Soko.
Despite the focus on men at the centre of the crisis, the Ibu Soko offers a glimpse into another side of Adat Perpatih, where women have long held a quiet but important place in the workings of adat.

Hence, the observance of International Day of the Girl Child on Oct 11 is a reminder of the contributions that women make to families and communities — contributions so familiar they often go unacknowledged.
HOW DOES IT WORK?
Adat Perpatih can appear bewildering to an outsider, but its basic structure begins with the family and works upwards.
A perut sits at the base of this social structure, comprising families who share a common female ancestor.
Several groups of these families make up a suku, or clan, and the clans live in a luak, also known as customary territory.

The Negri Sembilan society is traditionally structured around 12 primary suku — Biduanda, Batu Hampar, Seri Melenggang, Tanah Datar, Seri Lemak, Mungkal, Tiga Nenek, Paya Kumbuh, Anak Melaka, Anak Acheh, Batu Belang and Tiga Batu.
Leadership also rises through different levels. A Buapak looks after the affairs of families within his perut, while a Lembaga heads a suku.
At a higher level are the Undang, chiefs of the four principal luak of Sungai Ujong, Jelebu, Johol and Rembau.
The four Undang, together with the Tunku Besar of Tampin, have a constitutional role in choosing the Yang di-Pertuan Besar.
Unlike a system where authority simply flows from the top down, Adat Perpatih has traditionally placed great importance on consensus and selection through different levels of the community.
Running through it all is the maternal line.

Traditionally, a child belongs to the mother's suku, and members of the same suku do not marry one another as they are considered close blood relatives. Marriages are also matrilocal, meaning the husband will move in with the wife's family.

Knowing precisely who belongs where is therefore not simply family history. It not only determines marriage and inheritance, but it can also matter when deciding who has the lineage to hold customary office.
THE WOMAN WHO KNOWS
This is where the Ibu Soko becomes far more than a keeper of family history.
Traditionally a senior woman, she knows her suku, its genealogy, relationships and customs.
In a system where customary leadership grows from family and clan upwards, that knowledge can help establish who has the standing to lead.
Although men traditionally occupy leadership positions, such as the Buapak and Lembaga, the Ibu Soko can play a part in identifying, supporting or rejecting candidates from within her community.
Her knowledge of lineage therefore sits surprisingly close to the question of power itself.
It reveals one of the most fascinating features of Adat Perpatih.
Men may occupy many of its highest customary offices, but the lineage from which their claim to those offices emerges runs through women.
A 2023 Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia (UKM) study on the role of the Ibu Soko in Luak Johol described her as among the women most knowledgeable and experienced in Adat Perpatih.

Researchers Nurlisa Syuhada Mohd Radzi and Mohd Yuszaidy Mohd Yusoff found that the Ibu Soko was traditionally an elder who knew and understood the adat, with responsibilities towards individuals, society and the customary organisation.
They documented her practical duties, ranging from involvement in customary marriage practices, to receiving guests and ensuring traditions were properly observed.
The exact role can differ between luak, an important distinction at a time when interpretations of customary authority are themselves being contested.
The researchers also made a troubling observation — the Ibu Soko's role nowadays is becoming less understood, with many people no longer recognising its importance.
THE WOMEN WE DON'T SEE
Perhaps there's something familiar in that finding, even for those who never lived under Adat Perpatih.

Women everywhere have often carried the less-visible work of family and community — remembering relationships, stories and obligations, knowing who needs looking after and passing knowledge from one generation to another.
Much of it receives little recognition because it has simply come to be expected.
The Ibu Soko at least has a name for that responsibility, although her contribution is becoming less understood.
But this doesn't make Adat Perpatih a society ruled by women.
"Matrilineal" is a more accurate description than "matriarchal" because many prominent customary offices have traditionally been occupied by men.
Instead, it offers a more interesting understanding of power, where influence doesn't necessarily belong only to the person occupying the highest position.
WHAT WILL GIRLS INHERIT?
International Day of the Girl Child asks us to think about what girls need for their future, from education and equality, to safety and opportunity.
The story of the Ibu Soko invites another question: what are we teaching girls about the women who came before them?
For a girl born into an Adat Perpatih family, inheritance can mean ancestral property and a place within a maternal line stretching back for generations.
It can also mean understanding the knowledge and traditions that helped shape her community.
That's why the warning from the UKM researchers matters. If fewer people understand the Ibu Soko, there's a danger that the knowledge carried by generations of women will fade with them.
The present Negri Sembilan crisis will eventually pass, as will the names dominating today's headlines.
Long after that, the adat will still need people who know how it works and why it matters.
For generations, the Ibu Soko has been one of those people. For the girls who follow, perhaps the inheritance isn't simply knowing where they belong, but knowing enough to carry it forward.

c46893703f4038fb: There is something curious about the Football Association of Malaysia (FAM) being shortlisted for the Asian Football Confederation’s (AFC) Member Association of the Year (Gold) award.

Malaysian football has spent months grappling with questions about governance, eligibility and accountability. Now its governing body is in the running for one of the region’s top administrative honours.
The winner will be announced at the AFC’s awards ceremony in Bangkok on Nov 19. FAM shares the shortlist with the FA of Hong Kong, China Limited, and the All India Football Federation.
Perhaps FAM has done enough in certain areas to merit consideration. But what exactly does the AFC reward when it names a member association of the year?
A trophy can recognise activity. It should not substitute for scrutiny of the institution behind it.

AFC general secretary Windsor John says associations submit reports on their activities and programmes. A selection panel awards points for areas such as grassroots development, youth competitions and hosting, with three associations shortlisted in each category.
Asked how the assessment treats governance and accountability, and whether strong programme delivery can offset institutional weaknesses, Windsor said:
“The assessment takes into account a wide range of areas of football in an association. You score high in some, medium in some and probably no score in other areas.”

His answer suggests that the panel assesses associations across several areas, with varying scores. But it does not explain how much weight governance carries, or whether strong results in some categories can compensate for serious weaknesses in others.
That is a fair question about an award meant to recognise an association as a whole. It does not mean the AFC ignored governance when assessing FAM.
The criteria and their weightings should make clear how institutional accountability is judged.
For FAM, the timing makes that scrutiny unavoidable.

The naturalisation scandal has damaged confidence in Malaysian football. Fifa’s sanctions over the eligibility case exposed serious failures that the national association could not brush aside with promises to move on.
The affair raised questions not only about player eligibility, but also about the controls and oversight expected of the body responsible for the national game.

September’s extraordinary congress brought another test. The Football Association of Selangor (FAS) had objected to the eligibility of the electoral committee chairman, a concern also raised by Windsor.

FAM’s electoral code, endorsed at its June 4 congress, states that the chairperson and deputy chairperson of the electoral committee must be qualified to practise law. Yet the congress proceeded amid questions over whether the committee met that requirement.
Electoral rules protect the legitimacy of the process and the people it puts in office. An association that revises its rules must follow them, even when compliance creates an inconvenient problem.
FAM cannot demand respect for its authority while treating its own rules as obstacles to negotiate away.
Governance as part of the scorecard
There is also the AFC’s audit of FAM, which many have urged the association to release in full.

Only part of the report had been presented at the extraordinary congress in June and critics argued that the public deserved to know the full findings, warning that withholding them could fuel speculation.
Prepared by AFC deputy secretary-general Vahid Kardany, the report highlighted weaknesses in governance, accountability and organisational management.
It found that FAM’s administrative structure had not received formal executive committee approval.
It also pointed to decision-making concentrated around certain individuals and critical functions heavily dependent on them.
Weak systems for retaining institutional knowledge threatened continuity and could discourage staff from raising concerns.
These are not cosmetic flaws. A sports association needs clear lines of responsibility, systems that survive leadership changes and an environment where staff can report problems without fear.
Otherwise, the institution risks becoming dependent on a handful of people rather than sound processes.
Football development raises another pressing question.

Malaysia’s U-23, U-19 and U-16 teams have struggled to remain competitive in Asean and reach the Asian stage. Their results demand scrutiny of the system meant to prepare young Malaysians for international football.
The National Football Development Programme (NFDP) was designed to produce a technically superior generation by 2025.
Yet questions persist about its outcomes, coaching standards, talent identification and the number of players progressing to senior international football.
Malaysia has repeatedly reworked its structures while regional rivals continue to develop their talent pools. Academies, coaches and thousands of trainees are not proof of success by themselves.
How many players become professionals? How many earn senior international caps? How many fulfil the promise that justified the investment?
FAM has taken on a greater role in NFDP’s technical implementation. It now has an opportunity to show what a more focused system can deliver.
Another revamp, however, is not an achievement in itself. Results must follow.
The Malaysian Football League’s problems add to the wider unease. Salary arrears and Fifa sanctions involving clubs expose persistent weaknesses in the domestic game.

FAM and the MFL are separate bodies, so responsibility for individual cases must be established rather than casually assigned to the national association. Still, activity reports alone cannot capture the health of Malaysian football.
The AFC may have sound reasons for shortlisting FAM. The nomination does not prove the panel got it wrong, nor does it mean FAM has achieved nothing worthy of recognition.

But an award bearing the title Member Association of the Year suggests more than a tally of activities. If the AFC wants the honour to command respect, it should explain how its criteria assess both an association’s output and the way it governs itself.
FAM, too, should welcome scrutiny rather than hide behind the nomination. Recognition will mean little while questions about its elections, audit findings and development record remain unanswered.
A trophy can decorate a cabinet, but it cannot repair a governing system, develop a generation of footballers or restore public confidence.
Before anyone celebrates the award, the more important question is whether the association has done the work to earn the trust that the honour is supposed to represent.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
c5a9196aa0fbda49: ROME: Inter Milan pulled clear at the top of Serie A after coming from behind to beat Bologna 3-1 on Saturday, while Roma dispatched Genoa to jump into second and Napoli's torrid start continued with a shock defeat by Venezia.
The champions moved up to 19 points, although Lazio can go level with the leaders if they beat Juventus in Turin on Sunday.
A 2-0 win for Roma at the Stadio Olimpico moved them two points off top in second, while Napoli's loss left them a distant ninth, nine points off the title pace.
Inter came in for criticism after a disappointing midweek Champions League defeat against Club Brugge but bounced back with a comeback win ahead of the visit of Shakhtar Donetsk on Wednesday.
"Our strength is the group and the quality of the players," Inter assistant coach Aleksandar Kolarov told DAZN.
"We don't have anything to prove to anyone except ourselves. We want to be more intense with and without the ball."
Bologna started brightly as Tommaso Pobega fired them in front after 10 minutes before hitting the bar with a powerful shot.
But Inter, shorn of injured captain Lautaro Martinez after he was ruled out for a month, responded through a towering Marcus Thuram header.
Chivu's substitutions proved decisive as Carlos Augusto scored within a minute of coming on midway through the second half, before turning provider for fellow replacement Ange-Yoan Bonny late on.
- CASTRO SCORES STUNNER -
Just three days after throwing away a 3-1 lead to lose 4-3 in the dying minutes of a Champions League clash with Real Madrid, Roma responded strongly with a 2-0 win over Genoa.
With top scorer Donyell Malen suspended and several key players injured, Roma's young guns seized their chance as Santiago Castro and Emanuele Lulli scored their first goals for the club.

Both sides were denied by the woodwork in the first half, but an audacious flicked finish in a crowded box from Castro broke the deadlock after 50 minutes, before teenage wing-back Lulli made sure of the points with a close-range effort.

Genoa coach Daniele De Rossi, a celebrated former Roma player and coach, received a warm ovation from the home support but was unable to prevent counterpart Gian Piero Gasperini from claiming the 300th Serie A win of his managerial career.
- NICOLA'S DREAM DEBUT -
Venezia coach Davide Nicola masterminded a shock 1-0 win over struggling Napoli on debut as Kevin De Bruyne had a penalty saved.

Renowned survival specialist Nicola was appointed during the week to replace sacked coach Giovanni Stroppa after last season's Serie B champions failed to pick up a single point in their opening six games.
He made an instant impact as Akor Adams struck the winner early in the second half to seal Venezia's first Serie A win over Napoli since 1942.

Rested Napoli stars Rasmus Hojlund and De Bruyne came on as coach Massimiliano Allegri searched for an equaliser and Hojlund soon won a penalty, but the Belgian midfielder's spot-kick was saved by Filip Stankovic.
The Venezia goalkeeper proved decisive in the closing stages with a string of impressive saves as Napoli pushed forward in vain.

It marked a second defeat in a row for Allegri's side after their midweek Champions League loss at Villarreal, and the first time in 25 years that Napoli have lost five of their first nine games in all competitions.
Next up for Napoli is the visit of Bodo/Glimt in the Champions League on Tuesday.

"In football you get moments like this and there is only one way out: keep working seriously and professionally, be more focused and turn this disappointment into anger," Allegri told a press conference.
"It's up to us to turn this situation around, starting with the Champions League."
Napoli are ninth on 10 points, while Venezia remain bottom with three points.--AFP

0d73a911e3989e4f: KUALA LUMPUR: Examination of the Flying Doctor Service's Bo-105 helicopter engines, and a video of flames and smoke near the rear of its main gearbox captured during the helicopter's final moments near Long Lellang, Sarawak, could help investigators establish what happened, an aviation expert said.
This follows the release of the Air Accidents Investigation Bureau's (AAIB) preliminary report yesterday, which found no fault with the crashed helicopter's airframe, maintenance or pilot.

Universiti Kuala Lumpur Business School Associate Professor Major Dr Mohd Harridon Mohamed Suffian said a thorough examination of the engines was standard procedure to help investigators determine the likely cause of the incident.
"Dissection of aircraft components is needed to acquire the flight's wear-and-tear history, where it would tremendously aid investigators in their logical structuring of the incident.
"Stripping down the engine would allow each component to be scrutinised for patterns of malfunction and show whether its function was impeded during flight.
"The extent of damage could also be measured in detail, allowing investigators to pinpoint the nature of the incident," he added when asked on the preliminary report.

The AAIB report also stated that the engines had been sent to the manufacturer's facility for further examination, adding that any airworthiness implications for other engines of the same type had yet to be established.
The helicopter was fitted with two Rolls-Royce 250-C20B engines manufactured in 1989 and 1976.

On the AAIB's findings of a visible smoke trail and apparent flames near the rear of the main gearbox, as well as substantial fire and impact damage, Harridon said investigators would examine burn patterns and damaged components to determine where the fire started and how it spread.
"The rear section of the Bo-105 houses several critical components, including the exhaust system, fuel and hydraulic lines, tail rotor drive shaft and transmission system.
"Investigators will examine burn patterns to determine where the fire started and how it spread.
"Scorch marks and chemical traces on damaged components could also help establish the sequence of events. If the fire is intense, heat can spread quickly in different directions."
He added that the fire could affect the helicopter's flight controls, transmission and structural integrity, making it important to establish how it spread and whether it contributed to the crash.

"During an emergency, a rapid succession of problems may leave pilots with little time to react. Even if the initial signs appear minor, pilots must assess the situation carefully, as it could escalate into a more serious emergency."
In George Town, Transport Minister Anthony Loke said the final report on the helicopter crash was expected to be published within a year.
On Sept 8, a Flying Doctor Service Bo-105 helicopter carrying five people crashed near Long Lellang STOLport in Sarawak, killing all on board.
05d6792d8b585ed9: PORT KLANG: Only 63 per cent of Malaysia's vast maritime domain has been surveyed to modern high-density hydrographic standards, leaving 37 per cent yet to meet the benchmark.
Modern high-density hydrographic surveying refers to mapping the seabed in a comprehensive, accurate and high-resolution detail to produce nautical charts.

National Hydrographic Centre (NHC) director-general Rear Admiral Dr Najhan Md Said said surveying Malaysia's maritime domain was a major undertaking requiring extensive work to build a comprehensive picture of the seabed.
"Many people do not realise the true extent of Malaysia's maritime territory.
"In reality, our maritime domain is almost twice the size of the land mass we typically draw on maps, spanning 569,845 sq km," he told the New Sunday Times in an exclusive interview.
He said Malaysia's breakthrough came in 1998, when KD Perantau, a hydrographic survey vessel, began its service.
Switching from a single-beam to multi-beam echo sounder, the technology transition had enabled a comprehensive, accurate and higher-resolution seabed mapping process.
In 2018, the decommissioning of naval survey vessel KD Mutiara then left KD Perantau as the NHC's sole hydrographic survey ship.
Now, the ageing vessel faces limitations in covering Malaysia's vast maritime domain alone.
FLEET CONSTRAINTS
Najhan said surveying the remaining 37 per cent of the country's waters to modern high-density standards with a single ship is challenging.
"Relying on a single naval survey ship to complete high-density mapping across our entire maritime domain would take an estimated 55 years.
"Expecting one vessel to cover the waters off Peninsular Malaysia, Sabah and Sarawak is impossible," he said.

To ease the shortfall, Najhan said the National Security Council (NSC) had introduced a three-year strategic outsourcing programme, allocating RM30 million annually to lease commercial hydrographic survey ships.
"Before this NSC-funded contract took effect, modern survey coverage had not even reached 50 per cent.
"Through outsourcing, we doubled our surveying pace and raised modern coverage to 63 per cent.
"However, national security imperatives require a dedicated fleet of naval survey vessels."
TRADE AND SOVEREIGNTY
Najhan said hydrographic surveying was critical not only to navigation, but also trade, economic security and maritime sovereignty.
The stakes are high for Malaysia, whose economy depends heavily on maritime trade.
"Data from the Academy of Sciences Malaysia indicates that the nation's ocean-based 'Blue Economy' contributes 21.3 per cent to the national gross domestic product, or roughly RM300 billion in 2020.
"Yet, the public frequently overlooks the ocean's immense economic and strategic importance," he said.
Najhan added that hydrographic surveys could help authorities maintain accurate nautical charts by detecting changes in seabed depth and identifying underwater hazards.

"The absence of sufficiently detailed or updated data does not necessarily make an area unsafe to navigate, but it can limit the accuracy of information available to mariners and authorities responsible for navigational safety."
He cited the Strait of Malacca, where the NHC determines and verifies depth parameters for the global shipping standard known as Malacca Max.
"Commercial mega-vessels traversing the Strait of Malacca operate under strict draft limits of 22 to 23.
"However, heavy maritime traffic may continually shift the seabed sand dunes, making shallow areas even shallower over time.
"Global shipping lines rely on the NHC to ensure that declared draft limits on nautical charts are accurate.
"If a mega-vessel ran aground because of inaccurate depth charts, the economic fallout would extend beyond Malaysia and could bring global trade to a standstill," he said.
Malaysia's maritime depths vary widely — from 110m northwest of Pulau Perak in the northern Strait of Malacca, to 2,932m east of Permatang Ubi, Sabah, in the South China Sea.
Beyond navigation, seabed surveys provide scientific evidence of underwater features within Malaysia's maritime domain.
These support their identification and naming through international scientific processes.
However, where maritime sovereignty or jurisdiction is contested, hydrographic data must be considered alongside the relevant legal framework and other supporting evidence.
However, seabed mapping alone does not establish ownership of maritime territory.

Najhan said bathymetric data on submerged mountains, ridges and valleys was crucial when responding to foreign submissions to name undersea features through international bodies, such as the Sub-committee on Undersea Feature Names.

"Under international protocols, if a foreign entity attempts to register undersea features outside of our territorial waters but within Malaysia's Maritime Zones, we cannot simply object verbally. We must present our own verified bathymetric survey data.
"Accurate, updated hydrographic data provides Malaysia with the technical evidence needed to register native feature names and assert its maritime sovereignty."

b235cb0336d8a311: WE are flying through turbulent skies. Our air quality is awful because of open burning in Indonesia. Part of the problem stems from greedy actions by some Malaysia- and Singapore-owned giant oil palm companies.

So, as our collective anger rises against our largest neighbour for permitting this eco-tragedy, yet again, now's a perfect time to remember (or to learn for the first time) that the 18th century Scottish philosopher, economist and historian David Hume (1711-1776) took a stand against the dominant economic doctrine in Europe from the 1500s to the late 1700s.
That damaging doctrine was called mercantilism, which selfishly and incorrectly considered international trade a zero-sum game.

In Hume's 1758 essay Of the Jealousy of Trade (a summary of which is found here: www.longfinance.net/news/pamphleteers/the-jealousy-of-trade/), he explained that the mercantilist's view of any neighbouring country's commercial success being racked up at the expense of your own country's wellbeing is wrong.
By the way, does that argument remind you of the present-day rantings of Donald Trump against China, Canada and Mexico succeeding to the detriment of the United States?
Hume, in contrast, contended a nation would, on balance, benefit when its surrounding countries prosper because they could then become better trading partners and customers.

Subsequent to Hume's genius-level work almost 270 years ago, his friend and fellow Scotsman Adam Smith, the author of the 1776 seminal economics book The Wealth of Nations, pointed out the flawed mercantilist doctrine led the rulers of Europe's nation states to believe they could grow richer only by impoverishing their trading partners.
This ludicrous zero-sum view of trade is patently false, yet it gave rise to the "beggar thy neighbour" economic philosophy.

The fundamental flaw of mercantilism is that it confuses cash or money with genuine economic wealth. Both Hume and Smith correctly argued genuine wealth lies in the goods and services available to a country's residents, and the productive capacity of the country's businesses.
Sadly, bad ideas sometimes take a long time to fade into oblivion.
PROSPER THY NEIGHBOUR

More than 220 years after The Wealth of Nations was published, specifically in 1997, the year that saw the start of the Asian Financial Crisis (1997-1998), Malaysia's fourth prime minister Dr Mahathir Mohamad flipped the evil phrase "beggar thy neighbour" on its head to commendable effect.

Dr Mahathir stated, almost 30 years ago, that "prosper thy neighbour" would be a slogan that encapsulates Malaysia's view of how Asean should function. Within a year, as the Asian Financial Crisis deepened, the civilised goal of prospering Malaysia's neighbours within that successful economic grouping was a clear-sighted Malaysia-driven foreign policy doctrine in its interactions with other Asean members.
Asean expanded its membership roll to 11 countries with the addition of Timor-Leste a year ago, on Oct 26, at the 47th Asean Summit in Kuala Lumpur, under Malaysia's then chairmanship.
Timor-Leste's inclusion was the first expansion of Asean's membership since 1999's inclusion of Cambodia.
We have repeatedly seen that the building of figurative — and sometimes even literal — bridges is a better way to promote peace, harmony, amity and prosperity than putting up walls.

And speaking of administrations adept at raising walls, be they figurative or literal ones, the tedious fallout from the US and Israel's attacks on Iran that began on Feb 28 continues to gather destructive momentum.
REASONS TO FRET

A few days before I finished writing this column, Houthi attacks on Riyadh in Saudi Arabia caused multiple fatalities and injured more than 300 people. Those of us situated far from such insane violence probably felt relatively safe.

Yet the bad air filling our lungs and causing those of us with respiratory illnesses to suffer more than usual violates our fundamental human right to clean and breathable air. I suspect spikes in lung cancer over the coming decades will be tied to this eco-crisis.
So, with so many bad things assailing us, who will be held responsible? Sigh! I am pessimistic enough to assume no one.
There are, of course, other reasons to fret:

The global economic impact of stirring the hornet's nest that is Iran means that the high price of fuel is now embedded into the fabric of our interconnected global economy. I have never made a secret of my abysmal opinion of the current US leadership.
In addition to destabilising the Middle East, round after round of Trump's import tariffs are adding unwanted friction to the engine of global trade.

So, while most of us feel helpless as we are swept along by chaotic currents of change driven by local corporate greed, American hubris and violence that is spreading like a metastasising cancer across pockets of the world, what should we do?
1. Heed global developments;
2. Remain optimistic about being alive in a safe corner of Earth;
3. Pray for the current crop of sub-par world leaders to be replaced by wiser people;
4. Tighten our belts to reduce expenses to save more money;
5. Channel a slice of those savings into well-chosen investments;
6. Grow personal wealth over decades; and, finally
7. Give or bequeath some of that compounded wealth to try and create a better world tomorrow.

9c172c70ae8ccff2: OSLO, Oct 18 — Chinese-made cars filmed sensitive information during a Norwegian military exercise, including access codes at secure sites and officials’ comings and goings, raising concerns about the risks posed by connected vehicles.

During a security exercise at Oslo airport on September 14-18, soldiers waiting in their vehicles and tapping on the onboard screens discovered videos recorded by the cars’ cameras, the Dagens Næringsliv (DN) newspaper reported.
The recordings showed who was getting in and out of the cars, the routes taken and even the codes used to open gates or doors to military facilities.
In its report three weeks after the exercise, DN said the recordings came from rental vehicles — at least two of them Deepal cars made by Chinese state-controlled automaker Changan.
The vehicles were supplied to the army by Hertz Norge, which is indirectly owned by Chinese automotive group Geely.
“Yes, soldiers from the Home Guard found videos from the vehicles’ sensors stored in their systems,” Lieutenant Colonel Per Gunnar Grosberghaugen, Norwegian Home Guard spokesman, confirmed to AFP.
It was not known whether the recordings had been shared with a third party, particularly in China, but the officer could not rule out the possibility.
The case highlights a paradox: while Europe’s armies are strengthening their defences against espionage and hybrid threats, the vehicles they use can collect sensitive information.
Even after discovering the leaks, the military continued using the vehicles until the end of the exercise because there were no alternatives, and the soldiers deleted the videos, DN reported.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Chinese-made Deepal cars rented for a Norwegian military exercise reportedly recorded sensitive information, raising security concerns. — AFP pic

Judging that a general ban on Chinese-made vehicles would be disproportionate to the potential security benefits, the military said it preferred security procedures tailored to each site, including possible local bans on vehicles equipped with cameras and sensors, regardless of their origin.
Hertz Norge stressed that it complies with Norwegian and European regulations.
“Our customers’ data is safe with us,” Hallvard Nerbovik, its marketing and communications director, told AFP.

“No personal data related to our rentals is shared with car manufacturers, our owners or other third parties without explicit legal grounds,” he added, without specifying whether the onboard videos might have been transferred.
Changan did not respond to AFP’s questions.
App spies

Last year, tests carried out for Oslo’s Ruter public transport authority revealed that Chinese manufacturer Yutong could theoretically remotely immobilise its electric buses through their “over-the-air” update system.
Norway could one day use the buses to evacuate the population during an emergency.
Ruter has since introduced mechanisms to monitor and delay incoming signals to control updates, it said.
Modern vehicles are not the only potential Trojan horses.
Smartwatches and fitness apps such as Strava, popular with joggers, can also expose sensitive military information.
In 2018, data published by Strava made it possible to identify military sites and soldiers’ routes, particularly in Afghanistan and Syria.

In March, French newspaper Le Monde was able to locate the French aircraft carrier Charles de Gaulle in almost real time in the eastern Mediterranean, thanks to a sailor on board who was using the app.
The Norwegian National Security Authority (NSM) said modern vehicles are “rolling computers that collect information”.
“We don’t know for sure where the information is sent or what it’s used for,” NSM official Andreas Skjold-Lorange told AFP.

The organisation, which is responsible for minimising strategic risks, including digital threats, said Norway should be wary not only of the data collected but also of excessive dependence on a single country.
This is particularly concerning if that country does not cooperate with Norway on security matters.
“If we become too dependent on services or products from a given country, that makes us vulnerable, whatever that country may be,” Skjold-Lorange warned. — AFP
