The revamp focused on restoring the building’s appearance while preserving its architectural identity.

Istana Budaya deputy director-general (operations) Johan Cruyff Mohd Johari Md Nordin told Malay Mail the work concentrated on repairing worn areas and bringing approximately 90 per cent of the building back to its original 1999 condition.
“We have since refreshed and rejuvenated the interior and surrounding areas.
“While the restoration may not be 100 per cent complete, we believe the building is now about 90 per cent restored to its former condition.
“We want visitors, especially those who have been here before, to feel that Istana Budaya has regained much of its original appearance.
“We are grateful for the support we have received to carry out these improvements while preserving the building’s character,” he said.
Decades in the making
The story of Istana Budaya began in 1964, when it was first proposed as part of plans to establish Malaysia’s National Cultural Centre.
Construction of the National Theatre, then known as Panggung Negara, began in July 1995.
The building was completed in December 1998 and officially renamed Istana Budaya on September 15, 1999.
Today, it stands as one of Malaysia’s leading performing arts venues, hosting productions that bring together artists, performers and audiences under one roof.
Built for the big shows
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Renovation works continue on the exterior of Istana Budaya in Kuala Lumpur on October 14, 2026. — Picture by Raymond Manuel
Johan said the venue was specifically designed to accommodate performances that highlight the beauty, aesthetics and diversity of the performing arts.
“It was specifically designed to present performances that showcase beauty, aesthetics and the performing arts.
“Even the building itself reflects a combination of Malaysian cultural elements, and the performances presented here are closely connected to that artistic identity.

“Unlike commercial venues that operate primarily for profit, Istana Budaya also aims to provide opportunities for local productions to stage their work here, subject to certain conditions and guidelines.
“We want to give local artists and production companies opportunities to perform, particularly in theatre and concerts,” he said.

Johan added that the venue was particularly suited to large-scale musicals and theatre productions because of its specialised stage facilities, including an overhead rigging system and fly bars that allow scenery and other stage elements to move during performances.
These facilities enable production teams to incorporate elaborate sets, complex stage designs and technical effects that may be difficult to accommodate elsewhere.
“For productions that need these capabilities, Istana Budaya is often a preferred venue because of what its stage can offer,” he added.
More than a concert hall
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
An overhead view of an art installation displayed in the foyer of Istana Budaya in Kuala Lumpur on October 14, 2026. — Picture by Raymond Manuel
Istana Budaya continues to serve as a national platform for theatre, musicals and orchestral performances, supporting local and international productions while promoting Malaysia’s cultural heritage.
Johan said its emphasis on theatre and stage productions distinguished it from other venues, which focus more heavily on concerts.
“We also have programmes featuring the National Symphony Orchestra and traditional Malaysian orchestral music, as well as musical theatre performances accompanied by orchestral arrangements.
“Our role is to continue providing opportunities for artists and production companies while preserving and promoting Malaysia’s artistic and cultural heritage,” he said.
Calling first-timers
As Istana Budaya looks towards the future, attracting younger audiences and first-time visitors remains an important priority.
Johan said the venue aims to achieve this through consistent programming, including children’s theatre, musicals and productions catering to different interests and age groups.
“Attracting new audiences is important to us.
“While we appreciate those who have supported Istana Budaya for many years, we cannot depend only on our existing audience.
“We need to introduce the venue to people who may never have attended a performance here before.
“Our aim is to build a consistent programme from year to year so that audiences know there will always be something worth coming to see.
“Ultimately, we want to preserve the legacy of Istana Budaya while ensuring that new generations continue to appreciate theatre and the performing arts,” he concluded.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Istana Budaya deputy director-general (operations) Johan Cruyff Mohd Johari Md Nordin. — Pictures courtesy of Johan Cruyff Mohd Johari Md Nordin
What’s next

The next performances scheduled at Istana Budaya include Konsert Rindu Sumayyah – Hijjaz 3 Dekad on October 17, followed by Teater Muzikal Kanak-Kanak: Pengembaraan Sang Kancil from November 13 to 15.
The Istana Budaya team said both productions had recorded strong ticket sales, with tickets reportedly nearing a sell-out.
As the curtains rise once again, Istana Budaya’s challenge extends beyond restoring a landmark building.
It is about ensuring the stage continues to inspire audiences, support local talent, and keep Malaysia’s performing arts alive for generations to come.
dec128071537b64c: BANGKOK, Oct 18 — Rising energy and fertiliser costs are hitting smallholder farmers and driving up prices of agricultural commodities, fueling fears of a global food crisis, the head of the UN agriculture development fund told AFP.

Global agricultural prices jumped 13 per cent in the third quarter of the year, according to the International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD), which warned a “global food crisis is looming”.
The surge in energy prices due to conflict in the Middle East has sparked a sharp increase in the cost of fertilisers and fuel this year, driving up agricultural production and transport costs.

“Over the next six to nine months, we will see continued increases related to food prices, but also I would say even inflation in terms of food, which will impact most of the populations that actually can afford it less,” IFAD President Alvaro Lario told AFP in an interview on Tuesday.
Already, “almost one in three people in the world cannot afford a healthy diet”, Lario said.
“So I think the costs of a healthy diet, which means an increased cost on legumes, on vegetables, on meat, is just having a big impact on what people can afford to consume.”
Food insecurity affects around 260 million people worldwide, accord to UN figures.

Because food accounts for a significant portion of household budgets in developing countries, price hikes are felt acutely there, noted Lario, speaking on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank meetings in Bangkok.

Smallholder farmers — who account for one-third of global food production, and up to 70 per cent in many developing nations — are the most severely affected by the energy shock, according to IFAD, and were especially vulnerable to rising fertiliser prices.
“In the very short term, there is very little that governments can do. They can subsidise, for example, the price of fertiliser input... or fuel through subsidies,” he said.
G7 nations pledged on Thursday to mobilise US$2.5 billion (RM10.2 billion) to assist countries at risk of food insecurity, with a specific focus on fertilisers.
Lario called for longer term solutions to address underlying vulnerabilities.
“The important lesson is that these shocks will continue over time. So the most important lesson is that actually we should be building the resilience for the next three to five years,” he said.
“You need to diversify the type of value chains and crops that you are currently self-sufficient, and food security becomes now in many countries a matter of national security,” he added.
Lario also flagged the impact of climate change on small-scale farmers, who received less than one per cent of allocated global climate finance.

“It’s very clear that farming... starts with soil health, and it starts with availability of water, and both are very much affected by climate change. What we need to really do is to try to attract investments... in climate adaptation,” he said. — AFP
bd32b82931f1bfc4: NAIDIRI, Oct 18 — It had been decades since sharks last patrolled the reef off Fiji’s Naidiri Village, but they returned this year after a community-led effort to protect fish stocks and plant thousands of corals.

Manoa Duwai convinced his village in 2009 to establish a protected area within its customary fishing grounds on Fiji’s Coral Coast after growing concerned about the dwindling number and size of fish he was catching.
At the time, he was lucky to catch a fish as big as his palm.
“Man, imagine 10, 15, 20 years to come, what we going to have,” Duwai said after a fishing trip one night yielded only tiny, juvenile fish.
“What type of species are we going to have left in our customary fishing ground? We have to do something,” he said.
Duwai approached village elders with a proposal to protect part of their fishing grounds, initially designating a 30-by-40-metre area within the reef.
It did not take long for the plan to bear fruit, with larger fish finding a home in the protected area before spreading into neighbouring waters.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Fish swim among healthy coral at Naidiri Marine Biodiversity Park in Fiji on October 5, 2026, as community-led conservation efforts help restore the reef and replenish fish stocks. — AFP pic
Over time, the village expanded the protected area to 280 by 240 metres.
It is now flanked by a similarly sized area villagers call “the fridge”, which they temporarily close to allow fish stocks to recover.
Duwai’s vision of a thriving marine habitat that could sustain his village of 147 people has since earned global praise, with academics and charities seeking his insights.
Youth ownership
Joseva Kunagado, 21, leads Naidiri Village’s youth in preserving the health of its protected marine area.
The village formed a youth group in 2011 to manage what they call the “tabu area”, with members leading efforts to plant corals and encourage a healthy ecosystem.
In 2023 alone, the group planted 18,000 corals and 10,000 mangroves.
“When we started this we were small kids,” Kunagado told AFP.
“We used to take some barrels, cut it in half, tie the rope on it, and we pull it. We have to walk for maybe 20 minutes to get corals, come back and plant.
“From that to today, we can say that we are very happy on the work that we have done because we’ve seen big changes.”
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Healthy coral grows in the waters of Naidiri Marine Biodiversity Park in Fiji on October 5, 2026, where villagers are restoring the reef to protect marine life and fish stocks. — AFP pic

The protected area Kunagado and his friends have nurtured is now bursting with corals and home to hundreds of heat-resistant “super corals” that could help protect the village from rising sea temperatures.
Sharks have also started returning to the area.
Far from being frightened, Duwai said he shed a tear when they came back this year.
“When things started to come back, different types of fish species, invertebrates, all back, I’m like the most happiest person in the whole village,” Duwai said.
Kunagado said he had seen sharks on the morning of AFP’s visit, smiling with pride at the state of the fishery.
“We didn’t see this coming, like having tourists coming, having researchers, students from universities coming. So we’re proud of the work.”
Super corals
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Villagers watch the construction of a new house on higher ground near Naidiri Marine Biodiversity Park in Fiji on October 5, 2026, as coastal communities face growing climate change risks. — AFP pic
Researchers are interested not only in how Naidiri Village has protected its marine ecosystem but also in specific corals showing extraordinary heat resistance.
Duwai said water temperatures reached up to 39°C during a heatwave earlier this year, causing widespread bleaching among the thousands of planted corals.
At those temperatures, most of the corals should have died, but Duwai said 20 per cent survived and are considered “super corals”.
“The only corals we have here now are the ones who survived this 38, 39 degrees.”
Duwai said Naidiri is now transplanting its heat-resistant corals to deeper, cooler waters near the capital Suva to help protect them against future heatwaves. — AFP
87d58f87d80b5674: WASHINGTON, Oct 18 — This week in US politics, a candidate with the flu fell victim to a false rumour, a campaign ad aired in the wrong city, and packages with suspicious powder were mailed to election officials.
Here are some campaign highlights compiled by AFP ahead of the November 3 US midterm elections.
Real flu, false rumour
James Talarico, the Democratic Senate candidate from Texas, denied rumours that he had been secretly hospitalised in an Ohio psychiatric facility, calling it “the craziest thing I’ve ever heard.”
The 37-year-old candidate, who is neck-and-neck in a race in the Republican stronghold, actually had the flu, causing him to withdraw from campaign events for about a week.
Online conspiracy theories posted on social media by prominent right-wing users claimed Talarico was at an Ohio clinic because he had a mental health crisis.
The posts were amplified by his Republican opponent, Ken Paxton, and tech billionaire Elon Musk.
The facility in question confirmed that the candidate had never been there.
Talarico pointed out that he had participated in campaign events via videoconference while suffering from the flu and also attended a concert in Dallas during the time in question.
The episode was “a good reminder that you can’t believe everything you read on the internet,” Talarico said.
Which Portland?
A Republican campaign committee spent over US$25,000 (RM102,000) to run an ad against a Democratic candidate — in the wrong state.
The ad was shown in Portland, Oregon, not in Portland, Maine, on the other side of the country.
The advertising agency has since acknowledged its mistake and refunded the money.
The team of Democratic Senate candidate Troy Jackson, targeted by these ads, was quick to seize the opportunity.
His Republican opponent Susan Collins and her allies “are so out of touch with Maine, they apparently can’t find it on a map,” a spokesperson quipped to The New York Times.
Trump showers voters with money
Just weeks before the midterm elections, Donald Trump has found a way to try to address some US voter concerns about the cost of living: handing out cash.

In addition to a US$5,000 “dividend” he promised to pay to every voter if Republicans win the election — a measure whose legality and funding are questionable at best — his administration has begun sending US$500 checks to nearly one million Americans.
The sum has been touted as reimbursement for Obamacare health insurance costs that were allegedly too high under Joe Biden’s presidency.
The Republican billionaire also announced US$90 payments to more than 20 million seniors to offset Medicare contributions, the US health insurance program for those over 65.
“If you want to BUY midterm votes, maybe start by not gutting everyone’s health care in the first place,” suggested Democratic Senator Ron Wyden.
Suspicious substances
Authorities are investigating a series of letters containing suspicious substances sent to congressional and election offices in several states, US media reported.
Packages containing white powder led to the evacuation of election offices in Louisiana and Oklahoma this week.
Six workers in Democratic Representative Ritchie Torres in New York were exposed to white powder found in a letter on Friday, CBS News reported. The substance was determined to be harmless.

The mailings are reminiscent of other incidents during previous elections, when election offices received letters containing a white powder and, in some cases, traces of fentanyl, a potentially deadly opioid. — AFP
31fd2b523077d73f: BRASÍLIA, Oct 18 — Deforestation of the Brazilian Amazon has fallen to its lowest level in nearly 40 years, according to figures released Friday, in welcome news for leftist incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva days before a presidential runoff.

Between August 2025 and July 2026, 3,335 square kilometres of forest were cleared, a decline of nearly 42 per cent over the previous year and the lowest level since records began in 1988, official statistics showed.
“It’s an absolutely stratospheric drop... it’s like a dream,” Environment Minister Joao Paulo Capobianco told a press conference in the capital Brasilia.
The data was also hailed by Lula, whom polls show running neck-and-neck with conservative senator Flavio Bolsonaro ahead of the October 25 runoff.

Lula, a veteran left-wing leader, returned to office promising to end unlawful forest clearance by ranchers and illegal miners, which had soared under his far-right predecessor Jair Bolsonaro, the father of Flavio.
“Our goal is to achieve zero illegal deforestation by 2030,” he reiterated Friday on X, after the deforestation data was released.
Brazil is home to approximately 60 per cent of the world’s largest rainforest, which plays a crucial role in absorbing greenhouse gases responsible for global warming.
The official deforestation rate is measured using the “Prodes” satellite system, operated by the National Institute for Space Research.
Deforestation has been steadily decreasing in the Amazon since 2022, with a cumulative drop of 71.2 per cent over the four years since Lula was elected.
The figures, which have been attributed to greater monitoring and stiffer penalties for illegal logging, mark a dramatic about-turn since Jair Bolsonaro’s presidency, from 2019 to 2022.
The Amazon lost around 11,600 square kilometres of forest under his watch — almost 60 per cent more than in the previous four years, official figures show.
Flavio Bolsonaro has praised his father, who is serving a 27-year sentence for coup plotting, for having opposed what he calls a “radical environmental agenda.”
At the same time, he has proposed treating the environment as a “strategic asset” and pledged to end “illegal deforestation” by 2029.
There was also good news from the vast Cerrado savanna south of the Amazon, where deforestation fell to its lowest levels since records there began in 2001.
From August 2025 to July 2026, 5,517 square kilometres of native vegetation were destroyed, representing a reduction of almost 24 per cent in a year.
Marcio Astrini, executive secretary of the Climate Observatory, a network of over 100 civil society groups, praised the figures as a “historic victory.”
“This demonstrates that Brazil plays a leading role in protecting forests and that, with political will, it is possible to curb chainsaws and greenhouse gas emissions,” he said in a statement. — AFP
1fb61941d5b43ee1: From Jason Chuah
Malaysia has staked a good deal of its economic future on a few dozen strands of fibre lying on the seabed.

More than 20 international submarine cables land at over 10 stations in this country, and with its digital economy blueprint the government aims to make Malaysia Southeast Asia’s leading destination for cable landings.
They carry almost all of our international data, including the traffic behind Johor’s data-centre boom. Yet the criminal law that protects them was written for the telegraph.

The only provision aimed squarely at cable damage is Section 431A of the Penal Code. It punishes mischief by cutting or injuring “any electric telegraph cable, wire, line, post, instrument or apparatus for signalling”, with up to two years imprisonment or a fine.
The provision has three serious weaknesses.
First, it requires mischief, meaning intention or knowledge that loss or damage is likely.
A ship that drags its anchor across a cable through carelessness might well fall outside it, and so does one that merely claims carelessness.
That is exactly the explanation offered in almost every recent incident, from the Baltic Sea to the Taiwan Strait. Proving mischief will not be easy.
Second, it stops at the territorial sea. The Penal Code applies to offences committed “within Malaysia”, which takes in our 12-nautical-mile territorial waters but no more.
Its extraterritorial provisions reach Malaysian citizens and Malaysian-registered ships, but not a foreign crew aboard a foreign vessel.
Most of a cable’s route lies further out, in the exclusive economic zone and on the continental shelf.
The Exclusive Economic Zone Act 1984 and the Continental Shelf Act 1966 regulate the laying of cables but do not make damaging them an offence.
A foreign ship that cuts a cable 30 miles off our coast commits, so far as Malaysian criminal law is concerned, no offence at all.

Third, the language is out of date. Modern fibre-optic cables probably count as “apparatus for signalling”. The planned subsea power link carrying a gigawatt of Sarawak’s electricity to Singapore almost certainly does not.

International law regrettably does not fill the gap. The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), which Malaysia ratified in 1996, is better at protecting the freedom to lay cables than the cables themselves.

Article 113 obliges states to criminalise the wilful or culpably negligent breaking of cables, but only by ships flying their own flags and their own nationals. Malaysia’s law, which ignores negligence, arguably does not meet that obligation.
Worse, Article 97 says that when an “incident of navigation” occurs beyond the territorial sea, only the flag state may prosecute the master or crew.

Nor does it give any right to board a ship suspected of damaging a cable. So when a vessel flying a flag of convenience drags its anchor through a cable in our EEZ, UNCLOS refers us to a flag state that has neither the means nor the will to act.

This is not hypothetical. In May, the director-general of the Malaysian Maritime Enforcement Agency acknowledged that tankers carrying Iranian-linked oil choose to transfer cargo about 70km off Johor precisely to “exploit jurisdictional gaps”.
One monitoring group counted 42 such transfers there in about 10 weeks. They operate in the very waters where Malaysia’s criminal law stops.
The United Kingdom faced the same problem and offers a useful model. Its principal offence dates from 1885 but was long ago extended to the continental shelf.
In May 2026 the British government went further, announcing a new criminal framework covering damage that is intentional or reckless, with tougher penalties.
Malaysia should do three things.
First, replace section 431A with a dedicated offence covering intentional, reckless and culpably negligent damage to telecommunications and power cables, with penalties that reflect what is at stake.
Second, extend that offence expressly to the EEZ and continental shelf, applying to any person, whatever their nationality or flag.
Third, draft it with the enforcement problem in mind.
In August 2026 the Helsinki Court of Appeal revived the prosecution of the crew of the Eagle S, a shadow-fleet tanker accused of cutting cables in the Gulf of Finland.

The court held that the offence was committed where its effects were felt, in Finland. It also held that deliberate anchor-dragging is not a mere “incident of navigation” that UNCLOS reserves to the flag state.

The coastal state suffering the cable damage can therefore have criminal jurisdiction. A Malaysian statute that locates the offence where the damage is suffered, and defines it accordingly, would put our courts on the same footing.
Malaysia, which has long taken a robust view of coastal-state rights, is better placed than the great maritime powers to take this step. What it lacks is a law fit for the age of fibre.
Jason Chuah is chairman of the Board of Research at the Maritime Institute of Malaysia and an FMT reader.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
104410d7c32c5685: PETALING JAYA: The dialysis patient slipped on a long-sleeved shirt. There was nothing particularly unusual about it at first glance, save for the zipper running down one sleeve. She was told by the eager university students around her that this simple design feature was going to make her dialysis a little easier.

And then she noticed it … the personalised letter that came with it. “She teared up when she read the message and she said that this is really meaningful. She even gave me a hug!” recalled Navena Arumugam, 21, a member of the newly launched student-led social enterprise Aperta.

The long-sleeved shirt, named Aperta Libre, has a specialised zipper running from mid-bicep to wrist, allowing healthcare workers to reach medical access points without patients having to roll up their sleeves or remove their clothes.

“We were in touch with an oncologist and a surgeon and they told us how sometimes it is a struggle for dialysis patients to pull up their sleeves entirely during treatment,” explained Anna Natasha, 19, an Aperta team member.
“Some Muslim women feel uncomfortable fully rolling up their sleeves. And clinics and dialysis centres can be very cold. So, that’s why we thought this is something for us to address,” she added.
Aperta was created as part of the Youth Leadership Academy 2026, a programme that develops young leaders through leadership training, mentorship and social-impact projects.
The Aperta team consists of Teo Yan Khai, Anna, Navena, Loi Yong Xiang, and Natalie Ho, all from different colleges and universities.

“There's not much that can compare to the feeling that you’re actually helping people,” said team leader Teo, 22. “It's not really about making money or about selling things, but it's more about identifying a genuine need.”

Teo, a biomedical science student, shared that his team’s initial idea was a stoma-bag, which was rejected after consultations with medical professionals. One consultant surgeon told them bluntly that it had no product-market fit.
“It was very demoralising,” Teo said. “For us to kill an idea that we were working on, we were so invested in. That was a very big challenge.”
Instead of giving up, they went back to the patients, and Aperta Libre, which sells for RM55, was birthed.
Their latest feedback has already pushed Aperta to think ahead, including possible designs for central venous catheters and children who use PICC (peripherally inserted central catheter) lines.
They are also looking at working with sewing services that employ B40 women, allowing the social impact to extend beyond the patients who wear the clothes.

The team’s visits to clinics and dialysis centres have also produced encouraging feedback. Navena, a financial economics student, said even nurses who had worked for 13 years in the dialysis system had never seen clothing specifically designed for dialysis patients.
“Most of the patients just DIY their shirts. They just tear it and then they use it during their treatment,” she said.
But getting patients to trust a new product has not been easy. Loi, a psychology student, said convincing people has been one of their biggest challenges.
“Sometimes you might face critics who say you're just selling a product, creating business, you just want to take money from us,” the 23-year-old said. “But in fact, it's not.”
Thankfully, the students found great support from nurses who recommended the shirts to patients.
“One of our customers bought the shirt for her husband and she was like, ‘I'll make my husband the ambassador for you. Don't worry.’” said Navena.

The team knows that Aperta is still young but they have already learnt that solving a problem means being open to uncomfortable feedback, abandoning a much-cherished idea and spending time with the people they hope to help.
For Teo, that process has given the project its true meaning.

“If we were not on the ground doing door-to-door, we wouldn't have that conviction and belief,” he said. “Our current door-to-door efforts getting positive feedback has bolstered our confidence in what we are doing.”
And sometimes, that confidence comes in the form of a hug from someone who simply wanted to feel comfortable and cared for while receiving treatment.
Follow Aperta on Instagram.
66106a5b6b1dc664: KUALA LUMPUR: Enam wanita menerima pengiktirafan Yayasan Tuanku Fauziah (YTF) atas sumbangan dalam bidang teknologi, penyelidikan dan inovasi menerusi Anugerah Wanita dalam Teknologi YTF 2026.

Dalam kategori senior, Aini Ideris memenangi hadiah utama RM30,000, manakala Suraya Abdul Rashid dan Haniza Yon masing-masing menerima RM10,000 bagi Anugerah Bintang Harapan dan Anugerah Pengubah Industri.
Bagi kategori junior, Serene Lock Sow Mun membawa pulang hadiah utama RM15,000, sementara Marlinda Ab Rahman dan Afzan Ahmad Zaini masing-masing menerima RM5,000 bagi dua anugerah khas berkenaan.
Majlis penganugerahan dan makan malam di The Ritz-Carlton, malam tadi, berlangsung sempena ulang tahun ke-80 Raja Perempuan Perlis Tuanku Tengku Fauziah Tengku Abdul Rashid.

Turut berangkat Raja Perlis Tuanku Syed Sirajuddin Jamalullail, Raja Muda Perlis Tuanku Syed Faizuddin Putra Jamalullail dan Raja Puan Muda Perlis Tuanku Lailatul Shahreen Akashah Khalil, yang juga pengerusi YTF.
Tuanku Lailatul Shahreen bertitah, YTF komited membuka peluang dan mengangkat martabat wanita Malaysia yang berjaya dalam bidang berimpak tinggi.

“Kejayaan penerima ini adalah bukti jelas kepakaran wanita tempatan bukan sahaja setanding di peringkat global, malah menjadi tunjang utama dalam memacu pertumbuhan ekonomi berasaskan digital dan teknologi negara,” titah baginda.

Sementara itu, Presiden dan Ketua Pegawai Eksekutif Malaysian Industry-Government Group for High Technology (Might), Rushdi Abdul Rahim, berkata anugerah tersebut bukan sahaja mengiktiraf pencapaian individu, malah bertujuan mendorong lebih ramai wanita menceburi bidang sains, teknologi dan inovasi.
“Kami berharap pengiktirafan ini menjadi pemangkin inspirasi kepada generasi muda wanita untuk terus meneroka bidang sains, teknologi, dan inovasi,” katanya.
YTF ditubuhkan Tuanku Tengku Fauziah di Kuala Lumpur pada 19 April 2004 dengan moto Women in Search of Excellence (WiSE).
9b0564ac9f78a785: JERUSALEM: Israeli settlers on Saturday attacked a convoy of European diplomats in the West Bank and beat up a visiting French mayor, witnesses said, a day after an American photographer was similarly set upon as violence escalates ahead of bitterly fought elections.

The 78-year-old mayor said masked settlers yelled defamatory comments about France, kicked him and hit him with iron bars as he joined Palestinian olive farmers in the West Bank alongside the top French and Belgian representatives in Jerusalem and Polish diplomats.

"I think that if settlers are behaving like this, there is a tolerance on the part of the Israeli government," Bernard Baudoux, mayor of the northern French town of Aulnoye-Aymeries, told AFP after he was attacked.
"The whole world needs to know what's happening," he said. "For me, I'll go back to my country and everything will be fine. Those who continue to suffer the most are those who are here."
Baudoux, who was wearing a sash with the French tricolour, was seen collapsed on the side of the car after the attack but he did not need hospital care.

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said in a statement that Israel must "urgently halt criminal violence" and arrest those responsible for attacking Baudoux, with his Belgian counterpart issuing a similar call.
- ELECTION SEASON -
The attack came just one day after settlers beat an American photographer for The Washington Post, who was in moderate condition on Saturday after suffering broken vertebrae.
Israel's foreign ministry condemned the attack on the diplomats and Israeli police promised to open an investigation.
But Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is seeking to shore up support from the fiercely pro-settlement far-right in the Oct 27 election, instead alleged a "smear" campaign against settlers.
Netanyahu said the diplomats should have coordinated their movements with the Israeli military and pointed out that Baudoux is a communist known for supporting the Palestinian cause.
"We urge caution before drawing conclusions" about the attacks, Netanyahu's office said in a statement.

His main rival in the elections, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, strongly criticised Netanyahu over the violence, saying it was "burning away the little legitimacy the State of Israel still possesses."
The attacks are "Jewish terrorism, under the auspices of the Israeli government", Eisenkot said.
- ATTACKS ON CULTURAL SYMBOL -
Baudoux, the mayor, said he had come to the town of Taybeh, a Christian stronghold, along with his local pastor from France to sign a goodwill agreement.
He was attacked just as he joined the harvest as a symbolic gesture with the Palestinians, for whom olives are an important cultural symbol.

Extremist Israelis have issued calls to stop the Palestinians' annual harvest after months of escalating attacks in which settlers have stolen land and property. There has also been violence against Israelis, with a Palestinian shooting a settler dead last month.
Bashar Fawadleh, a priest in Taybeh, said settlers had already attacked the harvest and snatched olives before beating the mayor.
"One person was hit in the head and needed stitches. They also beat up an older lady in her 70s after insulting her with very bad words," the pastor told AFP.
The West Bank violence has shocked much of the world, with Britain spearheading economic sanctions that in turn led Israel to close the British consulate in Jerusalem.
Netanyahu had also sought to throw doubt on the circumstances behind the beating Friday of the photographer, Heidi Levine, suggesting that Palestinians and "far-left" activists caused trouble.

But President Isaac Herzog, who holds a mostly ceremonial role, took the initiative Saturday to call Levine in the hospital, saying the attack was "outrageous and shocking" and weighed on his conscience.
US Ambassador Mike Huckabee said the beating was "a despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards", and demanded Israel prosecute and jail the assailants.

Israel Gantz, head of an umbrella settler group, blamed recent incidents on "groups of provocateurs and terrorists" but implicitly acknowledged some Israelis' responsibility, saying that they harmed the settlers' cause.
Settlers earlier this month also beat up AFP photographer Jaafar Ashtiyeh as he covered the olive harvest tensions, fracturing several of his ribs and stealing his camera.
Netanyahu's government has ramped up approval of West Bank settlements, which are illegal under international law.
Some 500,000 Israelis live in the West Bank, which Israel seized in 1967, alongside three million Palestinians.--AFP

ef72725917af3aa3: BRUSSELS: Belgian police fired tear gas and water cannon to disperse hundreds of demonstrators in Brussels and Liege taking part in cost-of-living protests on Saturday, similar to violent rallies in neighbouring France.

74d2de2712942262: MANGROVES do more than line the edges of Malaysia's coast. Their tangled roots help hold shorelines together; their dense habitats shelter marine life and their ability to store carbon makes them an important part of the fight against climate change.

At Kuala Selangor Nature Park, these natural defences received a helping hand recently when 40 employees from Hektar REIT's asset and property management companies joined a conservation effort to plant 200 mangrove saplings under the guidance of the Malaysian Nature Society (MNS).

The exercise was intended to do more than put young trees into the ground. By helping to rehabilitate degraded areas within the park, the initiative contributes to the longer-term work of restoring a fragile ecosystem on which coastal biodiversity and marine life depend.

Mangroves are particularly valuable because their benefits extend well beyond the shoreline. They help reduce coastal erosion, provide breeding and nursery grounds for fish and other marine species, and support fisheries that sustain the livelihoods of coastal communities. They are also highly effective carbon sinks, with the capacity to store up to four times more carbon per hectare than most tropical forests.
ENVIRONMENTAL STEWARDSHIP

While 200 saplings represent a modest contribution to the wider conservation effort, their potential impact will depend on how well they survive and grow. MNS will continue to monitor and care for the trees, a crucial step in ensuring that the planting translates into lasting environmental benefits.
For Zainal Iskandar, executive director and chief executive officer of Hektar Asset Management, the initiative reflects the importance of turning sustainability commitments into practical action.

Says Zainal: "We believe meaningful sustainability efforts should translate into practical action on the ground. Through our collaboration with MNS, this initiative contributes to mangrove restoration efforts that support carbon sequestration, protect coastlines, conserve biodiversity and strengthen the resilience of coastal ecosystems."

He adds that environmental stewardship remained an important part of Hektar REIT's broader sustainability journey, with the organisation continuing to identify initiatives that encourage its employees to take a more active role in caring for the environment.

The planting also highlights the work of MNS, which manages and operates Kuala Selangor Nature Park on behalf of the Selangor state government. Beyond habitat conservation and research, the society conducts environmental education and community-based programmes to raise awareness of the country's natural heritage and the need to protect it.
RESILIENT ECOSYSTEM

Such efforts are increasingly relevant as coastal ecosystems face mounting pressures from environmental degradation and climate change. Restoring mangroves is one nature-based approach that can help address these challenges, although the long-term success of any planting programme depends on suitable conditions, continued monitoring and the survival of the trees.

The initiative aligns with three United Nations Sustainable Development Goals: Climate Action (SDG 13), Life Below Water (SDG 14) and Life on Land (SDG 15), reflecting the links between climate resilience, healthy marine environments and biodiversity conservation.

For Hektar REIT, the activity forms part of its wider environmental, social and governance agenda. For the park, the more immediate task is to ensure the young mangroves take root and become part of a healthier, more resilient ecosystem.

Ultimately, the value of the exercise will not be measured by the number of saplings planted on a single day, but by how many survive to strengthen the coastline and provide shelter for the wildlife that depends on it.

4719c20f0d3035a0: LISBON: Protesters pitched dozens of tents in Lisbon on Saturday demanding action to stem housing and living costs in Portugal, mirroring demonstrations that have gripped neighbouring Spain for weeks.
Hundreds of protesters rallied at night in Rossio Square -- located at the bustling, touristic heart of the Portuguese capital -- following a march that had rallied thousands of people nationwide.
The mostly young attendees vowed to stay overnight, with hundreds singing songs as they sat around the statue of King Pedro IV that dominates the square, AFP journalists saw.

"The Portuguese social class that pays taxes, that which keeps this country going, is under attack and is losing its rights, notably its right to housing," said Elena Costa, a 46-year-old social assistant.
"So we are all here together to try to explain that we are suffocating," she said.

Engineer Antonio Margado, 52, criticised the centre-right government for "a total liberalisation of rents; owners are protected more and more, while tenants who need a house are those who are protected less and less".
Portuguese housing prices rose by 124% between 2015 and 2024, roughly twice as fast as the EU average, according to official data.
The impact is especially harsh on the young and in Lisbon, which concentrates around one-quarter of Portugal's more than 11 million inhabitants including the capital's greater metropolitan area.

Another of the protesters, Isabel Guerreiro, told public broadcaster RTP: "As a self-employed professional, I obviously don't have the means to pay Lisbon's exorbitant rents -- and I'm a daughter of Lisbon."
Saturday's camp in Lisbon amplified a housing protest that started in the northern city of Porto, where dozens of tents are set up.
At the earlier protest in Lisbon called by the main CGTP union, demonstrators called for better public services, pensions and wages as well as measures against soaring housing costs.
Marching to the roar of drums, they held placards with slogans including "Their greed, our misery" and "the cost of living increases, the people can't take it anymore."
"There are many problems. Wages, housing, the cost of living: it's a matter of survival," Yolanda Silva, a 43-year-old civil servant, told AFP.
Earlier this week, prime minister Luis Montenegro said "we fully understand that people want answers" and to "express their outrage at what, in their view, may be omissions in public policies".

But he warned political rivals against "importing into Portugal climates of instability and protest that, in fact, have no support in Portuguese society", in a likely reference to violent protests that have rocked France.

The expanding Portuguese movement comes as Spain is gripped by housing protest camps and demonstrations that are entering their fourth week and have culminated in the calling of an early general election for Nov 29.
29ef1dc4a887cec6: MANCHESTER: Enzo Maresca is sweating on Erling Haaland's fitness after the Manchester City striker limped off following his double in Saturday's 3-2 win against Ipswich.

"We give credit to the players. They are not worried about people who judge from outside," Maresca said of the flood of criticism for City since the guilty verdict.

"The environment was very good. The club, the fans, the players are all together on this journey and this is the best feeling for everyone," he said.
55ecedeba970987b: PARIS: Clashes between police and protesters, massive looting and multiple blazes gripped France on Saturday, as nationwide marches against soaring inflation degenerated into street violence of "extreme intensity".
The widespread unrest follows weeks of student protests and deepens political uncertainty as the country readies for elections in six months' time to replace President Emmanuel Macron.
Whole streets in Paris "have been devastated", the city's mayor, Emmanuel Gregoire, said as groups of masked young men torched parked cars and ransacked many shops.
French prime minister Sebastien Lecornu, who earlier slammed the "violence of extreme intensity", said late Saturday that 1,200 people had been arrested and 150 police officers hurt.

The violence began on the sidelines of marches in the capital and other cities over the cost of living that the interior ministry said were attended by 550,000 people. The CGT union, which took part, said 800,000 people participated.

Police used tear gas and water cannon against protesters who threw projectiles and aimed fireworks. A 17-year-old boy had his right hand blown off by a crowd-control grenade in the southern city of Saint-Etienne.
Looting in many cities
During and after those demonstrations, gangs of youths roamed city streets, sporadically confronting police, while setting fires and attacking shuttered stores to break in and empty their shelves.

Scores of shops -- supermarkets, pharmacies, luxury boutiques, clothing retailers, opticians, cosmetic vendors and consumer electronics stores -- were looted in Paris, Marseille, Nice, Nantes, Bordeaux, Limoges, Lille, Toulouse and Strasbourg.

AFP reporters in Paris saw groups of half a dozen young men often attacking the shops in an organised way: wearing masks and gloves, they first disconnected security cameras before smashing windows to get in.
The looting added to a day of destruction and vandalism, with town halls in several cities targeted.

The one in the city of Limoges -- more than 140 years old -- was largely destroyed by a blaze set by masked protesters who broke in, according to the region's top official. Two others were broken into and vandalised in Marseille and Lille.
A police compound in Bordeaux was also vandalised, while in Lyon protesters set ablaze a tourist office.
Macron vowed on X that "those who carried out vandalism, attacked administrative offices or businesses, or carried out looting -- even in our town halls, will be prosecuted and punished".
Opposition politicians vying to replace Macron in presidential elections in April and May seized on the chaos.
Far-right candidate Marine Le Pen condemned "the rioters" and claimed that the party of her far-left rival for the presidency, Jean-Luc Melenchon, had "legitimised the violence".
She said on X that, if she came to power, she would protect the French "from the violence of the extreme left".
Melenchon, who had prominently supported the demonstrations and the student protests preceding them, urged demonstrators to stay away from any looting, describing it as "contrary to our methods".
A 'revolution'
France's Yellow Vest movement, which eight years ago staged street protests against Macron's government over planned fuel tax hikes, had called for Saturday's "yellow and youth" demonstrations.
The principal grievance was the cost of living, pushed up in part by the war in the Middle East that has helped send inflation soaring in Europe as elsewhere.
But there were other issues too.
In Paris, tens of thousands marched across the east and north of the city in one major march, some shouting "Everyone hates the police" and "Macron, resign".

High school student Kamil Alahyan, 18, said he was protesting "for so many reasons -- the elections coming up in 2027, politicians who lie, the ultra-rich who've been taking more and more wealth over the past 10 years".
Several protesters sought to draw parallels with the French Revolution of 1789.
"It's the Revolution -- we're taking the Bastille!" some shouted in Marseille during the forced entry of the mayor's offices.
In the western city of La Rochelle, marchers streamed behind a placard reading: "Revolution or death."
And in the southern city of Montpellier, a giant blue sign reading "The people will win" was unfurled above a central square.

"The government is trembling and it's right to tremble because when the French people are angry, they never let up," Ryad Rani, the head of the LSU high school student representative body, told journalists in Paris.
5bcae441451ee0bd: RIYADH: Saudi Arabia said on Saturday that it had intercepted a fresh wave of incoming drones, as its ally Egypt weighed sending the kingdom help in defending against repeated attacks from Yemen's Houthis.

Riyadh leads a military coalition supporting Yemen's internationally recognised government in its war with the Houthis, and a military spokesman for the Iran-backed group said Saturday that dozens of Saudi strikes over the past day had killed and wounded "numerous" people.

Since Yemen's conflict flared back to life in July after a years-long hiatus, Saudi Arabia has faced sustained Houthi missile and drone attacks targeting its oil installations, tankers and transit hubs, including one on Riyadh's airport last week that killed 13 people.
A spokesman for the Saudi coalition said on Saturday that it had "intercepted and destroyed four drones over the past few hours in the regions of Riyadh, the Eastern Province, and the South".
The interceptions came as the president of Egypt, which is also a member of the coalition, said he was willing to "carry out any measure to protect" Saudi Arabia if its leaders requested it.

President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said Egypt was not looking to intervene in regional wars, but added that it was "inconceivable" for Cairo to stand by while the kingdom was "harmed or its security and stability threatened".
"I'm not talking about fighting anyone or attacking anyone," he said. "We are speaking only about defence."
Though Egypt is a member of the anti-Houthi coalition, its role has mostly concerned Red Sea maritime security rather than the fighting in Yemen.
It and Saudi Arabia are historically close and have strategic economic ties.
Egypt's parliament will hold an emergency session on Sunday at Sisi's request.
The repeated Houthi strikes have prompted foreign embassies to warn their citizens not to use Saudi airports, or not to visit the country altogether.
The Saudi education ministry on Saturday announced the extension of remote learning measures for students in Riyadh and nearby Diriyah.
Residents of the Saudi capital received a mobile phone alert early on Sunday warning of a "hostile aerial threat" and to stay away from windows and doors. It was lifted after a few minutes.
'Political process'
Saudi Arabia has accused Iran of encouraging the Houthis' recent escalation, a charge Tehran denies.

Iranian foreign minister Abbas Araghchi said Saturday that Tehran supported a "comprehensive political process as the only practical and sustainable way to resolve" the conflict on the Arabian Peninsula.
He also repeated Iran's offer to mediate between the two sides.
Deputy foreign minister Saeed Khatibzadeh previously said Riyadh has not responded to Iran's overture.
But Yemeni foreign minister Afrah al-Zouba rejected Iran's offer in a statement on X Saturday, saying "the Tehran regime is a party to the war against Yemenis, not a mediator".
The Houthis are part of Iran's "Axis of Resistance" against Israel and the United States, but both they and Tehran insist the group acts independently.
Saudi Arabia has carried out daily airstrikes on the Houthis in Yemen, where government forces are seeking to roll back gains the group made in a lightning offensive in September.
On Saturday, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said Riyadh had conducted 53 strikes in the capital Sanaa and six other provinces over the past 24 hours, causing "numerous dead and wounded".
A Houthi-affiliated news agency had earlier accused Saudi warplanes of targeting "civilian residences" in Dhamar and Taiz provinces, killing 12 people and wounding more than 30.
It alleged that the strikes were carried out "using cluster bombs, which are banned internationally".
004a070a8fb42340: VATICAN CITY: Pope Leo XIV left hospital to enthusiastic cheers and applause from well-wishers and returned home to the Vatican on Saturday, four days after undergoing surgery for lung cancer.
The 71-year-old pope was seen crossing the lobby of the Gemelli hospital on foot and exiting the building, smiling as he shook hands and waved.
He spoke briefly to the doctors who treated him and hospital officials before pausing to speak with a Ukrainian girl, a cancer survivor who wanted to wish him well in his recovery.
Soon after leaving the hospital, the pope's black SUV was seen driving through a side entrance to the Vatican.
Leo's discharge capped days of uncertainty that rattled the Vatican and the world's 1.4 billion Catholics, less than two years into the Chicago-born pope's papacy.

Earlier Saturday, his doctors said the pope was "fit for discharge". Surgeon Stefano Margaritora later told Vatican News that Leo was in "absolutely satisfactory clinical condition," estimating another ten days before he is fully recovered.
The pope had been at the Gemelli hospital, north of the Vatican, since Tuesday when doctors removed the lower part of his right lung to extract a cancerous tumour.
On Sunday, Leo plans to recite the Angelus prayer from the window of the Apostolic Palace overlooking St Peter's Square, as is customary, the Vatican said.
Before his discharge, Leo celebrated mass at noon, according to the Vatican, as he has in recent days, in a room on the 10th floor where he has been recovering.
'Heart and soul'
News that the otherwise active pope had a cancerous tumour removed from his lung was met with trepidation among the world's Catholics and other supporters.
But his doctors have said Leo's recovery has been progressing well as they await the results of tests that will determine the next course of action to take.
Surgeon Margaritora told Vatican News that Leo's tumour had been discovered by chance, during a routine abdominal X-ray that captured the "little spot" at the base of his right lung.
While calling the lung operation "routine", he saluted the pope's commitment to his recovery, saying he "really put his heart and soul into it, like the most motivated patients".
"His determination to achieve a very quick and very effective recovery from every point of view was really commendable," Margaritora said.
Leo has resumed some work, making a call on Friday to Russian President Vladimir Putin to urge a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky.
Up in the air, however, has been a planned papal voyage to South America, scheduled for November 6-17 to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, where Leo spent two decades as a missionary.
But Margaritora said he believed there were "no clinical reasons why the trip should not go ahead".
"All in all I believe that in another ten days or so the pope could be fully recovered," he said.
Leo has cancelled all his audiences until Oct 20.
Varvara Struck, the 13-year-old Ukrainian girl who spoke with the pope outside the hospital, had earlier Saturday told AFP that she was rooting for him.
The cancer survivor said she had met the pope last year in Rome, "and he blessed me for a successful treatment."
"With his support, I've now overcome my illness, and I want to give him my positive energy so that he, too, can overcome his illness as quickly as possible."
ca4ba7c309dbfa7f: JERUSALEM: Israeli settlers on Saturday attacked a convoy of European diplomats in the West Bank and beat up a visiting French mayor, witnesses said, a day after an American photographer was similarly set upon as violence escalates ahead of bitterly fought elections.

The 78-year-old mayor said masked settlers yelled defamatory comments about France, kicked him and hit him with iron bars as he joined Palestinian olive farmers in the West Bank alongside the top French and Belgian representatives in Jerusalem and Polish diplomats.

"I think that if settlers are behaving like this, there is a tolerance on the part of the Israeli government," Bernard Baudoux, mayor of the northern French town of Aulnoye-Aymeries, told AFP after he was attacked.
"The whole world needs to know what's happening," he said. "For me, I'll go back to my country and everything will be fine. Those who continue to suffer the most are those who are here."
Baudoux, who was wearing a sash with the French tricolour, was seen collapsed on the side of the car after the attack but he did not need hospital care.

French foreign minister Jean-Noel Barrot said in a statement that Israel must "urgently halt criminal violence" and arrest those responsible for attacking Baudoux, with his Belgian counterpart issuing a similar call.
Election season
The attack came just one day after settlers beat an American photographer for The Washington Post, who was in moderate condition on Saturday after suffering broken vertebrae.
Israel's foreign ministry condemned the attack on the diplomats and Israeli police promised to open an investigation.
But Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is seeking to shore up support from the fiercely pro-settlement far-right in the October 27 election, instead alleged a "smear" campaign against settlers.
Netanyahu said the diplomats should have coordinated their movements with the Israeli military and pointed out that Baudoux is a communist known for supporting the Palestinian cause.
"We urge caution before drawing conclusions" about the attacks, Netanyahu's office said in a statement.

His main rival in the elections, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, strongly criticised Netanyahu over the violence, saying it was "burning away the little legitimacy the State of Israel still possesses".
The attacks are "Jewish terrorism, under the auspices of the Israeli government", Eisenkot said.
Attacks on cultural symbol
Baudoux, the mayor, said he had come to the town of Taybeh, a Christian stronghold, along with his local pastor from France to sign a goodwill agreement.
He was attacked just as he joined the harvest as a symbolic gesture with the Palestinians, for whom olives are an important cultural symbol.

Extremist Israelis have issued calls to stop the Palestinians' annual harvest after months of escalating attacks in which settlers have stolen land and property. There has also been violence against Israelis, with a Palestinian shooting a settler dead last month.
Bashar Fawadleh, a priest in Taybeh, said settlers had already attacked the harvest and snatched olives before beating the mayor.
"One person was hit in the head and needed stitches. They also beat up an older lady in her 70s after insulting her with very bad words," the pastor told AFP.
The West Bank violence has shocked much of the world, with Britain spearheading economic sanctions that in turn led Israel to close the British consulate in Jerusalem.
Netanyahu had also sought to throw doubt on the circumstances behind the beating Friday of the photographer, Heidi Levine, suggesting that Palestinians and "far-left" activists caused trouble.

But President Isaac Herzog, who holds a mostly ceremonial role, took the initiative Saturday to call Levine in the hospital, saying the attack was "outrageous and shocking" and weighed on his conscience.
US Ambassador Mike Huckabee said the beating was "a despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards", and demanded Israel prosecute and jail the assailants.

Israel Gantz, head of an umbrella settler group, blamed recent incidents on "groups of provocateurs and terrorists" but implicitly acknowledged some Israelis' responsibility, saying that they harmed the settlers' cause.
Settlers earlier this month also beat up AFP photographer Jaafar Ashtiyeh as he covered the olive harvest tensions, fracturing several of his ribs and stealing his camera.
Netanyahu's government has ramped up approval of West Bank settlements, which are illegal under international law.
Some 500,000 Israelis live in the West Bank, which Israel seized in 1967, alongside three million Palestinians.
af1ed09be6230652: ROME: Inter Milan pulled clear at the top of Serie A after coming from behind to beat Bologna 3-1 on Saturday, while Roma dispatched Genoa to jump into second and Napoli's torrid start continued with a shock defeat by Venezia.

- Castro scores stunner -

"In football you get moments like this and there is only one way out: keep working seriously and professionally, be more focused and turn this disappointment into anger," Allegri told a press conference.
"It's up to us to turn this situation around, starting with the Champions League."
Napoli are ninth on 10 points, while Venezia remain bottom with three points.

32750e74423d48e7: Today, I’m talking with Walter Piecyk, a partner and analyst at LightShed Partners who covers tech, media, and telecom, about SpaceX’s recently announced plan to become a major wireless carrier.

Last week, SpaceX agreed to buy a big chunk of low-band spectrum to expand the Starlink network, spectrum that’s been traded around the telecom business for decades now. SpaceX’s ambitious plan is to use that spectrum to help build “the world’s most advanced mobile network.”
Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.

Combined with news that the FCC approved the deployment of 15,000 next-gen Starlink satellites and the company’s previous agreement to purchase close to $20 billion worth of EchoStar spectrum last year, it’s now clear SpaceX is serious about competing with AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile.

I’ve covered the telecom business for a long time, and I’ve always known that these companies can say they want to do something until they run into the harsh reality of how expensive it is to actually do it. The telecom graveyard of pivots, bad ideas, and failed acquisitions is vast.

Walt has been closely monitoring SpaceX’s acquisition, and he’s correctly predicted that the company was headed in this direction for months now. So I wanted to dig into whether SpaceX can pull this off, why Walt thinks the existing telecom giants have really fumbled their response to SpaceX’s growing threat, and what happens when Elon Musk’s rocket company jumps headfirst into a business everyone loves to hate.
Okay: LightShed Partners’ Walter Piecyk on SpaceX’s plan to expand into mobile. Here we go.
This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
Walter Piecyk, you’re a partner and a tech, media, and telecom analyst at LightShed Partners. Welcome to Decoder.
Thanks for having me. I’m looking forward to it.

I’m excited to talk to you. I feel like we’ve been tweeting or posting around each other for many, many years, but I’m a telecom nerd at heart. I’ve been covering the space for ages. SpaceX is going to make a big splash. It’s going to be the fourth major mobile carrier in the United States and maybe the world. It bought some spectrum to do it.

It’s EchoStar spectrum by way of private equity. It is at once very simple and also very complicated. Give us the state of the state. SpaceX bought 800 Mhz spectrum for $8 billion. They spent nearly $20 billion already on separate EchoStar spectrum. What is SpaceX trying to do here?

It’s definitely complicated, but maybe less complicated than trying to figure out how to put a data center out in space and making that work. Or something on the moon. But they don’t typically want to own spectrum and spend for spectrum. If you think about how Starlink was built, satellite companies don’t typically pay for spectrum. And then as the business evolved and as they saw the opportunity in telecom, they purchased some spectrum initially from EchoStar.

The feedback they got from investors at that time was very positive and they said, “Wait a minute, you should do more here.” This is a trillion-dollar enterprise value business in the US alone. Obviously they have global aspirations both for Starlink as well as what they’re doing with this mobile telephone service. So they bought more. They went back to EchoStar. That’s a key thing to pay attention to, in that they bought some spectrum and then they went back and bought some more.

Because with a lot of things that Elon Musk does, he learns as he goes. He bought the spectrum, got feedback, talked to people in telecom, and bought some more spectrum. Then we didn’t hear from them for a while. Now, you have this thing that happened last week where they bought some more spectrum, and I can go through the history of it if you care, but it’s long, wonky telecom stuff. This was originally the Nextel spectrum, if you remember that company.

I do. Actually, I do want you to go through the history because I think the telecom business is best understood as a bunch of lobbyists trying to make everything more complicated than it should be. Yes, spectrum auctions are complicated and what spectrum is good for what is deeply tied to the physics of the radio spectrum and all that.

But here it’s the 800 MHz spectrum from the Nextel service, the old push-to-talk, walkie-talkie service that Sprint had to divest as part of the deal to get sold to T-Mobile. They’ve been trying to sell it for ages. They sold it to this company, Grain Management. They’ve been sitting on it, and when Starlink showed up, Elon bought it. Nobody else wanted it. What did he see in the spectrum that no one else did?

When you realize that you need to build a terrestrial network to support what you’re doing with satellites, because satellites work fine if you’ve got your dish on the top of your house and you’re getting your broadband, but when you’re trying to connect with a phone that doesn’t have the same type of power or you’re going inside a home, you’re going to need better coverage.

Sirius Satellite also has supplementary towers. There are not that many of them, but sometimes when you get out of Sirius coverage, you will connect to a tower. When they bought that EchoStar spectrum and then got FCC approval, and if you looked into those details of that FCC approval and what was required, you would see that they can’t do this by satellites alone. There had to be terrestrial.

Then SpaceX, as Elon is wont to do, tries to send some diversions like, “We’re going to do Femtocell, we’re not going to do macrocell, this, that, and the other thing.” But they realized that they were going to build a terrestrial network. Now they finally realized, “If I’m going to offer mobile service, I need some form of a terrestrial network.”

At the same time, the telcos are not going to help them out. They’re not going to give them a wholesale agreement. Then when they go back and say the companies that had the lowest churn, what is the fundamental value you need in a terrestrial network? It’s low-band spectrum. Why? It travels further, you can get better coverage, and you have that connectivity.

So getting this low-band spectrum piece was just an important part, not to make the satellites work better, but to actually give them the spectrum assets that they need to build a terrestrial network. That’s why the stocks reacted, because people finally came to terms with the fact that Elon is actually going to build a terrestrial network.

I’m less interested in the stock and more interested in just the cost structure of how this works. If I rewind my brain to being a baby blogger at Engadget 100 years ago, the FCC told all the TV networks they had to stop broadcasting on 700 MHz and we were going to run an auction.

Verizon and AT&T bought big chunks of 700 MHz spectrum and that’s what 4G is built on. That’s the low-bandwidth spectrum that you’re talking about. It goes everywhere. This was a big victory that we reallocated 700 MHz, and 800 MHz was sitting right there the whole time. This is the Nextel spectrum. If it is so valuable, why wasn’t there a market for it until Elon showed up just now?

It was part of this transaction. T-Mobile ended up having to sell it because the government said, “If we’re going to allow you to take out the fourth competitor, which was Sprint, then in order to enable another fourth competitor out there, we need to have you guys give up some of your low-band spectrum.”

Part of the deal that T-Mobile and Sprint had with the government was that they would sell it to EchoStar. Why? Because Charlie Ergen, CEO of Dish at the time — it’s EchoStar now — was going to be the fourth competitor. This was the rationale that they gave in terms of the approval of the transaction. Dish needed low-band spectrum. The problem is Ergen went about his business, he was trying to build a network, and then he just couldn’t afford to buy that.

They had the rights to buy. Then at that point when Ergen failed on the bid to come up with the dollars to buy that spectrum, it enabled T-Mobile and actually forced them to put it up for auction. Now, your question: Why didn’t someone else show up then? Again, from SpaceX’s standpoint, as I mentioned at the start of this podcast, their strategy has been evolving over time.

In terms of the other telcos, they can’t really use it. There are some limitations that they have. But in hindsight, maybe Verizon or AT&T should have bought this 800 MHz spectrum for whatever it was, let’s call it $8 billion. They’re probably losing more in enterprise value over the concerns of what’s happening with SpaceX than what it cost them just to buy it in what’s known as foreclose. They basically just take it, even if they don’t use it or do whatever they need to meet those build out requirements and stop SpaceX from having unnecessary assets. I don’t think even these companies were taking Elon seriously and thinking that he would actually build the network.

Do you think that’s colored by the failure of Dish? We covered the promises of Dish Network to build a fourth wireless carrier in this country so closely. Their attempt was predicated on some amount of technology innovation.

They were going to build this thing called an O-RAN network, which had a more competitive supplier base instead of just Nokia or Siemens or whoever, and they were going to run it on AWS and that was going to reduce costs. Man, eventually they supported one Motorola handset in Vegas and even that was backstopped by AT&T. They literally could not do it. These promises never came true. Dish is a different company and Charlie Ergen’s a different CEO and their ability to just throw money at a problem until it’s solved is very different from Elon.

But if they couldn’t innovate to make a cheaper, faster network, what’s the evidence that Starlink can stand up an entire terrestrial network at a cost basis that allows them to compete selling service to consumers, while they’re also standing up an entire network in space? Because that feels like adding up a lot of cost.

I’m going to go back even deeper than that. Remember when Sprint was struggling, Masayoshi Son from SoftBank was claiming the same thing. They were going to cut their CapEx to nothing and they were going to use these small cells. They innovated how wireless was going to get delivered. That failed. Obviously, they had to get bailed out through the purchase when T-Mobile bought Sprint effectively for just the spectrum.

That network got completely decommissioned. To your point, Dish got a network built, but they couldn’t resonate in the market. The difference between Dish and SpaceX is Elon’s ability to get customers. That’s where Dish truly failed. They built the network. The network worked fine. They had the wholesale agreements that they needed.

I’ll push back on you a little bit there. I have a very funny email from a Dish PR person from several years ago where they said, “We’d like to issue a correction to your story. Our network does exist.” That was the level that they were competing at, where they had to insist to us that the network was real, even though we could not find it in our tests in the various cities they claim.
Maybe there was a network, they built some amount of network, but they had not built anything that competed at the national scale with the big three.

Absolutely. It’s not like your phone. The phone that I was using, I had an iPhone that it was mostly going to roam onto the AT&T and T-Mobile wholesale agreements that existed. The theory is you get the customers, you have a go-to-market strategy, and then you backfill the network. This is probably going to be something similar.

You can even go back to when John Legere first took over T-Mobile. They had a crappy network, and then Legere promised, “We’re going to build it,” taking on customers saying that the network was great before the network was great. Then it caught up because they actually finally got the Germans, Deutsche Telekom, to give them the money to invest in the network.

The same thing can happen here where SpaceX will sell something that’ll probably rely on other assets that are out there, even if the telcos themselves are circling the wagons. They have the satellites for certain benefits in terms of coverage and then they can build the capacity over time. The point is it’s going to take time. You can’t just turn on a network overnight and start selling service on that.

This has always been my framework of how to think about telecom companies. You can try to run the network cheaper or you can run some kind of different technology to make that cheaper. Or you can just spend and have the best network, which was the Verizon strategy for years and years and years.

Then you’ve got to acquire and manage your customers. That was the T-Mobile strategy. That was John Legere. He was just nicer to people than AT&T was, and he picked up a lot of customers and that drove some investment.

Then you’ve got to get some devices. You have to have the iPhone. We can set that aside because it feels like that era of competition is over. We’re not doing exclusive devices anymore. But those are the two. I’m just looking at the network here. It does not seem to me, from the outside, that Starlink is proposing to build a cheaper network.

It feels like they’re proposing to build a vastly more expensive network because they need the satellites. They’re going to launch 15,000 more satellites to support this network. Then they’re going to build a terrestrial network by investing in spectrum on the ground and building some set of base stations.

Then they’re going to have to convince one of the big three to let them roam over as some sort of mobile virtual network operator (MVNO). The big three do not want to do that. So they’re going to overcharge them for that. I’m just stuck at that being a lot of cost, even if you’re Elon Musk and you can make some set of people buy whatever you’re selling.

The third thing you said is obviously the most challenging. That’s the tent and the pole that prevents you from launching services sooner rather than later. But without necessarily getting a wholesale agreement, there might be other ways. Roaming agreements exist out there. There are roaming partners that exist that these telcos still rely on. It’s very expensive. It’s not something you can build a high-margin business on, but it perhaps provides an entry to the market sooner rather than later.

As Apple has pitched in terms of satellite connectivity, some people are in the middle of the Utah desert texting because they’re injured. There’s value there. But it’s the soccer field. We have, maybe not in the cities, but in the suburbs, plenty of areas that the telcos have effectively given up on trying to provide coverage because of NIMBY-ism, meaning people just don’t want these cell sites. This satellite coverage can give you not just this basic text messaging that Apple has been doing through the Globalstar constellation, but a true cellphone-type experience.

So that’s a positive. The second differentiation is the fact that these telcos have 60 percent earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) margins. So there’s a lot of fat there that can be eaten off of, that when you’re selling other services in terms of Elon, like home broadband, maybe this becomes an entree in terms of pushing Grok and people’s usage. You don’t necessarily need 60 percent margins, in this case, for him to justify building this network.

They also talk about other data connectivity that these satellites are going to enable. Again, in the current constellation, you need a lot of power and you need a dish. But if you don’t have that, if you have the cell phone-type power, then the internet of things (IOT) and other types of opportunities that exist there become another revenue opportunity that they look at.

It’s just funny. The IOT story — that’s what all these companies promised us about 4G. That’s what they all promised us about 5G. There’s something about this business that just rhymes every time. They’re going to do self-driving cars and robot surgery. I’m confident we’re going to hear about self-driving cars and robot surgery when it comes to Starlink and Tesla and Optimus.

There’s something about these applications for next generation networks that just recurs, and we hear about them all the time. Then I think about our consumer audience at The Verge, and they want long battery life and fast service and [connectivity] all the places they go. I’m not sure how that squares with your phone is going to connect directly to a satellite in the middle of a soccer field. There’s something about that that also seems challenging.

It’s just the performance if your phone does connect to the satellite on the soccer field and it works. A lot of the things that people said wouldn’t work on Starlink in terms of airplanes or even getting customer-premises equipment (CPE) down below a certain price, they’ve delivered on. Obviously, Elon sometimes delivers on them a little later than some of his initial optimistic promises, but they ultimately get delivered on.

There is the ability with these new constellations to give you that type of connectivity on these spaces. Is that enough to differentiate with consumers? I don’t know. The telcos have attacked this by saying, “No one cares about our direct-to-device (D2D) services.” Well, your D2D services are not good. It’s just sending basic text messages. What they’re talking about is giving you that blanket coverage where you get what you expect from your cell phone wherever you go.

That’s fine, but you still have to give it to the person in the middle of the building where their cell phone works today and provide the volume at a cost that is going to be attractive to that consumer. So those are longer-term things that are going to require some amount of terrestrial network build. Then the question is: how much? A lot of the attacks that have been out there have been referencing $100 billion, $200 billion. I get that. Why?

Telcos each spend $10 billion to $15 billion a year, but they are maintaining massive customer bases. To get that initial network up where you have that usage, where you use that low-band spectrum to get into buildings, is not those types of numbers. You’re probably talking like $10 billion, $15 billion for that initial build in terms of CapEx.

The dynamic there is really interesting. I’m just thinking about AT&T when the iPhone came out. The network immediately got overloaded because there was a surge of customer demand that took four years to truly resolve. Part of that resolution was just putting the iPhone on the other carriers.

How do you think that will play out for Starlink here? Because right now, Starlink customer service is not the best in the industry. Their actual service, people love it. And then when they need customer service, it’s a bunch of automated systems and people complaining on Reddit. So there’s some challenge there if you’re running a consumer business at this scale.

For consumer businesses, think about all the advertising that’s done. The fulfillment, dealing with the phones, phone subsidies, and that’s a big part of the financing. How many customers are we talking about? So for the amount of spectrum that they have now in the network that I’m talking about for $10–$15 billion, you’re not taking 50 percent share overnight. I don’t think that would be that expectation from day one.
