b32f0e3a029c0656: BANGKOK, Oct 17 — Coconut farmer Sombat Chuekrod travelled more than 200km to join hundreds on the streets of Bangkok yesterday demanding that the International Monetary Fund and World Bank change how they deal with the developing world.

Finance ministers, central bank governors and other top policymakers gathered this week in the Thai capital for the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings, as decision-makers tackle an inflation crisis fuelled by the US war on Iran and other economic shocks.

The message from the IMF has been clear: after years of economic crises starting with the pandemic and continuing through the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, worldwide debt is too high and governments need to cut spending.
For the hundreds at the protest in Bangkok, as well as for rights groups and analysts interviewed by AFP, that message is the wrong one.
“We want the IMF and World Bank to rethink their role,” said 51-year-old Sombat, as he walked alongside banners demanding reform of the institutions.
“Thai people are already poor. Please don’t make them any poorer.”
Protest organisers called on institutions like the IMF to focus on climate financing and tax reforms that aid poorer citizens rather than demand governments cut subsidies and social spending.

“Governments across the Global South are being forced to squeeze vital spending on public health, education, and social protection just to service illegitimate debts to wealthy nations and private creditors,” Lidy Nacpil, one of the protest organisers, said in a statement.
‘Inequality emergency’

Speaking to AFP on the sidelines of the meetings, Oxfam Executive Director Amitabh Behar said the world was facing an “inequality emergency”, and that the IMF’s calls for fiscal consolidation were code for cutting spending on essential social support during the war-fuelled inflation crisis.
“It will lead to (more) price rises. It might lead to hunger,” he said. “You will see cuts further happening in terms of health, in terms of education, in terms of basic social security.
“So all that is going to suffer in a time when you actually need it more.”

The IMF this week upgraded its world economic outlook, citing unexpected “resilience” in economic growth. But it warned that that prosperity was fragmented, with vulnerable countries falling even further behind.
It highlighted oil-importing low-income countries not exposed to the boom in artificial intelligence investment as being the most vulnerable.
Yet the Fund’s advice to all countries at a time of rising global debt levels has been to cut spending and rebuild fiscal buffers after years of spending on crises.

Asked what vulnerable countries should do, IMF deputy chief of research Petya Koeva Brooks told AFP that while their situation was indeed “more difficult”, they had “no other choice” but to address their fiscal balances by either cutting spending or increasing revenues.

The IMF has proposed making energy and food subsidies offered in the wake of the Iran war more targeted, even as the UN Development Programme warned this week that if such subsidies were cut entirely, it could plunge 130 million people into poverty.
Protest organiser Nacpil questioned in an interview how one could draw a line between who deserves a subsidy and who does not.
“How poor do you have to be for them to think that you will need some support?” she asked.
Trading off
Reza Baqir of Alvarez & Marsal’s Sovereign Advisory Services said he has experience with the difficult trade-offs policymakers in low-income countries face in such crises.

“During my time as Pakistan’s central bank governor, I saw firsthand how difficult it can be for countries to balance the needs of the countries’ citizens with the needs of the IMF programme,” he said.

“At the same time, it also reinforced the importance of addressing domestic governance challenges, so countries can build their own resources and fiscal buffers, reduce their reliance on the IMF and support their citizens in a targeted and prudent manner.”

Christina Segal-Knowles of the Rockefeller Foundation said developing countries are “effectively being given two bad options” — either take on debt at currently sky-high interest rates, or make extraordinary spending cuts and potentially give up on development goals.
She proposed a “growth and investment reset” that ramps up funding to countries in need as part of a set of measures designed to provide sustained support at concessional rates.
On the streets of Bangkok yesterday, protesters prepared to spend the night under a flyover.
“We are raising our voices because we believe that the network of citizens present here are key stakeholders in the negotiations,” said activist Supaporn Malailoy.
“This is not merely a matter of borrowing money; it is about shaping the very structure and direction of the nation’s development.” — AFP
8d18356feeda01ec: BEND, Oct 18 — Kristen Vanetsky and her family moved to Bend, Oregon, after a shooting in their New Mexico neighbourhood, choosing Silver Rail elementary for her grandson because they considered it safer.
But their world was shattered this week when a 16-year-old entered the school and opened fire, shooting dead three children and a teacher, and leaving another child and educator critically wounded.
An armed bystander who pursued the gunman into the school shot and killed him.
The tragic events, Vanetsky told AFP on Friday morning outside the school, are “unthinkable.”
The 52-year-old, whose 10-year-old grandson attends the school, said the mass shooting “just took away all the innocence” of the school’s children, disrupting their sense of safety.
She said she went to the school “trying to make sense of what’s going on.”
“Who would do this to little kids?”

Thursday’s massacre in Bend — a city of about 100,000 people in central Oregon — is the latest of 371 mass shootings that have occurred in the United States just this year, according to the tracker Gun Violence Archive.
It “just doesn’t stop,” Vanetsky said.

She said she is grateful for the actions of the man who fired back against the shooter, but notes the scenario’s inherent contradictions, which underscore the ongoing debate over gun control in the United States.
“It’s very weird, to have a gun solve the problem of a gun,” she said. “I can’t wrap my mind around it.”

“The whole thing could’ve been a lot worse had somebody not stepped in and shot the shooter,” she continued. But now, “the shooter has to live the rest of his life knowing that he shot a 16-year-old to keep other babies from being shot.”
“It doesn’t make sense,” she said tearfully.
‘Devastated’
Bend, a popular destination for its natural beauty and outdoor recreation scene, “is devastated,” Vanetsky said.
“We’re a close town of people, and we look out for each other.”
And yet, the perpetrator of Thursday’s attack was a resident of the city itself.

Authorities have not yet offered details regarding motive or any connection to the school. They did specify that a long gun was used, and media reports indicate the shooter’s mother had purchased the weapon.
“I don’t understand why a mom would buy a teenage boy a weapon like that,” said Vanetsky.
Less than 24 hours after the shooting, Silver Rail Elementary School, which serves more than 400 students, was cordoned off with yellow crime-scene tape.
A few cars and bicycles remained stranded in the parking lot.

At the school’s main entrance, neighbours and parents had created a memorial with flowers, candles and toys to honour the children — aged five, eight and 11 — and the educator whose lives were cut short Thursday.
Vanetsky said her grandson was struggling at home in the wake of the trauma he’d been through.

“My grandson should be in his classroom, with all of his friends,” she said, her gaze turning towards the school’s second floor. “Everybody should be in there learning, having fun, looking forward to their weekend, and it’s just vacant.”
“There’s nothing. Even the birds are not here.” — AFP
1b0fda0f6a693537: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 17 — The ringgit is expected to trade within a tight range with an upward bias next week, between RM4.07 and RM4.09, following Malaysia’s higher-than-expected advance estimate of gross domestic product (GDP) growth for the third quarter of 2026 (3Q 2026).

c3a2b9f0b6d12cd5: KIGALI, Oct 17 — Viewed by some as “sportswashing” and by others as an overly ambitious, grandiose project, the prospect of a Formula 1 Grand Prix in Rwanda has provoked reaction at home and abroad.
The government touts the initiative as a significant “investment in Rwanda’s future”, slated for some time in the early 2030s.
On Tuesday, Kigali put on a glitzy ceremony to announce the “historic” agreement between Rwanda, the organisation that owns Formula 1, and the International Automobile Federation (FIA).
A landlocked country still widely associated with a horrific genocide in 1994, Rwanda has used sports to revamp its image, attract tourists and impress investors with its organisational efficiency.
The event promises glamour — replete with champagne-quaffing celebrities — set against the backdrop of Rwanda’s verdant hills and rich wildlife, all broadcast to a global audience.
Formula 1 markets itself as the third most-watched sporting event on the planet, trailing only the Olympic Games and the Fifa World Cup.
However, the project has drawn dismay from some quarters, including Amnesty International, which immediately condemned it as an act of sportswashing.
The NGO accuses Kigali of “buying into the world’s biggest sports to polish its image and deflect from its appalling human rights record”.
This same criticism has been levelled against Formula 1 on several previous occasions.
In its pursuit of global expansion, the sport has forged numerous partnerships with governments with questionable rights records, including China and Azerbaijan.
Sports diplomacy
Last year, Rwanda became the first African nation to successfully host the World Cycling Championships.
Through its “Visit Rwanda” campaign, Kigali also sponsors several major European football clubs, including Paris Saint-Germain (PSG), as well as the NBA’s Los Angeles Clippers.

However, while President Paul Kagame is credited with a strategic vision that has driven Rwanda’s economic transformation over his decades-long tenure, he has faced repeated accusations from opponents of suppressing political dissent.
Reacting to the news, Kenneth Roth, the former director of Human Rights Watch, noted on X Rwanda’s “invasion via its M23 proxy of eastern Democratic Republic of Congo”.
The armed M23 group, backed financially and militarily by Kigali, has forcibly seized vast swathes of the DRC.
During the Kigali ceremony, Kagame said it was an “honour” to be selected for Formula 1.
He described it as an “investment in Rwanda’s future” that would bring “jobs, skills, tourism and new business to our country and our region for decades to come”.
But one foreign attendee voiced concerns, telling AFP in English: “I am really hoping Rwanda is not chewing what it cannot swallow.”
Formula 1 is an expensive pursuit and far wealthier nations have already seen their ambitions backfire.
The Qatar model
India and South Korea — which built circuits specifically to host Formula 1 — eventually withdrew as their financial losses mounted.
European organisers, including those in France and, more recently, the Netherlands, have encountered similar setbacks.
In comparison Rwanda, despite its economic boom, remains a low-income country with a GDP per capita barely exceeding US$1,100 (RM4,500).
It ranks 159 out of 193 countries on the United Nations’ Human Development Index, although it is steadily improving.

Critics question whether the hundreds of millions of dollars required to build a modern racetrack might be better spent on healthcare or education — not to mention the tens of millions of dollars F1 Grand Prix organisers typically charge host countries for the privilege of holding the event.
A source close to the FIA said Qatar was “supporting” the Rwandan project.
The Gulf country is also building a new international airport in Bugesera, 40km from Kigali — near where the racetrack will be constructed.
Jean-Guy Africa, CEO of the Rwanda Development Board, pointed to the “tremendous interest” from the private sector.
“You cannot miss out on the 100,000 people who will come. From a business standpoint, you stand to benefit,” he told AFP.
While several Rwandans told AFP of their pride that their country will soon host the pinnacle of motor sports, Kigali entrepreneur Amon Niyigena, took a more pragmatic view.
“The economics of hosting F1 in Rwanda will not be for everyone, but for a tiny percentage of the already rich,” he said. — AFP

cd060138da3227e2: PARIS, Oct 17 — After weeks of student protests, France faces broader, nationwide demonstrations today over the cost of living, setting up a potentially fraught six months heading into a presidential election.
President Emmanuel Macron appealed for “calm” on the eve of the protests that authorities fear could see the two movements merge, perhaps with violence.
The country’s Yellow Vest movement, which eight years ago staged street protests against Macron and his government, called today’s “yellow and youth” demonstrations.
It has appealed to teachers and students, workers, pensioners and farmers to take part in an online call spread through social media.
“We’re expecting a pretty big turnout,” Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told France 2 television.
Macron called yesterday “for calm and respect,” adding the right to protest went hand in hand with “respect for people and property”.
A police source told AFP that authorities estimated nearly 200,000 people could take part, with 40,000 in Paris.
“I have a feeling that (today) will be a sort of culmination,” 18-year-old Marie-Lou, a protesting university student in the city of Lille, told AFP.
“We’ll be joined by workers and by the Yellow Vests, who are also mobilising again. There’s a sense of hope that all these different struggles might converge.”
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has ordered a crisis cell to monitor the demonstrations. On Thursday he said he feared clashes after what he called “urban violence” during the student protests.
Lecornu is attempting to get parliament to pass a cost-cutting budget, while protesters are demanding greater protection from inflation and more spending on public services, particularly education.
Anger at police
There is also public anger at perceived police brutality during the student protests. Several teenage protesters have been seriously injured and thousands arrested.

“It’s not just a Yellow Vest movement, it’s not just a student movement, it’s all the people who are rising up and that’s why those in power are afraid,” said Benjamin Ball, an activist working on a website for today’s demonstrations.
The unrest is weighing on the final months of Macron’s presidency, ahead of elections in April and May to choose his successor.
It has been seized upon by Opposition parties and their candidates.
Jean-Luc Melenchon, leader of the far-left France Unbowed party, has backed the student protests and marched in a demonstration Tuesday supporting them.
Far-right candidate Marine Le Pen, the election frontrunner according to surveys, has positioned her National Rally party on the side of the police.
Macron this week said he believed the “legitimate” demands of the students were being “exploited for political purposes”, according to a government spokeswoman.
Prepared for violence

Organisers of today’s demonstrations have set up a website showing more than 600 demonstrations planned across France, and hundreds more protest “actions” such as blocking motorway toll booths or service stations.
Authorities and demonstrators were preparing for possible violence.

Paris police banned a major march through the tourist and business heart of the capital, and are locked in negotiations with organisers over an alternative route. The main Paris demonstration was to kick off at 2pm (1200 GMT) at the Bastille square.
Paris police chief Patrice Faure banned demonstrations around the Elysee presidential palace, the prime minister’s office, and the Champs-Elysees shopping avenue, among other key locations.

Nunez told France 2 that officers could use stun grenades in case of “extremely serious urban violence”. He had previously suspended their use during the student protests after one stun grenade blew off the hand of a 15-year-old.

“Disturbances are expected, especially in the demonstrations in Paris and other big cities,” an interior ministry official told AFP on condition of anonymity, citing a risk of violence from “the ultra-left movement”.
“Actions blocking major roads or large, essential facilities will not be tolerated,” the official said.
Demonstrators have set up their own smartphone app giving the real-time location of police, tear gas and helicopters. — AFP

3f7e90810183cd15: BANGKOK, Oct 17 — International Monetary Fund chief Kristalina Georgieva said today this year’s Annual Meetings with global policymakers were marked by “optimism and worry” about the global economic outlook as the event wound down in Bangkok.
Georgieva also said her organisation had a “responsibility” to help low-income countries struggling with price shocks stemming from the US-Israel war on Iran.

Meetings in the Thai capital this week brought together finance ministers, central bank chiefs and other top officials from around the world, with surging inflation, spiking bond yields and economic growth driven by artificial intelligence at the top of the agenda.
“(The meetings) were marked by both optimism and worry,” said Georgieva, who was speaking at a press briefing alongside Saudi Finance Minister Mohammed al-Jadaan.

“Optimism from the resilience of the global economy, the promise of AI, the dynamism of Asia. But AI is also recognised to be a source of worry, and so are inflation, high levels of debt, wars, climate risks.”

All week, the IMF has warned that high levels of debt and rising bond yields in advanced economies are tightening financial conditions just as central banks need to focus on bringing inflation down, likely by increasing interest rates.

Global energy prices have spiked since late February, when the United States and Israel launched the war on Iran, with Tehran’s retaliatory actions targeting Washington’s Gulf allies and curtailing oil and gas supplies.
The price increases have rippled across the globe, fuelling inflation in economies across a range of income groups.
The most vulnerable to the shock, the IMF has said, are low-income oil-importing countries that are not exposed to the boom in AI investment that has propped up growth in many advanced economies.
“I can tell you that people everywhere, but especially in poorer countries, they don’t like inflation. Inflation is like a tax on the poor,” said Georgieva.

She said such countries needed to set spending targets such that they prioritised growth and protecting the most vulnerable people, adding that the Fund had a “relentless pursuit of more resources for low-income countries”.
Higher global interest rates and bond yields, however, were driving up debt repayments for low-income countries, she said.
The share of debt repayments as a percentage of government revenue had gone up from 8 to 14 per cent for low-income countries in recent years, the IMF chief said.

She said her organisation had a responsibility to help countries to restructure debt if needed; to assist with domestic resource mobilisation; to bring in international finance; and to create conditions for private investment.
“When we do our best, it translates into better lives for people.”

On the AI investment boom, Georgieva said that member countries had recognised its value in propping up growth, but “when we are dependent on one particular driver of growth, it is like we stand on one leg”.
A key debate at this year’s meetings has been on whether the technology’s most advanced frontier models require regulation and guardrails.
The question has grown more urgent after recent revelations of security incidents involving autonomous AI agents.
Georgieva said she was “impressed” by the spirit of cooperation between AI companies, governments and other stakeholders that she witnessed in Bangkok on the issue. — AFP

44e84b9497a21540: Late Sunday night, a still-unknown cybercriminal or group hacked thousands of remote-controlled refrigeration systems across hundreds of French grocery stores, spiking temperatures, spoiling food, and sparking fires. This is part of an ongoing trend of attacking physical systems that can do damage in the real world. In August, a ransomware attack disrupted building-management systems at a Canadian hospital, affecting door access controls, central HVAC monitoring, and the issuing of staff access cards. And three years ago, cyberattacks hit Las Vegas casinos, causing slot machines to go dark, preventing payment kiosks and ATMs from spitting out cash, and locking guests out of their rooms when the electronic keys stopped working. Not all digital intrusions remain in cyberspace, and attackers don’t need to encrypt files and steal data to cause chaos. Hitting physical systems often produces more severe consequences - and turns up the heat on executives to pay an extortion demand. “There was one gig where the customer was refusing to pay, and so the threat actor was like, ‘Hold my beer, have fun getting into your offices,’ and locked everybody out,” Tim Beasley, a senior incident response consultant at Semperis, told The Register. Beasley won’t name the customer, or provide any incriminating information, but said the incident response involved police smashing glass in addition to his team recovering compromised data. “The cops had to break in, and literally get into the building, breaking some windows, so the customer was able to finally get back in,” he said. We asked if the customer paid the ransom demand, and Beasley yelled: “Oh, hell, no!” A report published earlier this month by ServiceNow’s Armis Labs found increasing evidence of ransomware attackers using physical consequences as leverage in their intrusions. “Today’s BAS operate at the intersection of IT and OT worlds, creating unprecedented exposure,” the report said. Ransomware with physical consequences Building automation systems - BAS - are the critical systems that control and monitor facilities’ HVAC, lighting, energy usage, and water consumption. They also oversee badge readers, door locks, surveillance cameras, fire alarm control panels, and other physical safety equipment. As such, BAS make very attractive targets for ransomware operators looking for high-pressure ways to extort organizations into paying multi-million ransom demands. These systems also appeal to government-backed goons and hacktivists looking to ensure maximum psychological and physical impact during destructive cyberattacks. Armis Labs found 73 percent of organizations own BAS that have been used in ransomware attacks, and this same percentage have known exploited vulnerabilities in at least one of their building automation systems. Additionally, 91 percent of BAS communicate over insecure protocols - opening up an even bigger attack surface for cyber-miscreants wanting to cause physical harm. “The primary thing that we see with any attack on building management systems or physical systems: It’s a great place for the threat actor to hide,” Michael Freeman, ServiceNow’s senior director of threat research, told The Register. “It's easier for them to compromise, and it's easier for them to hide in.” BAS and operational technology (OT) in general have fewer security controls than IT systems. Most require continual uptime, which makes them harder to patch or even scan for vulnerabilities and misconfigurations as this may lead to outages. “One case in particular, against a very large financial institution, the threat actors were staying low and quiet by attacking their BMS systems, and then pivoting into the IT environment,” Freeman said. The intruders were routinely caught - and booted from - the financial institution’s IT systems, so they built backdoors into the BMS to ensure persistent access to both OT and IT networks. “We're also seeing threat actors using AI to understand more building automation systems, especially ones that are using obscure OSs like VxWorks, older Unix-type systems,” Freeman said. AI has entered the chat As multiple security experts have told us in previous interviews, security through obscurity is dead. Not only does AI make it easier for attackers to find bugs – some very obscure and decades old - but it also means criminals no longer need to be OT experts to carry out destructive cyberattacks on critical networks and facilities. Instead, they can use AI to learn all about the obscure protocols and proprietary hardware and software that historically made industrial control systems black boxes. “It’s easier to understand what the controls are,” Freeman said, using the example of an attacker trying to take down a plane, or some similar catastrophic cyberattack. Historically, even advanced, government-backed hacking squads would “be quiet, because you don't know what changing certain settings is going to do,” Freeman explained. “Now you can use AI to say, ‘If I compromise a weight and balance system for airlines, all I need to do now is move this number here to this number, and I just told the system to load heavy stuff on the right side of the plane instead of equal distribution.'” Freeman told us he has seen attackers break into airlines’ OT gear in the past. “But they didn’t know what they were getting into, and so they left them alone,” he said. “Those do cause me concern because in the past I've helped to kick people out of those types of systems.” Industrial orgs increasingly under attack OT security provider Dragos tracks ransomware groups’ claims against industrial organizations on the criminals’ leak sites, along with publicly disclosed intrusions affecting manufacturing and other critical sectors. To be clear: claims on leak sites aren’t always accurate or even true, and the claim itself doesn’t mean operations or control systems were hit. Since 2022, however, “the numbers have been consistently increasing,” Lexie Mooney, senior threat analyst at Dragos, told The Register. The cybersecurity firm tracked 995 ransomware attacks against industrial orgs in 2023, a 49.5 percent increase from 2022. That number jumped more than 87 percent in 2024. Active ransomware groups targeting industrial orgs also grew in 2024 to 80 groups, up from 50 the year before. Dragos tracked 119 ransomware groups impacting more than 3,300 industrial organizations in 2025, and the incidents have steadily increased every quarter this year: 1,020 incidents in the first quarter of 2026 and 1,140 incidents in Q2. “The vast majority of cases are opportunistic,” Abdul Alamri, a senior threat analyst at Dragos, told us. “In some of the cases that we have seen an operational impact, either physical systems or an OT operation, it’s just the nature of the opportunism on the part of those ransomware groups.” This is partially due to the complexity of OT systems, he added. “Ransomware groups want to disrupt operations, and put pressure on the victims to pay the ransom,” Alamri said. “They don’t want to invest that time and effort to target complex systems." It’s usually quicker and easier for financially motivated crims to affect operations via IT systems - as the extortionists did in the August 2025 Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) breach, which halted manufacturing and crippled business operations for months. Internet-connected OT: the next 'low-hanging fruit' The other side of this complexity, however, is that many organizations themselves still lack visibility into their OT environments. Dragos estimates that fewer than 10 percent of OT networks worldwide currently have sufficient network monitoring in place. Plus, in 30 percent of incidents the security firm responded to in 2025, the investigations did not begin with a detection alert, but with someone noticing that “something seemed wrong” in operations. This lack of visibility, combined with threats from AI, worries Alamri. “If you compare the risk that we have seen from humans, to what we are about to face in the near future with AI agents who might continuously try to break into those systems - it’s a pretty dark future if we don't take the right measures to protect ourselves against it.” As organizations get better at patching and securing IT systems, attackers will likely look to internet-connected OT systems where digital compromises have real-world consequences, according to Matt Hayden, VP of cyber and emerging threats at General Dynamics Information Technology. “We all anticipate that as we get better at reducing the IT low-hanging fruit, OT will become a vector of much more scrutiny and much more attention,” Hayden told The Register. Before joining GDIT, Hayden served as the assistant secretary for cyber, infrastructure, risk and resilience policy at the US Department of Homeland Security. Compliance vs. security “There is a big focus on the hardware being connected for the purpose of compliance - and to make sure that, in the name of compliance, we aren't opening back doors, to devices that traditionally wouldn't have to be connected to facilitate their service,” he said, using refrigeration units as an example of one such system that is now internet-connected for compliance purposes. This was prior to the French supermarket hacks. Refrigeration units’ monitoring systems connect to the internet so their owners and operators can prove to regulators that the units maintain their uptime and temperature in accordance with regulations. “So if the health department comes by, they say, ‘Look, my refrigerator was at 27 degrees for the last 72 days,' and they have a check mark, and they get their A plus. But that simple connectivity is also a vector in which that particular refrigerant unit could be targeted for disruption,” Hayden said. About a week after our interview, criminals did exactly that. “The recently reported exploitations of commercial refrigeration units represent a significant example of devices without digital value, no sensitive data or extended enterprise access, being exploited by being connected to the internet with unpatched firmware,” Hayden told us in a subsequent email. He said he expects the attribution to be “less nation-state, and more likely those looking for targets of opportunity to identify what could be done with the unpatched systems.” “The consequences are food supply degradation at a small scale, but it is an important example of what could happen at scale very quickly with more consequential operating equipment,” Hayden said.®
a73522a3fefcaa29: Close to 1 billion meetings take place each day around the world. CEOs spend nearly three-quarters of their workdays in meetings. Planning for and spearheading meetings eats up the lion’s share of managers’ time. In much of the industrialized world, meetings are both the metronomes and menaces of people’s working lives.

Given the enormous time spent in workplace meetings, do we know what they accomplish or how to make them as worthwhile as possible? For decades, the answer was… not really. Meetings weren’t a particularly accessible subject of study. But that has changed. Once a tiny niche area, “meeting science” is a growing specialization among organizational and social psychologists. The field is accelerating as archived virtual meetings provide vast swaths of data. And it is providing a fascinating window into human behavior.

Meeting to talk helps fulfill basic human needs to connect, communicate, and cooperate. People have long come together—in caves, fields, market squares, and town halls—to get something done, share ideas, get on the same page, or just to remark on the weather. But meeting scientists define their subject as gatherings of people “with some goal or structure to the event,” says organizational psychologist Liana Kreamer of the Florida Institute of Technology, who coauthored a review of over three decades of meeting science in the 2026 Annual Review of Organizational Psychology and Organizational Behavior.

d9ad1ab514e787dd: From P Kamalanathan
Last week, a young student at AIMST University asked me: “Datuk, did Rajinikanth go to university?”
I smiled.
Rajini studied in a Kannada-medium school and worked as a coolie, carpenter and bus conductor in Bangalore.
He joined a film institute at 25, an age when we tell our youth, “You are late.”
Last week, Jailer 2 was breaking box-office records again. At 74, he is still a superstar.
We celebrate his punchlines, but we ignore his lessons on education.
As a former deputy minister of education who oversaw five million students, I see five lessons from Rajini that our new National Education Plan 2026-2035 is trying to teach.
First: Learning agility beats certificates
Rajini had no degree. But he had what the ministry now calls “learning agility”. From stage plays to learning Hindi for Andha Kanoon to learning motion capture for Enthiran, he never stopped.
In Switzerland this year, I saw Swiss CEOs with no MBAs but 10 micro-credentials in AI. That is the Rajini model: lifelong TVET.
Second: Discipline is education
Director SP Muthuraman once said that Rajini was the first to arrive and the last to leave. In 50 years, there has been no “Rajini late” headline.
We chase tuition, but our students fail because they cannot wake up at 6am. Discipline, like that of the Bangalore bus conductor punching tickets at 5am, is the first certificate.
Third: Humility is Karamah Insaniah
The National Education Plan speaks of Karamah Insaniah, or the recognition and uplifting of human dignity. Look at Rajini.
He is a superstar, yet he sits on the floor, touches elders' feet and says, “I am a small child of K Balachander.”
In an age of TikTok arrogance, he teaches adab. My mother always taught me that education without humility is noise.
Fourth: Reinvention in the AI age

Rajini, at 74, is learning AI filmmaking for Jailer 2. If a 74-year-old can act with de-ageing technology, our youth can earn Google AI certification, which the United Nations Institute for Training and Research (UNITAR) offers free in Selangor.
Fifth: Do well, do good

Rajini famously said, “Money comes, goes. Give.” He built schools quietly. This is what I tell my colleagues at the Public Relations Practitioners Society of Malaysia: sustainability is a competitive advantage. Rajini has sustained a 50-year career because people trust his goodness.
That student asked if Rajini passed his exams. I told him: He did not pass with straight As, but he passed the hardest exam: life.
This Deepavali, when we watch Rajini on screen, let us tell our children:
Don’t copy his style; copy his discipline.
Don’t just whistle for the superstar; learn to be a superstar in your own trade, whether as a welder, coder or teacher.
Because, as Rajini said in Padayappa: “En vazhi, thani vazhi”, or “My way is my own way”.
Let our education system allow every Malaysian child to find their own way.
P Kamalanathan is an MIC central working committee member and a former deputy education minister.

7f491fb78fd52845: Amazon wants to ensure you have a personal AI that you can carry with you anywhere, listening in on your conversations so it can remind you of key details – and give you personalized shopping recommendations, of course. The global online bazaar has unveiled two new AI-based products from Bee, a startup in wearable devices that it acquired last year in a deal said to be worth $300 million. Bee’s original product for Amazon was tried out and sort of given approval by friend of The Register Corey Quinn, Chief Cloud Economist at Duckbill, earlier this year. One new gizmo, Bee Frontier, is designed to be worn like a watch or one of those fitness trackers, although to our mind it looks more like you are wearing a doorbell. The other, Bee Eclipse, is a slimline and lightweight device about the size of a credit card that attaches to the back of your phone magnetically, like a limpet. Both are intended to listen in to your conversations and help you remember important details, like when you are meeting your friend for a pint later and at which hospitality outlet. The devices take note of the details you might otherwise forget, and then turn them into useful conversation summaries, to-dos and reminders, Amazon says. The pair of devices feature a single button to turn on or off, and a visible indicator that lights up when one is listening in and its AI is summarizing the conversation. When enabled, the eavesdropper gathers context from your conversations to provide insights and recommendations. Summaries of your conversations can be accessed via a Bee mobile app on iPhone or Android (linked via Bluetooth), or an all-new desktop app. These can be organized using templates for things such as lectures, or users can just review memories from the past few days to see what you discussed. The Bee devices pick up on trends or themes that recur, and recommend personalized goals and actions. That sounds alarm bells for us, as it suggests the AI is designed to get to know you, and what you like. Along with the new hardware, Bee has now gained the ability to connect to Amazon’s Alexa+ AI assistant and Amazon.com, which means that you can ask Alexa for a meeting summary - or get personalized shopping recommendations from Amazon based on what your personal earwig has gleaned. However, Amazon says that the latest Bee products respect user privacy, as audio is processed into insights in real time and not stored, while transcripts are encrypted and only the user can access them. Bee Frontier is claimed to have IP67 water resistance, up to seven days of battery life, and has a USB-C charging port. Bee Eclipse also has a USB-C port but is said to last for more than 21 days of use from a single battery charge. Both devices come in a choice of colors, with Bee Frontier available now for $74.99 and Bee Eclipse due to be available shortly for $99.99. ®
768c5b134c4c2d56: The UK Space Agency needs a name for its Active Debris Removal Mission and has decided that the great British public are the people for the job. The agency confirmed the operation earlier this week and selected ClearSpace UK to lead it. The plan is to remove two UK-registered satellites from Low Earth Orbit, with the clean-up due to begin in 2029. The UK government is backing the effort with more than £60 million, and it expects the disposal to be completed by 2032. The spacecraft will grab each satellite, drop it into a lower orbit for disposal by burning up in the Earth's atmosphe, then climb to a higher one to await its next job. Less suicide dive, more cosmic bin round. And because it’s refuellable, the UK government says it "can help make a difference and sweep space for years to come." Launch is planned from SaxaVord Spaceport in Scotland. But first, the quest needs a name. The Active Debris Removal Mission hardly trips off the tongue, and the UK Space Agency gave inspirational examples of other project names, such as NASA's Mercury program (named after the Roman god) or Tim Peake's Principia mission (inspired by Sir Isaac Newton's Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica). Oddly, the agency didn't mention the poll to brand a scientific research ship, which was eventually named Sir David Attenborough rather than Boaty McBoatface, the most popular suggestion. The tag must consist of two words – so no "Itsy bitsy teeny weeny orbit debris clear machiney" – and 150 words to explain the name and how it reflects the theme. So no backronyms, for example Broom (British Robotic Orbital Object Manipulator). Starry McBinface? Obviously, swear words are not allowed, nor is anything deemed "potentially offensive" or political. Using anything that might attract copyright or intellectual property lawyers is also out. Letting the public suggest a name feels potentially riskier than the mission itself, though it should generate some engagement. It's a high-risk, high-reward campaign; there are plenty of dead satellites cluttering orbit, and the ability to remove them is becoming increasingly important. Rob Atchison, Managing Director of ClearSpace UK, said, "Our next step is to design, build and test a spacecraft that can get close, safely, to an object never designed to be caught, and take control of it." If you're getting a sense of déjà vu about this expedition, you're probably right. The European Space Agency (ESA) announced ClearSpace-1 in 2019, which the agency called "the first space mission to remove an item of debris from orbit" with a launch set for 2025. At the time, ClearSpace founder and CEO Luc Piguet said: "This is the right time for such a mission." In latest announcement, Piguet called the UKSA's selection "an important milestone." This is far from the first mission to grapple an object in orbit. Most recently, Katalyst Space sent its LINK spacecraft to rescue NASA's Swift observatory. That was intended to capture the Swift spacecraft and raise its altitude, but failures with LINK doomed it. Perhaps things might have gone better if the public had been given an opportunity to name the spacecraft? ®

814a9ce3b76d1166: Apabila sesebuah kerajaan Malaysia memasuki tahun ketiga pemerintahan dan membentangkan belanjawan untuk tahun berikutnya, ada satu soalan yang lazim ditanya, apatah lagi jika belanjawan menawarkan pelbagai inisiatif yang dilihat baik untuk rakyat. Yang bertanya termasuklah ahli politik terutamanya pembangkang, penganalisis dan ahli akademik, media, dan orang ramai.
Pertanyaannya ialah, adakah belanjawan yang dibentang satu belanjawan pilihan raya? Mengapa ditanya sedemikian ialah kerana banyak goodies yang diberi menerusi belanjawan itu.

Most of the time yang diluah bukan pertanyaan. Sebaliknya, ia satu syak oleh orang yang bertanya. Si penanya sudah membuat kesimpulan sendiri sebelum bertanya, hence giving a statement under the guise of a question. Lalu orang yang bertanya mensyaki goodies bertujuan untuk mengambil hati rakyat supaya mengundi parti memerintah yakni pihak yang membentangkan belanjawan apabila pilihan raya diadakan kelak.
Adakala apa yang disyaki memang benar. Adakala tidak. Boleh dikata semua kerajaan pernah menghadapi persoalan seumpama itu.

Tempoh hari Anwar Ibrahim membentangkan belanjawan untuk 2027. Like PMX or not kena akui it is a good budget. Banyak memberi manfaat kepada pelbagai lapisan rakyat sekali gus menimbulkan 'syak' this is an election budget. Sebenarnya sebelum Anwar bentang belanjawan pun, ada pihak sudah kata apa yang akan dibentang ialah belanjawan pilihan raya meskipun mandat kerajaan akan hanya tamat pada Februari 2028.

Semasa belanjawan dibahaskan di Parlimen, ada yang timbulkan soal election budget. Ketua Pembangkang Hamzah Zainudin mendakwa belanjawan kali ini sarat dengan pengumuman berbentuk apa yang beliau sifatkan 'gula-gula'. Kata beliau, "banyak manis-manis mungkin pilihan raya tahun depan".

Berkata begitu boleh dilihat Hamzah menjangkakan rakyat akan termakan 'gula-gula'. Mungkin Hamzah bimbang 'gula-gula' akan memberikan kesan negatif ke atas pembangkang apatah lagi apabila ada pemimpin kanan PAS menyambut baik belanjawan itu. Lalu Hamzah mendakwa bantuan atau 'gula-gula' bukan faktor penentu undi.

Kata-kata itu meskipun boleh dilihat sebagai perli dan menyerang kerajaan, mungkin juga disuarakan untuk menenangkan pembangkang, jika mereka sudah cemas. Juga menaikkan semangat untuk melawan. Pendapat saya mudah: Tak kisahlah bajet pilihan raya atau bukan, janji rakyat dapat manfaat.

Lantas saya setuju dengan pandangan kawan lama saya, Kassim Muhamad, bahawa gagasan ekonomi tidak semestinya kedengaran berdegum-degum. Belanjawan yang manusiawi juga gagasan ekonomi kerana ia melibatkan orang biasa.

"Bagi sesetengah orang gagasan ekonomi mestilah kedengaran gah dan besar biar berdegum. Bagi orang biasa seperti saya, nasib orang biasa yang bergelut mencari sesuap nasi, segala bentuk bantuan itu sangat bermakna," kata si kawan lama.

Kassim memberi contoh: Bantuan kepada pesara RM750. "Ini bukanlah bentuk gagasan berdegum. Orang boleh saja melabelnya gula-gula. Seperti juga hasrat supaya warung di bandar kita diberi perhatian juga tidak gah tetapi jelas aspek sifat manusiawinya."
Bagi beliau ini bukan belanjawan pilihan raya. Ia bajet yang punya sifat manusiawi. Ini elemen penting walau apa pun bajet itu digelar.

e3450c0821b6e75b: Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim likes to quote renowned thinkers in his speeches. Critics have said he likes to parade his erudition, which they argue is pointless because he fails to follow through with implementation.

In his budget speech the other day, he cited Isaiah Berlin, the Latvia-born and English-naturalised philosopher, famed for inventing the “hedgehog and the fox” metaphor in a celebrated essay on Leo Tolstoy’s meditation on history.

Berlin divided history’s seminal thinkers into hedgehogs and foxes: hedgehogs being those who relate everything to a central vision (Marx, Nietzsche); while foxes (Shakespeare, Montaigne, Sophocles) pursue multiform, even contradictory, insights to their finale.
He held that Tolstoy was a fox, a brilliant discerner of particularities, who towards the end of his life flirted with disaster by trying to be a hedgehog.

The metaphor sheds light on the concerns raised by Puncak Borneo MP Willie Mongin about schoolchildren refusing to sit next to classmates because they eat prohibited foods or wear religious symbols of other faiths.
Willie did not say from where the aversion stemmed but few would have difficulty in knowing the motivation.

Interestingly, the problem of polarisation among school pupils can be helped by understanding Berlin’s musings. He said that human beings have to be both hedgehogs and foxes; we maim our sensibility if we choose the exclusivity of the one and dissolve into nihilism if, fox-like, we opt for contradictions that lead nowhere.
Willie has highlighted a problem during the tenure of a prime minister who, in his youth, championed a cause that has contributed to the dilemma facing our education system.
Fortunately, the same leader has access to the ideas needed to free those trapped by a form of exclusivity that harms. He is aware of the way out. Would that he opted for it.
Our children should be open to being both hedgehog and fox.
Terence Netto is a senior journalist and an FMT reader.

4d556263d22f1c96: The prime minister’s announcement that the government will phase out the contract system for medical officers and offer permanent posts to more than 9,000 contract doctors in 2027 has injected some hope into the healthcare workforce.
Budget 2027 also raised the post-basic incentive for nurses and paramedics from RM100 to RM200 a month, and the Air Health Service incentive from RM30 to RM100.
These moves recognise that a health service cannot run on buildings and equipment alone. It depends on people who are trained, supported and willing to stay.

These are significant commitments. However, success will ultimately depend on whether the government can recruit these healthcare workers, relocate them and provide the support they need to remain where their services are most needed.
Recent figures show why the situation remains troubling.
In the latest round of medical officer postings, only 673 of the 1,055 medical officers offered placements in Sabah and Sarawak had reported for duty.
Those who did not report cited relocation costs, personal and family circumstances, health concerns and limited opportunities for specialist training.

In all fairness, the health ministry has made significant strides over the past few weeks in addressing these concerns and taking immediate steps to retain healthcare workers, particularly young medical officers.

For doctors moving to East Malaysia, the government had already agreed in February to allow eligible contract doctors offered permanent appointments in 2025 to claim transfer and relocation costs, with claims of up to 100% for inter-regional moves.
Earlier this month, the ministry also confirmed approval for claims by specified cohorts.
This represents significant progress, but it is important to clarify that this is not a newly introduced allowance.
On social media, officers continue to express frustration over the lack of clarity and transparency in the application and payment processes.

Clear rules on eligible expenses, advances, documentation and payment timelines are needed. Most importantly, these rules must be communicated to relocating officers in a timely manner so they can access the support before relocation costs become a barrier.
Additionally, on Oct 8, the health minister said that eligible medical officers returning to their home regions could receive a disturbance allowance equivalent to one month’s basic salary.

Later that week, the minister also announced that the ministry was studying a proposal to allocate a dedicated 30% share of Federal Training Award places to medical officers serving in Sabah and Sarawak. Both measures could make postings more attractive, but the proposed training quota remains under study and has yet to be implemented.
For those who are unclear about the issue, it may be helpful to explain the allowances available to officers.

Bayaran Imbuhan Wilayah (BIW) supports eligible officers serving outside their home regions. Bayaran Imbuhan Sara Hidup (BISH) is a cost-of-living allowance linked to locality, while Bayaran Insentif Mengikut Lokasi dan Tahap Kesusahan (BIMLTK) applies to designated facilities in remote or difficult areas, with rates determined by hardship level.
Under the current rules, BIMLTK is tiered, while BIW has fixed rates for newly eligible officers and protections for existing recipients.

One concern raised relates to BIW. Previously, the allowance was calculated as a percentage of salary. Following the change to a fixed-rate structure, some officers have seen their actual payments fall significantly.

BISH is determined by locality and officers’ grades, which may not accurately reflect actual living costs. Meanwhile, BIMLTK eligibility is tied to designated facilities rather than rural status alone.

The overarching concern is the lack of clarity over why an individual qualifies for, or is excluded from, a particular allowance. With different rules and arrangements being implemented, officers have little transparent information on how their entitlements are determined.

Therefore, the government should publish the relevant claim rules, required documents, processing deadlines and payment dates within the next fortnight, and allow advances to be paid before relocation.

Within the next three to six months, the government should establish a centralised digital service linked to ePlacement, allowing officers to check their entitlements, apply directly, upload documents once and track the progress of their cases.
It should also review the fixed BIW rate and assess remote sites across Sabah, Sarawak and qualifying parts of Perak, Kelantan, Terengganu, Pahang and Johor against consistent criteria.

In the longer term, the government should work with state governments to prioritise the repair and maintenance of health service residential quarters in rural and remote areas, while developing clear rural career pathways for doctors, nurses and other healthcare workers.

A coordinated, phased approach to these measures should help address the barriers preventing younger officers from taking up their postings. The issue should not be reduced to a question of willingness to serve, nor should it be attributed to a lack of interest or patriotism.
Over the past fortnight, the government has made several welcome commitments to the healthcare workforce, further reinforced by the 2027 Budget.
The next test is delivery: clear entitlements, timely relocation support, fair regional allowances and credible career pathways.
A posting letter can fill a vacancy only when the terms make the move possible — and give people a reason to stay.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
d25a41d84637b5f6: The recent announcement that Budget 2027 will provide funding for public transport is a good step forward. Hopefully, more funding will go beyond the Klang Valley, with Johor Bahru and other state capitals receiving their allocations by June next year.

Between now and June, there is still time to undertake a proper demand assessment, a fundamental component of transport planning. Without a proper understanding of travel patterns, passenger volumes, origins and destinations, even expensive infrastructure projects can fail to deliver their intended benefits.

Unfortunately, transport planning in Malaysia has so far been biased towards road transport, driven mainly by federal government decisions and funding, and often mired in political considerations rather than based on a comprehensive assessment of actual needs and demand.
The Johor Bahru-Singapore corridor is a classic example. For decades, demand for travel between the two cities has exceeded the capacity of the transport infrastructure and services available.

Hundreds of thousands of people cross the border daily for work, business, education and other activities. The pressure on the Causeway is known and well documented. Sketchy improvements in the form of costly new technology — such as QR codes for documentation processing — have not eased daily congestion, especially when systems break down as they often do.

Despite this longstanding demand, the question remains: have we made the best use of our existing infrastructure, especially the rail facilities, before committing ourselves to more expensive solutions?
The Tebrau shuttle service: a missed opportunity?

Keretapi Tanah Melayu Berhad’s (KTMB) rail lines across the causeway may be old tech by today's standard, but the Tebrau shuttle service between Johor Bahru and Woodlands has demonstrated the value of rail travel across the border. The actual train journey takes only five minutes, making it considerably faster than travelling by road during peak periods.
However, the service has historically been constrained by limited seating capacity and ticket availability, and the difficulty of accommodating the large number of commuters who wish to use it.
Between 5am and 7.30am, a train departs every 30 minutes. After 7.30am, passengers may face waits of up to 1½ hours for the next departure.

This raises an important question. If demand for cross-border travel is so substantial, why has the existing railway service not been upgraded more aggressively to accommodate the high passenger volume?

Why are the intervals between trains so long, resulting in lengthy waits? Why must every passenger buying a ticket be assigned a seat when the journey takes only five minutes each way, when some may be willing to stand?
The answer cannot simply be that its replacement — a new, modern and technologically more advanced railway system — is already under construction.

What if we first examined the operational and regulatory constraints, existing railway capacity, options for increasing service frequency, border immigration arrangements and the feasibility of expanding operations?
Railway infrastructure is expensive to build. Where tracks and stations already exist, improving the utilisation of those assets should be an obvious starting point, and could cost much less.
The RTS Link: necessary, but an incomplete solution

It has been said that the Johor Bahru-Singapore Rapid Transit System (RTS) Link will transform cross-border commuting. With a journey time of about six minutes between Bukit Chagar and Woodlands North and planned intervals of around 10 minutes or less, the RTS Link will offer commuters an alternative to road travel across the Causeway.

Its importance should not be underestimated. However, the RTS should not be regarded as a stand-alone or final solution to Johor Bahru's transport problems. Its success will depend heavily on how passengers travel to and from Bukit Chagar station.

If commuters must depend on buses, private cars, taxis or ride-hailing services to reach the station, congestion could simply shift from the Causeway to the roads surrounding Bukit Chagar. The station's passenger-handling capacity, pedestrian access, bus connectivity, drop-off facilities and integration with other public transport services will need to be planned and integrated seamlessly.

More importantly, it has to be recognised that the RTS primarily serves a specific cross-border corridor link. It does not automatically solve the wider mobility problems faced by residents travelling between different parts of Johor Bahru, Permas Jaya, Iskandar Puteri and the surrounding Johor Bahru conurbations.
We must therefore distinguish between a project that improves a cross-border link and a transport system that improves mobility throughout the city. They are not the same thing.
How does KTMB fit into the bigger picture?

KTMB has more than one line in Johor Bahru. Apart from the new double-track intercity line linking central Johor Bahru with Gemas and Kuala Lumpur, there is also a branch line from Kempas Baru, north of Johor Bahru, to Pasir Gudang in the east.

Another branch line just south of Senai forms a triangular route with the main line, connecting Senai to Iskandar Puteri and Tanjung Pelepas in western Johor. It is also possible for a train from Tanjung Pelepas to travel to Senai, Sedenak, Kluang, Gemas and all the way to Kuala Lumpur.
Using the same line, a train can also provide services from Tanjung Pelepas directly to Senai, using the Kempas Baru junction to get to Pasir Gudang or go directly south to Johor Bahru and Woodlands.

Unfortunately, such services (or a configuration of my imagined passenger services) are currently not available, even though the tracks there are all in good order and condition, and obviously underutilised, reportedly because there are no suitable coaches and locomotives to run such services.

This is one of my concerns: has sufficient attention been given to the future role of KTMB’s existing railway infrastructure network. i.e. whether it can be turned into an effective passenger commuter service? Reports suggest that funding has instead been directed toward an elevated autonomous rapid transit system.

The Tebrau shuttle service should not be abandoned once the RTS Link is up and running. Instead, it should be combined into the wider KTMB network mentioned above to serve different travel demands and purposes.

Like the RTS Link, public transport in Johor Bahru should not be planned piecemeal or in isolation from other services. Integrated planning and demand management must be comprehensive, free from political influence, and considered within the broader framework of transport planning for greater Johor Bahru.
There is an opportunity to extend the Tebrau shuttle service to Senai town and eventually to Senai International Airport. From there, the service could branch towards Pasir Gudang via Kempas Baru.

While the RTS will provide a higher‑capacity link to Woodlands North, the KTMB network could serve as a feeder line, collecting passengers along existing routes that are not easily reached by other transport modes.
There is nothing wrong with providing two rail network options into Woodlands from more than one location in Johor Bahru.

The challenge is determining how these services can complement one another rather than leave gaps in growing transport demand. Johor Bahru’s public transport network should follow future demand, not politics.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
e90bf8500398a4f9: Open-weight models more than quadrupled their share of spending through Vercel's AI Gateway between June and September, when they processed more than seven in 10 tokens. "In August, open-weight models processed the majority of AI Gateway token volume for the first time," the biz said. "The money is now following. Open weight's share of spend has more than quadrupled over the last three months, from one in twenty gateway dollars in June to nearly one in four in September." AI Gateway, like OpenRouter, acts as an intermediary that allows customers to purchase tokens from different AI providers through a common interface. While it works with popular harnesses like Claude Code and Codex and provides access to proprietary and open-weight models, it doesn't see usage through other gateways or from customers who access AI models directly from vendors or through on-premises hosting. While gateway spending in September was about 13x higher than recorded in December 2025, the average price per token was about 47 percent lower, according to Vercel. At the same time, almost one in three teams changed their most-used AI provider in September, suggesting that market competition may be limiting vendor lock-in. The most popular model in September was TypeSafe AI's Jev. In just 14 days, it reached 35 percent of paid teams using Vercel's AI Gateway, the company said. Its popularity didn't generate much spending due to the model's architecture – usage accounted for only 1 percent of the month’s tokens and 0.15 percent of spending. US-based models from Anthropic and OpenAI still attract the largest portion of spending in September, with 11.03 percent going to Claude Opus 5.5, followed by GPT-6 Astra at 4.86 percent. But models from Chinese AI providers have become more popular. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash ranked third in spending, at 4.19 percent. More than two-thirds of the September spending on Chinese models went to US providers serving those models, up from less than a tenth in December 2025, Vercel said. Moonshot AI, maker of Kimi, captured 3.6 percent of gateway tokens and 13.2 percent of spend in September; DeepSeek took 58 percent of tokens for just 6.6 percent of spend; and Z.ai, maker of GLM-5.3, took 7.2 percent of tokens and 4.5 percent of spend. So efforts to ban or limit open-weight models, something considered by the current US administration, would affect American businesses serving those models and their customers. Even if the US continues to dither on AI policy, trade barriers affecting AI models may alter market dynamics. China on Friday proposed adding 40 technology items to its export control list, 23 of them related to AI. The Associated Press notes that Moonshot’s Kimi K3 and Alibaba’s Qwen 3.8-Max are among the models that meet the parameter threshold set by Chinese authorities, though the official message did not identify affected models. "This introduces significant uncertainty for US businesses that host or rely on Chinese models," Chris McGuire, a senior fellow for China and emerging technologies at the Council on Foreign Relations, said in a social media post. "Particularly given that Chinese AI labs are moving toward licensing the use of open-source models to generate revenue, the Chinese government stating that it has the ability to curtail those licensing agreements at any time should make US businesses more hesitant to rely on those models going forward." McGuire said the US needs to adopt a comprehensive regulatory framework governing the use of US AI technology overseas and include Chinese AI models used or hosted in the United States in its domestic AI regulations.®
